Elsewhere in New South Wales a woman was found decapitated in her home and an elderly woman had been allegedly stabbed to death in Bondi by a relative.

News.title: Ofsted graded inspections must be halted amid 'risk to life', union demands
News.content:
Ofsted graded inspections must be halted amid 'risk to life', union demands

Paul Whiteman, NAHT's general secretary, said: 'The clear theme emerging across all the feedback we have received is that this Ofsted framework is even more stressful than the one that preceded it'

View Image A new inspection system was intended to address fears over wellbeing following the tragic death of 53-year-old primary school headteacher Ruth Perry in 2023 (Image: PA)

Ofsted's graded inspections must be halted, a major union has demanded amid warnings of "a risk to life".

The call for action from the biggest school leaders' union - NAHT - comes almost 12 months on since the introduction of a revised inspection system.

England's school watchdog replaced the old regime - an overall single-word grade ranging from 'outstanding' to 'inadequate' - with a new 5-point grading scale last year.

It was intended to address fears over wellbeing following the tragic death of 53-year-old primary school headteacher Ruth Perry in 2023.

She had been told her school - Caversham primary school in Reading, Berkshire - was being downgraded from "outstanding" to "inadequate", the lowest possible rating.

A coroner at the time had said an Ofsted inspection "likely contributed" to her mental health deterioration and death.

NAHT said it had raised concerns at the start of a new framework that replacing an overall single-word grade would not ease the intolerable pressure on leaders.

The union said a survey of more than 5,000 of its members - conducted in June - found nearly three quarters (72%) felt the direction of travel on inspection had worsened.

It has led NAHT to call for the government to halt the inspection system - and conduct a review.

Paul Whiteman, NAHT's general secretary, said: "The clear theme emerging across all the feedback we have received is that this Ofsted framework is even more stressful than the one that preceded it.

"It poses a real and present danger to the well-being and mental health of school leaders and teachers, possibly even a risk to life."

"We warmly welcome the new Education Secretary's recent words stating how seriously she takes leader wellbeing and her determination to get not just the Ofsted framework, but the whole culture of accountability, right."

He added: "Really fundamental changes to inspection are needed, and we stand ready to work with the new government to achieve that.

"In the meantime, there remains a risk to the safety of school leaders, which is why we are calling for graded inspections to be halted."

An Ofsted spokeswoman said: “Ofsted exists to raise standards for children and to provide clear reporting to parents.

“Over the last three years, we have worked closely with teaching unions to deliver significant reforms to how Ofsted inspections work, to reduce unnecessary pressure on teachers. And we involved parents to make sure our new-look inspection reports worked for them – presenting clear, colour-coded grades and detailed information about the school.

“We will continue to engage closely with trades unions – but we will also continue to grade schools.”

Speaking earlier this month, the new Education Secretary Lucy Powell committed to working with headteachers and others to "make sure that we get this Ofsted framework, but also the culture, the whole regime, right".

She told LBC in early September: "There's nothing that is more concerning to me as Education Secretary than the idea that our accountability regime in this country would lead to a headteacher to taking their own life.

"It's just absolutely awful and that is not at all what we should be about, the kind of culture and atmosphere that that is created here.

She added: "So, I take incredibly seriously teacher, headteacher wellbeing and yes, of course we need an accountability structure and regime to continue school improvement.

"But I want to see one that that is much more kind of supportive and understanding of the great jobs that the majority, in fact, you know, almost all headteachers are doing around the country and support them with that."

News.title: NHS issues first-ever urgent organ donation alert with 9 people dying every week
News.content:
NHS issues first-ever urgent organ donation alert with 9 people dying every week

The NHS has launched an urgent organ donation response plan to get a million more Brits to sign up, as transplant waiting lists hit a record high

View 7 Images NHS launches unprecedented response to donation crisis (Image: Getty Images)

The NHS is launching its first ever urgent organ donation response plan after a fall in donations.

‌



A record transplant waiting list means nine people a week are currently dying because no suitable organ is available. NHS Blood and Transplant (NHSBT) says donor numbers are 9% below this time last year, and is launching an urgent appeal for people to sign the organ donation register.

‌



Some 8,700 patients are now on the waiting list desperately waiting for a transplant because fewer grieving families have been consenting to donate their loved ones’ organs since the COVID-19 pandemic. Family consent rates are down almost a fifth in the last five years, having dropped from 68% down to 59%.

‌



View 7 Images Mirror campaigner Max Johnson is alive thanks to a decision by the family of Keira Ball

NHS transplant landmark sees turbo charged lungs ‘breathe’ outside of body READ MORE :

Health chiefs say there has also been a shift in the circumstances in which people are dying, meaning there are fewer opportunities for organ donation. NHSBT is making an urgent appeal for one million Brits who have never registered before, to confirm their wishes on the NHS Organ Donor Register this year. Each donor can potentially save up to nine lives.

Anthony Clarkson, director at NHS Blood and Transplant, said: “We are facing one of the most challenging periods for organ donation in over a decade. The sharp decline in donors and the rising number of people waiting for a transplant need urgent action.

‌



“We have already adapted significantly to changes in the donation environment. But, saving lives and reducing the waiting list needs collective effort across the NHS and society.”

View 7 Images Miriam died from a sudden unexplained cardiac arrest

Miriam’s Gift of Life

Miriam Lee died when she was 17 from sudden cardiac arrest.

‌



The teen from Northamptonshire had signed the NHS Organ Donation Register so parents Nicola and David knew her wishes and consented to her donating. Miriam’s liver went to Ollie Jolliff, from Dorset, who needed a transplant at 11-months-old in 2016 due to a genetic condition.

Nicola said her daughter's death was "completely out of the blue". She said: “Miriam had registered on the Organ Donor Register when she was registering to give blood and as a part of the process, she had also told us her wishes. So, we knew we had to honour them. She wanted to offer everything she could and positively impact as many lives as possible.”

The transplant saved Ollie’s life but came after his elder brother Kieran had died from the same condition four years earlier.

‌



Their mother Hannah Jolliff said: "Sadly, a transplant wasn't an option for Kieran and he passed away at four years old, having spent most of his life in hospital. It was incredibly difficult and we miss him every single day.

"Ollie was on the list for 11 months, time which we spent in and out of hospital, unable to travel in case we got the call, and desperately hoping that Ollie would get the transplant he needed. We got the call to say that a match had been found for Ollie on the morning of what would have been Kieran's 10th birthday.

View 7 Images Hannah and Mike Jolliff with their son Ollie meeting Nicola and David Lee (Image: NHSBT/PA Wire)

‌



"It's 10 years this year since Ollie received his transplant and he's doing so well - he's going into his last year of primary school, he's got passions and interests and he's living his life like any other 10-year-old boy. We feel incredibly lucky."

Nicola said: "When we heard from Hannah and Mike and learned that Miriam's liver had gone to tiny Ollie, it was such an emotional moment. Meeting them was more emotional still and it has been a true honour to see Ollie grow up."

Mrs Jolliff added: "Ollie knows he's got a special liver, and he knows that Miriam is the special girl who gave it to him. We're so aware of how different things could have been had Miriam and her family not made the decision to donate. It was a difficult and completely selfless decision, and we are so grateful to them.”

‌



Only 1% of people in the UK die in circumstances where donation is possible and the pool of eligible donors has reduced by around 20% since the pandemic. The main causes of death for eligible deceased organ donors are severe brain injuries, strokes and a sudden lack of oxygen to the brain.

There has been a reduction in trauma-related deaths particularly among younger people in recent years. Road traffic collisions have reduced and there have been improvements in care for major trauma and major head injuries.

View 7 Images Whether or not you have registered your decision can be critical

‌



As the population ages those eligible people who do die from trauma-related injuries tend to be older - more likely to have other health conditions which prevent organ donation.

New figures released today show that over 700 potential donations did not go ahead in the period between April 2021 and March 2026, because families did not know for certain what their loved one would have wanted and so vetoed it.

Each deceased donor will donate three organs on average, which means there were 2,127 missed opportunities for transplant. NHSBT says that families support donation 90% of the time when they know their loved one’s decision but this falls to around 50% when no decision is listed on the organ donor register.

‌



In the past decade around 5,000 people have died waiting for a life-saving transplant.

View 7 Images Mirror poster boy Max Johnson has encouraged people to donate (Image: Daily Mirror)

The unprecedented NHS urgent response plan is getting hospitals together with clinics and healthcare partners to increase donation opportunities.

‌



The Mirror campaigned for Max and Keira’s law in the name of Keira Ball, who died, aged nine, in a car crash, then saved the life of Max Johnson, nine, who received her heart.

The law change which came into force in 2020 and was credited with helping keep organ donation going during the Covid crisis. It meant there would be a presumption in favour of donation but bereaved next of kin would always retain their right to veto transplants.

View 7 Images Max before lawmakers voted to Change the Law for Life (Image: Daily Mirror)

‌



‘Mirror readers helped change the law - now we need your help to save lives’

Rommel Ravanan - chief medical officer at NHS Blood and Transplant

"The Daily Mirror's Change the Law for Life campaign helped transform the conversation around organ donation in the UK. But today, despite that progress, we face a new and urgent challenge.

"Organ donation rates, family consent and patients who are eligible to be donors have all fallen significantly since the pandemic and we are yet to discover exactly why.

‌



"That's why we have responded to these challenges by implementing an urgent response plan to address what is becoming the most challenging period for donation in more than a decade.

"NHS teams across the country are working together to maximise every donation opportunity, but there is also a simple action Mirror readers can take that could save lives - make your organ donation decision known and join the NHS Organ Donor Register.

"Over the last five years, more than 700 potential donations did not go ahead because families were unsure what their loved one wanted. That uncertainty led to more than 2,100 missed transplant opportunities.

‌



"While the law around organ donation has changed, thanks in part to campaigns like the Mirror's, families still play a vital role in the process.

"Speaking with the family helps to understand the person’s wishes, support them and give them the opportunity to ask questions and understand what donation involves. Most importantly, families can provide clinicians with vital information about their loved one's health and lifestyle which may be critical to the suitability of organs for transplant.

"We know that when relatives are aware of a loved one's decision to be a donor, they support donation in 90% of cases. That is why NHS Blood and Transplant is calling on an extra one million people to confirm their decision for the first time on the NHS Organ Donor Register by the end of the year.

Article continues below

"It takes just two minutes. Recording your decision and sharing it with your family removes doubt at a difficult time and ensures your wishes are respected.

"Mirror readers helped change the law. Now we're asking them to help save more lives by making their decision known."

To find out more and to register an organ donation decision call 0300 123 23, visit organdonation.nhs.uk or use the NHS app.

News.title: Keeping Nigel Farage out of Downing Street is 'moral responsibility', Lib Dem leader says
News.content:
Keeping Nigel Farage out of Downing Street is 'moral responsibility', Lib Dem leader says

EXCLUSIVE: Sir Ed Davey raised concerns over the recent £72million donated to Reform by Crypto billionaires Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, and vowed his party would be a 'firewall'f against Reform

View 2 Images Ed Davey vowed to stop Nigel Farage becoming PM (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Keeping Nigel Farage out of Downing Street is a “moral responsibility”, and the “most serious” task of his political career, the Lib Dem leader has claimed.

‌



Sir Ed Davey raised concerns over the recent £72million donated to Reform by Crypto billionaires Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, and vowed his party would be a “firewall” against Reform.

‌



Earlier this year ministers brought in a £100,000 ceiling on the sum of money that can be donated to political parties by anyone living abroad, which would also be enforced for the first 12 months after British expats come back to the UK.

‌



Addressing the recent donations scandal, the Kingston and Surbiton MP said: “With this new money, it is deeply threatening.

View 2 Images Ed Davey said the Lib Dems were a 'firewall' against Reform (Image: Getty Images)

‌



“Having dismantled the blue wall at the last election, we now have an orange wall, which we want to defend and expand. That, I think, is the way to keep the Tories out and stop Reform.

“I deeply worry about Reform, who increasingly are openly racist and dividing our country, and one thing I hope Burnham will do is to focus a little bit more on where that populism and extremism is at its worst.

“I feel a heavy responsibility on me and our party, because I genuinely think we are a firewall against Reform in areas where Labour just aren't playing. It's a moral responsibility and I don't think I've had anything more serious to do in my political career.”

‌



His intervention comes as the UK elections watchdog announced political spending limits will be reviewed.

Vijay Rangarajan - the head of the Electoral Commission - said the rules needed to be "fit for purpose" and maintain public confidence in campaign financing.

He told the Sunday Times: "Our review will look across the campaign spending framework as a whole, including spending limits, the interaction between party and candidate spending, and the reporting requirements that support public confidence in the system."

‌



He was tasked to set up the review in July by ministers.

Under existing restrictions, parties standing candidates in Britain must not spend more than £34 million in the year before a general election.

Elsewhere at the Lib Dem conference, Sir Ed urged the PM to cut fuel duty by 10p a litre at least until Christmas to ease cost-of-living pressures.

Article continues below

The party also wants to slash bus fares to £1, cut rail fares by 10% and make driving electric cars cheaper by cutting VAT on public charging.

News.title: Life-changing child birth injuries at record levels in UK - scale of maternity ward failures laid bare
News.content:
Life-changing child birth injuries at record levels in UK - scale of maternity ward failures laid bare

EXCLUSIVE: Care Quality Commission data analysed by the Lib Dems shows that 1 in 10 women - roughly 54,000 mothers every year - are left alone during late stages of labour or childbirth

View 2 Images CQC data shows that that 1 in 10 women are left alone during late stages of labour or childbirth (Image: Getty Images)

Britain’s maternity wards are seeing “mothers and babies are being failed across large parts of the country”, damning new figures reveal. .

‌



Care Quality Commission (CQC) data analysed by the Lib Dems shows that 1 in 10 women - roughly 54,000 mothers every year - are left alone during late stages of labour or childbirth.

‌



The data shows life-altering childbirth injuries reached a record high in the first half of 2026, with NHS data showing that 3 in every 100 women undergoing a vaginal birth now suffer severe 3rd or 4th-degree tears.

‌



These are agonising injuries so profound that patients must be rushed to an operating theatre for surgical repair. The rate of these severe tears has surged by 29% since 2021.

Now Sir Ed Davey, the leader of the Liberal Democrats, has urged the PM Andy Burnham to step in to end the crisis.

View 2 Images Ed Davey urged Andy Burnham to save Britain's maternity wards (Image: Getty Images)

‌



It comes with wards facing severe shortages of senior midwives and consultant doctors, while overworked staff are left without adequate training to read vital CTG heart monitors or identify women at risk.

The crisis extends to life-threatening postpartum haemorrhages, with 2026 recording peak rates of severe bleeds involving a blood loss of more than 1.5l.

The most recent quarter (April-June) had the highest level ever recorded - at 33 women per thousand and 2026 has seen a higher level than any previous year.

‌



Speaking to this newspaper as his party conference begins, Sir Ed said: “The number of injuries and deaths to mothers and babies seems to be rising, which is shocking.

“I think that Britain should be the safest country in the world to have a baby given our NHS and given what we've achieved in the past, so we're going to keep pushing that until that vision is achieved.”

Pointing the finger at decades of Tory austerity, he added: "The genesis of this is all those years where the Conservatives just ignored it, and I think they have to bear a big responsibility for the mess of our NHS and maternity services in particular.”

‌



It comes after the Mirror told how mothers-to-be in Devon feared having problem births by the roadside with no one to help. A lack of consultants and obstetricians has meant births, including C-sections, as well as triage appointments to see if mother and baby have any problems, have been suspended at North Devon District Hospital in Barnstaple.

The Lib Dem leader also praised Mr Burnham for his willingness to work with him on improving maternity wards.

He said: “I felt Starmer didn't really get a grip of this, and I get the impression that Burnham will listen.

Article continues below

“Starmer never met me, never invited me in for cross-party talks on anything. So there's no doubt there's been a change of tone, and there's no doubt that I welcome that. But I've got to be honest, the proof of the pudding will be the eating, won't it?”.

A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: "Every woman deserves safe maternity care and the new Health Secretary has made this issue a personal priority. Through the National Maternity and Neonatal Taskforce that she is chairing, this Government will deliver the reforms needed to ensure the very highest standards of safety and care for every mother and baby.”

News.title: Call to shut down 'Jenrick hotels' in attack on Tory turncoat Reform MP Robert Jenrick
News.content:
Call to shut down 'Jenrick hotels' in attack on Tory turncoat Reform MP Robert Jenrick

EXCLUSIVE: In a fiery attack on Reform's Robert Jenrick, senior Lib Dem Max Wilkinson will urge ministers to look to Europe to shut down 'Jenrick's hotels' - pointing to the MP's 2022 brag

Robert Jenrick speaks about 'ramping up' asylum hotels in 2022

Dozens of "Jenrick's hotels" housing thousands of asylum seekers must finally be shut, ministers will be urged today in a fiery attack on the Reform MP.

‌



Lib Dem frontbencher Max Wilkinson will lash out at Tory turncoat Robert Jenrick, who famously bragged about securing hotels when he was Immigration Minister. In a keynote speech, Mr Wilkinson, the Lib Dem home affairs spokesman, will tell the Lib Dem conference that the Reform MP and his colleagues are "shamelessly" exploiting a small boat crisis they helped to create.

‌



He will call on the government to look to sign up to a new EU migration pact to clear up the mess left by Mr Jenrick and co. Mr Wilkinson is expected to say: "Was it not Robert Jenrick himself who bragged about opening up more asylum hotels when he was Immigration Minister?

‌



230 most dangerous areas for knife crime in UK identified with plans to increase CCTV and police patrols READ MORE :

View 2 Images Lib Dem Max Wilkinson will launch a scathing attack on Robert Jenrick's record on Monday (Image: Getty Images)

"And was it not the Tories in the Home Office who stopped processing asylum cases leaving taxpayers to foot the bill for a huge backlog? We have seen their politicians visit Dover and Calais over and over and over again to shamelessly point at the mess that they created."

In an interview in 2022, as the asylum backlog grew, Mr Jenrick told Sky News: "More hotels have been coming online almost every month throughout the whole of this year. So, (fellow Reform defector) Suella Braverman and her predecessor, Priti Patel, were procuring more hotels.

‌



"What I have done in my short tenure is ramp that up and procure even more because November, historically, has been one of the highest months of the year for migrants illegally crossing the Channel."

Nigel Farage later branded Mr Jenrick a "fraud" when sharing the quote on X. But this did not stop Mr Jenrick defecting to Reform in January after being sacked from the shadow cabinet by Kemi Badenoch, who got wind of his plan.

Blaming Brexit for the small boats crisis, Mr Wilkinson will call for the UK to join the EU's Migration and Asylum Pact, which sees participating nations agree to co-operate on screening and returns. Other countries that are not part of the bloc, including Switzerland, Norway and Iceland, have adopted elements of the agreement.

‌



Mr Wilkinson will say: "Before the (Brexit) referendum, not a single small boat crossed the Channel. Since then, more than 200,000 people have tried to make that dangerous journey - some, tragically, never making it to safety on those flimsy rubber dinghies.

View 2 Images Mr Wilkinson will turn his fire on Robert Jenrick, who defected to Reform in January (Image: Getty Images)

"The new status quo created by the Tories and Reform and then weaponised by them has led directly to the unrest and mistrust we see across the nation.

‌



"There is a solution: to enter EU's landmark new Migration and Asylum Pact. To put a stop to dangerous Channel crossings and the criminal gangs’ business model once and for all.

"And to close down Jenrick’s hotels, which never worked for communities or asylum seekers, despite costing taxpayers a fortune. This is the solution we need to build an asylum system British people can trust - that is fair and effective for all."

Last week Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the pact should not be viewed as a "silver bullet", telling MPs: "It is a real mistake to think that that pact is the future and if we were in that, this problem would go away - because I promise you it would not."

Article continues below

Since leaving the EU, Britain has not had a Europe-wide returns agreement, but last summer Keir Starmer reached a one-in-one-out deal with France. This has seen around 1,400 small boat arrivals returned so far in exchange for people deemed to have legitimate claims coming the other way.

Labour has vowed to close the remaining asylum hotels by the general election by shifting people onto large sites while their applications are processed. At its peak there were over 56,000 people living in around 400 hotels.

At the end of June there were 16,021 in under 160 venues.

News.title: RNLI warned of cyber attack after volunteers abused for saving migrants by far-right thugs
News.content:
RNLI warned of cyber attack after volunteers abused for saving migrants by far-right thugs

Online security experts have warned that the identities of RNLI members could have been leaked or fallen into the wrong hands

View 2 Images RNLI volunteers were labelled as traitors online by far-right thugs for rescuing asylum seekers in the Channel (Image: Barry Williams/PA Wire)

RNLI members have been warned they may have been hit with a cyberattack amid a heightened threat from far-Right agitators.

‌



Volunteers for the organisation were told their data may have been stolen by hackers - just days after they suffered online and physical abuse for rescuing 120 migrants from a dinghy in the English Channel.

‌



Online security experts have warned that the identities of RNLI members could have been leaked or fallen into the wrong hands after a cyber-attack on a third-party software provider. In a letter accompanying the autumn copy of its Lifeboat magazine, the charity warned supporters that their "name, contact details and records of interactions with the RNLI" could have been breached in the raid on Beacon CRM.

‌



View 2 Images Balaclava-clad followers have protested in both Dover and Portsmouth in recent weeks

NHS says 20 women had breasts removed unnecessarily as hundreds of cancer patients suffer significant harm READ MORE :

Orlando Bloom begs for international aid at world's largest refugee camp as cuts fuel crisis READ MORE :

The RNLI said it was advised last month by the provider to "assume that data held within its systems was taken" in a cyber-attack that affected around 1,500 charities in late July.

"At this stage we're not aware of any misuse of your personal information and have no evidence that your information has been published or shared," the charity added.

‌



The RNLI has suspended its services in Portsmouth since its staff were subjected to relentless abuse and branded "traitors" by anti-migrant protesters.

Peter Sparkes, the charity's chief executive, condemned abuse of its volunteers as "wholly unacceptable in civilised society", adding that the RNLI worked to save lives at sea irrespective of whose they are.

The latest data breach has fuelled concerns that lifeboat volunteers will face "doxxing", which involves the publication online of a person's home address.

‌



Dr William Allchorn, a senior research fellow at Anglia Ruskin University's International Policing and Public Protection Research Institute, said that those on the far-Right could exploit the data breach.

He told the Sunday Telegraph: "They use open source maritime tracking and endto-end encryption, but beyond that I don't know how sophisticated their set up is."

"It is the chill effect," he added. "For those on the fringes of the movement this information could be quite key."

‌



Andy Burnham hit out at "appalling" abuse directed at hero crews after they were labelled as traitors online by far-right thugs for rescuing asylum seekers in the Channel and bringing a dinghy to safety in Portsmouth, Hants.

Hundreds of protesters blocked roads overnight on September 6 and vowed to stop migrants from leaving the port.

The boat, reported to be carrying about 140 migrants, is thought to have made one of the longest journeys of any small boat and landings as far west as Hampshire are rare.

‌



The Mirror later revealed two RNLI heroes were named and pictured online by Portsmouth protestors who condemned them as "collaborators" and "traitors" for rescuing asylum seekers.

The RNLI issued security advice warning volunteers and staff not to wear the charity’s branding because of “unacceptable abuse”.

A spokesman for the RNLI said: "Beacon CRM works with many charities and organisations across the UK and Ireland, and while they cannot confirm exactly which records were accessed or downloaded, it advised all affected organisations, including the RNLI, to assume that data held within its systems was taken.

Article continues below

"At this stage, there is no evidence that information relating to RNLI supporters has been published, shared online or otherwise misused."

News.title: Key takeaways from BBC interview as Earl Spencer defends claims about King
News.content:
Earl Spencer has told the BBC writing his book about sister Princess Diana, which has made headlines for its criticism of King Charles, was his "duty...as an eyewitness to history".

In an interview with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg ahead of the memoir's release on Tuesday, Earl Spencer said he wanted "to put things down once and for all that were true".

Among claims made in Swan Song about the King, who was then the Prince of Wales, was that he said "we'll forget her soon enough" during an argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in Diana's funeral procession.

In a strongly worded response, Buckingham Palace said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".

Here are the key moments from Earl Spencer's interview, which include his first account of how he was told about Diana's death and criticism of press coverage of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.

News.title: Specialist courts for rape cases to be rolled out across England and Wales
News.content:
Labour promised in its 2024 manifesto to halve violence against women and girls within a decade.

"For too long, victims of rape and serious sexual offences have felt let down by our justice system," Burnham said.

"Prosecution rates for rape remain shamefully low, with many victims waiting years for justice. This is not good enough."

The changes were "long overdue" and would make a "significant difference" but focusing on prosecution alone would not be enough, he added.

"So as well as ensuring victims get justice, we will step up action to prevent these horrific crimes from happening in the first place," the prime minister said.

Nichols spoke publicly for the first time about being raped when she accused the then Justice Secretary, David Lammy, of using crime victims as a "cudgel" to push through his reforms of the legal system.

She was criticising the Courts and Tribunals Bill's plans to limit jury trials to cases with a likely prison sentence of three years or more.

She said she had waited 1,088 days to go to court, with every day being "agony" and the "trauma" made worse by her role in public life.

Her attacker, she said, was acquitted at crown court but subsequently ordered to pay compensation after she won a civil case against him.

"It is because I have been raped that I am as passionate as I am about what it means for a justice system to be truly victim-focused," she said.

"It is because I have endured every indignity that our broken criminal justice system could mete out that I care what kind of reform will actually deliver justice for survivors and victims of crime more widely."

Responding to news of the specialist courts being rolled out, the Conservatives said tackling delays to criminal rape trials was "long overdue" and they pushed Labour to commit to scrapping plans to restrict jury trials.

"The fact that victims have been withdrawing their cases because they have taken too long has been a disgrace," said shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy.

"Labour need to get courts sitting throughout the year, end the delays and clear the backlog â not undermine our right to a trial by jury."

Last year another charity, the Salford Survivor Project, said victims of rape and sexual assault were being "failed by the system" as court backlogs reached a record high.

The long delays for cases to go to trial were having a serious impact on victims' mental health, it said.

Also last year, a woman who says she was sexually assaulted by a taxi driver on her 21st birthday told BBC News she had dropped the case because of court delays.

She reported the alleged incident in early 2022 and gave evidence in court in December 2023 but the case was adjourned until September 2024 when the judge fell ill.

"I made the decision, even though I hate the statement, to drop the case," she said. "I couldn't let this hurt me further."

The Crown Prosecution Service said that, without her testimony, the case had been dropped because of insufficient evidence.

News.title: Union calls for halt to graded Ofsted inspections over health concerns
News.content:
England's biggest school leaders' union has called for a halt to graded Ofsted inspections, saying they could pose a "risk to life" for school staff.

The National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT) said the change to inspections, rolled out nationally just under a year ago, had been severely harmful to school leaders' welfare.

It said schools should instead be rated using short narrative reports that set out their strengths and areas they could improve.

Ofsted said it had worked closely with unions and parents to develop the new report card inspection system, and would continue to grade schools.

Ofsted, England's schools' inspectorate, introduced the report card system to replace its previous one or two-word judgements last November, following the death of head teacher Ruth Perry, who took her own life after Ofsted downgraded her school from "outstanding" to "inadequate".

An inquest ruled that an Ofsted inspection had contributed to her death in January 2023.

That led to a change in how Ofsted assessed schools, bringing in report cards designed to grade schools on several areas, rather than focusing on one overall grade for the whole school.

News.title: Burnham hails Greenland deal ahead of expected first Trump meeting
News.content:
"Donald Trump is trying to claim he's got a success in Greenland, but actually, all he's got is almost a carbon copy of the agreement that's persisted since the 1950s," he said at a Q&A with members at party conference.

"So let Donald Trump try to pretend he's had a victory. The truth is, Europe, Nato, countries like Canada stood up to him and won."

Trump had tried for months to purchase or annex the semi-autonomous territory, arguing that it was vulnerable to adversaries, including Russia and China.

In the wake of the deal, Frederiksen said she was "pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement" for all three parties, which was expected to be signed at the UN General Assembly next week.

The deal "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" while also recognising "the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination", she said in a joint statement with Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen.

The agreement would still need to go through "the necessary parliamentary procedures to enter into force" once signed, the statement noted.

Burnham has spoken with Trump at least twice since entering Downing Street and No 10 said he intends to use the UNGA to "drive forward work on issues that matter to people at home" including the cost of living and the war in Ukraine.

News.title: Kelsey Parker welcomes baby after 'devastating' stillbirth last year
News.content:
Kelsey Parker, the widow of The Wanted singer Tom Parker, has welcomed a baby after last year announcing a "devastating" stillbirth.

The podcaster and author, 35, had two children with British boy band star Tom Parker before he died in 2022, aged 33, after being diagnosed with terminal brain cancer.

She is now in a relationship with Will Lindsay and last June revealed the "earth-shattering news" that they had lost their baby Phoenix.

On Sunday, a post on her Instagram account showed a photo of a newborn baby's arm next to a pink sign with the word River. "Welcome to the world, River. Our little bit of hope," the caption said.

Celebrities including The Saturdays singer Rochelle Humes, TV presenter Susanna Reid and reality TV star Holly Hagan-Blyth have congratulated Kelsey Parker on social media.

"Congratulations angel," Rochelle Humes wrote.

"Oh my goodness â this is so wonderful â welcome River," Susanna Reid said.

Hagan-Blyth commented "I am SO happy for you xxxx".

Kelsey Parker's Instagram bio says "turning life's hardest moments into hope".

Last year she posted a poem online after the loss of her stillborn baby.

It was called Born Sleeping, Forever Loved, and began "the world grew quiet as you arrived, So loved, so longed for, yet not alive. Our precious boy, our angel light, Born with wings, took silent flight".

News.title: Jailed teacher convicted of sexual abuse secretly released early in Indonesia, BBC finds
News.content:
In January this year, after hearing that Bechi may have been released early, BBC undercover reporters attended an annual prayer event at the Shiddiqiyyah Islamic boarding school in East Java.

The reporters saw Bechi wearing a mask and sitting beside his father. Just before he appeared on stage, filming and photography was prohibited, a marked difference from previous years.

Then in March, BBC reporters again captured Bechi on hidden camera at another prayer event for Eid at his family home located in the same compound as the school.

The BBC sought comment from Bechi, his mother and the Shiddiqiyyah school but there has been no response.

The students who testified, including the girl he was convicted of sexually assaulting, were placed under witness protection and Indonesian law requires them to be informed of Bechi's release.

But they were not informed, Ira and another former student who testified told the BBC. They were stunned by the undercover footage of Bechi because they believed he was still in prison.

The ministry said that victims need not be informed because Bechi remains on parole, but the witness protection agency disputed this, saying the victims must still be informed.

Ayu Masuroh says she was never abused by Bechi but she started investigating the allegations of abuse against him after hearing about them from schoolmates. She lives close to the school and says she is frightened about Bechi being out of prison.

"He hates me. His supporters have threatened to kill me many times. I will never feel safe here. I don't feel safe living in Indonesia."

Speaking publicly for the first time, she told the BBC she collected testimonies from at least 10 other female students, all of whom alleged that they were sexually assaulted or raped by Bechi.

According to her, some said Bechi told them they were "chosen", and one of them said Bechi raped her after calling her for a "personal interview".

These accounts were part of the closed-door trial, which alleged years of abuse at the school, according to court records seen by the BBC.

News.title: Russia's elections had few surprises - but how the Kremlin uses the results is far from clear
News.content:
Many things about Russia are hard to predict.

The result of this election wasn't one of them.

In a political system tightly controlled by the Kremlin, the party of power â United Russia â had been widely expected to maintain its grip on parliament.

There was no upset. No surprises. No other party came close.

Preliminary results suggest that United Russia is on course to retain its constitutional majority in the State Duma.

And that's after more than four and a half years of war against Ukraine, which have resulted in huge battlefield losses for the Russian army, sparked economic hardship, as well as petrol shortages due to Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil facilities.

It appears that those parties which have crossed the 5% threshold and made it into the new Duma are the same ones that were in the last parliament.

And that Duma was fully behind the Kremlin and the so-called special military operation.

News.title: Brigitte Bardot's ballet flats and diamond rings to be sold at auction
News.content:
Personal possessions of late actress Brigitte Bardot â from Repetto ballet flats and diamond rings to her copy of the Kama Sutra â are being sold at auction on Monday with proceeds going to her animal charity.

Fans of the iconic figure, who died last December at the age of 91, have been coming en masse to contemplate the nearly 300 lots on display at the Drouot sale rooms in central Paris.

The items are from Bardot's two homes in Saint-Tropez as well as her Paris flat, parts of which are recreated in the display.

"Each item on sale bears the trace of an encounter, an involvement, a moment of happiness, a stage of her life. They tell the story of the woman as well as the legend," said her secretary for many years, Frank Guillou.

Bardot is seen today as one of the most important female personalities of the late 20th century. As a model and actress from the 1950s, she became an emblem of modern femininity and the sexual revolution before later taking up the cause of animal rights.

But later in life she was also criticised for making homophobic slurs and was fined multiple times for inciting racial hatred.

News.title: Homes evacuated over fears fire at seaside hotel weakened building's structure
News.content:
Speaking to the BBC, John Dighton, who was evacuated from Pavilion Court, said that he was told to leave his flat at about 19:00 on Saturday.

The 50-year-old said: "We don't know how long we will be out for but we have grabbed stuff for a couple of days.

"The worst thing is the not knowing. We are at a hotel over the road from the flats."

Ross Honeycomb, 39, was staying at the hotel with his family and told the BBC on Saturday how they were woken by fire alarms at about 01:00.

He said: "I thought I was dreaming, it was horrifying.

"We looked out and there was smoke billowing from the underground car park. Later we started hearing explosions."

Kevin Crawford, 91, and his wife Kathleen, 82, said they had booked in for a two-week stay at the hotel.

The couple, from London, told the BBC that they were in their room on the sixth floor when they heard a fire alarm.

"We saw the fire but we thought the fire brigade had it under control," said Kevin.

"We managed to sleep through it. At the time, we didn't realise how bad the fire was."

The council's chief executive, Susan Priest, said on Saturday: "The extent of support of organisations, including Three Hills, Morrisons and the Salvation Army, has been amazing and helped to ensure that visitors and residents were looked after, supported and had food and hot drinks.

"This was an extremely difficult day, firstly for the hotel guests and this evening for our residents who have had to move out of their homes."

News.title: The deadly new drugs making Scotland's fight against addiction even harder
News.content:
Efforts to bring down Scotland's sky-high rate of drug deaths are being frustrated by the arrival of hundreds of powerful new synthetic substances that experts warn are making the deadly drugs crisis even more dangerous.

In the past three years, there has been an explosion in the supply of new synthetic cannabinoids and opioids, transforming the illicit drugs trade and increasing the risk of fatal overdoses.

Annual figures to be released on Wednesday are expected to show a rise in the number of drug-related deaths in Scotland, which already has an unenviable record as the drugs death capital of Europe.

"The illicit drug supply in Scotland is getting more and more dangerous," said Dr Lorna Nisbet of Dundee University's Leverhulme Research Centre for Forensic Science.

News.title: Billionaire Man United owner loses moral high ground after tax exile, Labour chair says
News.content:
The Labour Party chair has said Sir Jim Ratcliffe loses "the moral high ground" by making statements about the UK while living in tax exile.

Speaking to Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Bridget Phillipson said she would take the billionaire businessman's comments that the UK was "on the slide" with a "pinch of salt".

Sir Jim, the founder of petrochemical giant Ineos and Manchester United's co-owner, told the BBC he has lost confidence in the UK due to a combination of high taxes and high immigration.

He has been a tax resident in Monaco since 2020 and said "things would have to get better" in the UK for him to return.

When questioned over the remarks, Phillipson said Sir Jim loses "the moral high ground" by "making these kinds of pronouncements while choosing to make decisions, that he is within his rights to make, to become a tax exile".

Pushed on whether it bothers her that people who create jobs and pay a lot of tax were leaving the UK, the minister said she was "optimistic about our country's prospects".

Other high profile billionaires have left the UK, including including steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal and most recently the UK's third biggest taxpayer, hedge-fund boss Chris Rokos.

But, Philipson argued the country was in a good position ahead of the Budget next month, and Andy Burnham has shown a "sense of hope and optimism whilst recognising that many families are still struggling and there is more to do."

"Of course, there are challenges, including big international headwinds, but I fundamentally believe that we are in a strong position going into this budget because of the decisions taken over the last two years, and I believe our country's best days lie ahead of us," she said.

Philipson declined to speculate over whether there would be tax rises in the Budget on 28 October, and said the government remained committed to being disciplined about its spending rules.

News.title: Tens of thousands of fridge freezers left at docks as household collections suspended
News.content:
People have reported storing broken fridges and freezers in their gardens for months because some council collections have been suspended.

It follows the closure of specialist treatment facilities and a wider shortage of capacity to process cooling appliances, the Local Government Authority (LGA) said.

Recycling company Unimetals, which had dozens of sites in the UK, filed for liquidation in 2025 leaving tens of thousands of fridge freezers at Newport Docks.

The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said it was working to manage the capacity shortages.

Almost a quarter of Welsh councils say they have suspended household collections of fridge-freezers due to a shortage of space at disposal sites.

Cardiff is one of these and Lee Young, who lives in the city, has been trying to get rid of his broken fridge-freezer for two months.

"I tried to take it to the recycling centre in July but was told it wasn't accepted. Someone said the council would collect it, but they won't either."

It has been sitting in his back garden ever since and he does not know when council collections will resume.

News.title: Human extinction fears make me want to flee AI and live on an island
News.content:
Since headlines broke about claims AI advancement could lead to human extinction, James Downs has felt his anxiety rising.

"It makes me almost feel powerless. Like, what can I do as an individual?" said the mental health campaigner from Cardiff.

This sense of fear has led him to check his phone for more news.

"And the more you look at it the more your attention's drawn to the negative or scary things and the worse and worse it can seem," said the 37-year-old.

Earlier this month, a top safety researcher at Anthropic warned AI was advancing so quickly he believed there was a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.

Then computer scientist and Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton, known as the "Godfather of AI", told the BBC that the claim was "not unreasonable", external.

On Tuesday, amid rising public concerns about the risks, the boss of ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said people should have more faith in AI firms to keep the tech safe.

News.title: Ed Davey calls for immediate 10p cut to fuel duty
News.content:
Sir Ed Davey is calling on the government to immediately cut fuel duty by 10p a litre until Christmas as part of a package of policies aimed at cutting the cost of living.

The Liberal Democrat leader is also urging the government to scrap a permanent increase in fuel duty which is set to take effect in January.

Fuel duty was frozen under the Conservatives in March 2022 and Sir Keir Starmer's government continued the freeze, deciding in May to push back a planned 3p increase in September until the end of this year.

The Lib Dems claim cutting 10p from fuel duty now would mean fuel would drop by 12p per litre at the pump.

Sir Ed claimed drivers should be supported and a temporary three-month fuel duty cut would pay for itself by stimulating the economy.

"Petrol and diesel prices are higher than they've been for a long time because of Trump's mad war with Iran, and people need help now," he said.

The policy would cost about Â£2bn, he said, adding: "It's a three-month package, a temporary package, but if you look at the extra money the government will get through the energy profits levy, from gas taxes, from VAT and fuel duty, it's self-funding."

In a speech to his party's conference on Tuesday, Sir Ed will make further calls to cut the bus fare cap from Â£3 to Â£1, and reduce rail fares by 10%.

He will also call for VAT to be dropped from public charging points for electric vehicles and a review of network costs the Lib Dems have labelled unfair.

Chancellor John Healey is under pressure to raise taxes or cut spending at his Budget next month, amid soaring government borrowing costs.

Asked about Sir Ed's call for a fuel duty cut, Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson told Laura Kuenssberg: "I'm sure John Healey will be open to any and all suggestions ahead of the budget but actually this is an area where the Labour government has taken action on fuel duty already.

"Whilst I recognise what the Lib Dems have to say on this topic, this is the element of politics about it - they've got their conference, they're making their pitch, good luck to them."

Sir Ed also ruled out scrapping the state pension triple lock after party grandee and former business secretary Sir Vince Cable said at a fringe event it was unsustainable and should be "phased out".

Speaking at Q&A on the conference stage, Sir Ed said the policy had been introduced by the Lib Dems during the Conservative coalition to address inequalities and there was still work to do to tackle pensioner poverty.

"It has not finished the job," he told party members, who were split in a show of hands about whether the triple lock should be scrapped if the Lib Dems win power.

The triple lock guarantees that the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases or 2.5% - whichever is the highest - but critics say it is unaffordable and unfair to younger people.

News.title: JLR suppliers call for shift to aerospace
News.content:
Major Jaguar Land Rover suppliers have urged the government to help automotive manufacturers move into aerospace and defence, warning that large-scale car production in the UK faces long-term decline.

In an open letter to the prime minister, chancellor and West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker, industry leaders argued Britain's automotive supply chain was "not in decline" but "in the wrong market".

The intervention comes nearly a fortnight after JLR announced plans to cut 4,000 jobs.

The Treasury said it recognised the uncertainty facing workers and was supporting the automotive sector through grants, lower energy costs and investment in electric vehicle production.

JLR has its global headquarters in Coventry and plants in Solihull, Wolverhampton and Halewood.

Signatories to the letter said the redundancies were "the first visible crack" in a UK automotive supply chain supporting about 183,000 manufacturing jobs.

News.title: Maddy Cusack 'more than a number on a shirt' as anniversary falls during inquest delay
News.content:
Sitting on a bench dedicated to her memory, Maddy Cusack's sister and cousin fondly remember her as their sunshine and someone with a real sense of fun.

Olivia Cusack says her big sister was the person "I looked up to my whole life", while for Emily Reilly, her cousin Maddy's the one who "used to get us in trouble with my dad".

But as they come to remember the former Sheffield United footballer on the third anniversary of her death, they're still waiting for answers.

An inquest examining what happened to Maddy Cusack, who was 27 when she was found unconscious at her home in Derbyshire, started in June and should've finished in July.

But it has been paused for months while her former club Sheffield United looks for documents linked to her medical records.

It means her family will have to wait until at least December to hear more evidence, a wait Olivia describes as "extremely overwhelming".

"It is very emotional and you can find yourself frustrated at times," she tells BBC Newsbeat.

"They're very difficult days."

Kemi Badenoch has pledged to bring back tax-free shopping for tourists by reversing a post-Brexit rule change.

The decision to scrap the VAT refund scheme for international visitors in 2021 left the UK “less competitive” than many other European destinations as the country left the EU, the Tories said.

The Opposition leader, who was a Treasury minister at the time of its abolition, said retailers were being “let down by a policy that is driving their customers away.”

open image in gallery Business chiefs including the head of Fortnum & Mason welcomed the pledge (Yui Mok/PA) ( PA Archive )

Business chiefs including the bosses of Fortnum & Mason, Paul Smith and the parent company of Claridge’s hotel hailed the policy change as “pro-growth” and “pro-jobs”.

Visitor numbers to the UK have returned to near pre-Covid levels, but real-terms spending remains 8% lower than before the pandemic, according to estimates from tourism agency VisitBritain based on data from 2024.

The Tories said returning the VAT refund would be partly offset by a proposed “crackdown” on so-called “health tourism”, including more consistent charging of patients ineligible for free treatment.

Tax-free shopping could also be extended to cover EU tourists subject to evidence, with the rollout complete by the end of the next Parliament, the party said.

In a joint statement backing the pledge, business leaders said: “As some of the leading businesses in tourism, retail and hospitality, we welcome this pro-growth, pro-jobs announcement from Kemi Badenoch and her team.

open image in gallery The Tories scrapped the VAT refund scheme in 2021 (Stefan Rousseau/PA) ( PA Wire )

“With its heritage and the quality of our products and service, Britain is well placed to compete with the world’s finest destinations. The restoration of tax-free shopping for tourists will allow us to win back those who may have taken their custom elsewhere in recent years. When taking the full economic benefits and other taxes paid into account, we believe this will be a net benefit to Britain.”

The business leaders are: chef and TV personality Angela Hartnett; co-founder of Inception hospitality group Charlie Gilkes; chief executive of Me+Em fashion brand Clare Hornby; Burlington Arcade managing director Jamie Reuben; chief executive of Maybourne, which owns and manages The Berkeley, Claridge’s, The Connaught and The Emory hotels, Marc Socker; Paul Smith executive chairman Ewan Venters; Fuller, Smith and Turner executive chairman Simon Emeny; and Fortnum & Mason chief executive Tom Athron.

Mrs Badenoch said: “Britain should be the place where the whole world comes to shop.

“We have iconic retailers, inventive designers and brilliant manufacturers, but they are being let down by a tax policy that is chasing their customers away. Holidaymakers are choosing rival cities in other countries for the simple reason that it saves them money.

“British retailers are closing down shops with the knock-on effects damaging small manufacturers, suppliers and jobs across the UK. I want them to know I’m on their side and Conservatives will sort out taxes so companies can create jobs and grow our economy.”

Labour accused the Tories of a “spectacular U-turn” over the policy pledge.

“Kemi Badenoch used to say tax-free shopping was a costly giveaway and now she’s trying to sell it as an economic miracle,” a party spokesperson said.

“If they really think it’s such a great idea, they should explain why they scrapped it in the first place and how they’d pay for bringing it back.”

A Treasury spokesperson said: “The UK is one of the most-visited countries in the world with international tourism driving billions into our economy. We are supporting the continued growth of this industry and the Government is working to meet our ambition to welcome 50 million international visitors a year to the UK by 2030.

“Visitors can still claim VAT relief where the items purchased are shipped directly to their home country as exports.”

A federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent reportedly shot and wounded a man in Austin, Texas, early Sunday afternoon during the latest instance of government violence allegedly tied to President Donald Trump's mass deportation campaign.

The unidentified victim was hit once in the torso and rushed to a local trauma center, where he was in serious but stable condition, Austin-Travis County EMS Chief Robert Luckritz said during a news conference. He couldn’t confirm whether the man was shot in the front of his body or from behind.

Officials said city police officers weren’t present during the shooting, which took place near a highway overpass in the 800 block of Anderson Square around 12:55 p.m. local time.

Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said she was told the shooter “is an ICE agent,” and Mayor Kirk Watson said he was “very angry” over the shooting.

“Part of what makes me angry about this, part of what makes me so unhappy about it, is that we live in a time where there's a politics of fear, where people are trying to create fear,” Watson said.

open image in gallery A car at the scene of the shooting in Austin, Texas, appears to have bullet holes in it ( Reuters )

Watson said there was “no reason for us to be surprised” by the shooting, given “the nature of ICE and how it’s doing its business” in other cities. He called for an independent, third-party investigation, saying it “would not be appropriate” to let ICE conduct the probe.

Davis said, “I trust the Texas Rangers, and I trust [the Texas Department of Public Safety]...to work alongside us and to get — to get answers. Absolutely.”

Spokespersons for ICE and the Department of Homeland Security didn’t immediately return inquiries from The Independent.

Photographs taken at the scene show a dark blue Toyota Corolla with damage along its passenger side and what appear to be two bullet holes in the rear window.

The police chief said she couldn’t confirm a report that the car was sideswiped and that the ICE agent fired multiple shots through its rear windshield.

“That's not what I'm hearing. I'm hearing that it was out on foot...there was a small foot pursuit,” she said, adding that “this is all very preliminary” and that she hadn’t been briefed by federal officials.

open image in gallery Austin Mayor Kirk Watson says there’s ‘no reason for us to be surprised’ by the shooting, given ‘the nature of ICE and how it’s doing its business’ ( The City of Austin, Texas/ATXN )

Democratic U.S. Rep. Greg Casar, whose district covers the shooting scene, said, “I think the obvious should be said, that there is a reason that people in Austin and across the country are deeply suspicious of anything that ICE has said.”

“People in the community don't know all the facts, but people are hurting and upset because they see how ICE has shot and, in some cases, even killed people with impunity in other parts of the country,” he said.

Casar also called on ICE to end what he called its “surge of officers here” and to instead “be focused on transparently working on issues of crime, not what they've been doing consistently here in Austin before this event.”

The mayor said local officials “have seen an increase, we believe, in the number of incidents where ICE has detained somebody, stopped somebody, those sorts of instances.”

“And it happened in a relatively brief period of time,” Watson said. “I think in one week we saw it go from: count them on one hand to in the thirties, and that happened in less than a couple of days.”

open image in gallery US Rep. Greg Casar says ‘there is a reason that people in Austin and across the country are deeply suspicious of anything that ICE has said’ ( The City of Austin, Texas/ATXN )

The incident in Austin follows a string of immigration-related shootings by federal law-enforcement officers carrying out Trump’s pledge to conduct the “largest mass deportation program in history,” which has a reported goal of expelling 1 million people a year.

In Minneapolis, two American citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were fatally shot while separately protesting ICE operations in January, leading to the ouster of then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, who falsely accused them of domestic terrorism.

ICE officers also allegedly killed Mexican national Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston and Colombian national Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford, Maine, during separate traffic stops in July, even though neither was the target of an investigation.

Their slayings led Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to order a temporary halt to vehicle stops by ICE. Trump immediately criticized the directive, leading Mullin to countermand it the following day.

Reports also revealed that the ICE officer who allegedly shot Durán Guerrero, David Brouilette, had a history of mental illness that led military recruiters to reject him before he went off his medications and was able to enlist in the Maine National Guard and later join the Army in January 2010.

Brouilette was deployed to Afghanistan from May 2012 to February 2015, with an immediate relative telling The Associated Press that the tour of duty "destroyed him."

"They took someone who was extremely mentally ill and turned him into a killing machine," the relative said.

At just 22 years old, Eman David has spent much of her life in and out of hospital.

Diagnosed with kidney failure at seven, she was handed a lifeline in 2014 when she had a successful kidney transplant, which allowed her to finally enjoy her childhood.

But in 2021, she received the heartbreaking news that her body had started to reject the organ and that she would need another transplant. Six years later, she is still waiting.

“Right now I’m just doing maths at college. But I can’t focus on anything but dialysis and the transplant and when they’re going to call me.”

“I’m always looking at my phone, I’m always thinking that it’s them [the hospital] calling me.”

Ms David, from Manchester, is one of 8,700 patients in the UK waiting for an organ transplant – a record high – with nine people a week dying while waiting to get a lifesaving call, according to NHS Blood and Transplant (NHSBT). At this rate, it could mean 468 deaths by next summer if nothing changes.

The situation has reached crisis point and is now so concerning that NHSBT, the body responsible for organ donation, has had to take the “unprecedented” move to trigger its “urgent” organ donation response plan.

John Richardson, assistant director of Organ and Tissue Donation and Transplantation, told The Independent: “In organ donation, it’s unprecedented that we’ve moved to this footing; it’s the highest list we’ve seen. Up to nine people each week will die waiting for an organ transplant, so it is significant.”

open image in gallery Eman David is still waiting for a donor three years on ( Patient Handout )

Despite a change in the law to introduce opt-out donations – which assumes people have opted in to donate organs unless they have explicitly stated otherwise – families can still decline a deceased relative’s wishes. The latest data shows family consent rates have dropped from 67 per cent in 2020-21 to 57 per cent last year.

Mr Richardson explained the issue likely driving this is that people do not make their wishes clear by registering to donate, and so families who don’t know what their loved one wanted can often decline donation.

That leaves people like Ms David in limbo and facing lengthy waits.

‘Dialysis just drains you’

She is one of the 80 per cent of transplant waiting list patients waiting for a kidney, with 7,200 currently in limbo.

Ms David and her parents were first told she would need a transplant and weekly dialysis when she was seven.

“Since then I’ve just had to basically live at Manchester Royal Infirmary. I think I missed about two, three years of primary school.”

At 11, Ms David and her family got some hope, and she received a kidney from a donor.

“My life changed so much, you know; I finally was able to travel. I remember that a year after my transplant, I went to Spain. I’d be more active. I get tired a lot because I even wanted to eat without restrictions.”

However, in 2021, doctors discovered that her body was rejecting her kidneys, which were functioning at just 15 per cent, and she would need to go back on dialysis.

“It wasn’t really scary because I was thinking like, “What do you mean it’s not working?” I was doing all these blood tests, all these tubes taken out on me, you know. I was thinking, ‘Is this going to ruin my education again?’”

“Dialysis just drains you.”

Initially, she was too ill to even be eligible for a transplant, but she was eventually placed on the waiting list in 2023. She is still waiting.

Fiona Loud, policy director at Kidney Care UK, and a kidney transplant recipient herself, said: “It’s experiences like Eman’s that really highlight the impact that waiting for a transplant can have. To be waiting in limbo for so many of her formative years is heartbreaking. It really hits home that every number on that waiting list is a person with hopes and dreams just waiting for that life-changing call.

“We hope that after reading Eman’s story, people will understand more about the difference organ donation can make and register their decision to be a donor.”

open image in gallery Becca Moore, 31, has been waiting for a new kidney for 18 months ( Handout )

Becca Moore, 31, was treated for recurring urine infections (UTI) during childhood due to a condition which means her urine travels the wrong way from her bladder to her kidneys, causing organ damage.

When she turned 16, the infections “came back with a vengeance” and UTIs made her so sick she was unable to properly take her GCSEs.

After a few years of stable health, she was admitted to hospital in 2008 with a significant UTI and suspected sepsis, a blood infection that can be fatal. The UTIs had done such damage to her kidneys that she needed dialysis.

“It was devastating. My life turned upside down. I worked so hard.”

“When I got my GCSE results, I was told, ‘You ain’t gonna make anything good’. I’d been so poorly during them that I didn’t do the best I should have, or what they expected of me.

“However, I worked myself up working in care homes, daycare centres, and I’d really conquered a job that I absolutely loved. I was a deputy manager of a supported living unit for adults with learning disabilities and mental health issues.”

She added, “I’d gone from having nothing with GCSEs to get where I wanted to be, then losing it again, due to my illness that I didn’t understand. So it did affect me...I had quite severe anxiety. I thought I was going to die.”

In July 2019, Ms Moore received a transplanted kidney from her cousin who was a match. However, devastatingly, in 2023, her body rejected the kidney.

Again in 2025, when her health deteriorated further, she began haemodialysis treatment, where a machine filters waste products and excess fluid from the blood.

Ms Morten has to travel to the hospital for this three times a week and her closest treatment centre is three hours away.

While she waits for a transplant, Ms Moore has been able to move to home dialysis, which has allowed her to work again and go on her honeymoon this month. However, she desperately needs an organ donor.

Chief executive of Kidney Research UK, Fiona Carragher, said: “We all have the power to help turn the tide. Saying yes to organ donation, recording your decision on the NHS Organ Donor Register and making your loved ones aware of your decision is vital if we are to reduce those waiting times.

“But we also must do more, and science holds the answers. It is only through research that we’ll be able to make more kidneys suitable for transplant and find ways to make transplanted kidneys work better and last longer, giving patients the best possible chance of a healthier future.”

Kenyan growers who produce black tea for British supermarket shelves have warned that climate impacts are damaging crop harvests and further diminishing their already "scarce" household incomes.

The East African nation currently provides half of all black tea consumed across Britain, but local farmers face increasingly unpredictable weather patterns, lower crop yields and quality, alongside escalating operational expenses over recent years.

These compounding issues have driven up global tea costs, leaving supermarket shoppers in the UK paying noticeably higher prices for their favourite beverage.

Yet impoverished farmers at the start of the supply chain see little financial gain from higher market prices. Harvesting smaller crops while spending more to maintain them, growers watch as intermediaries, brokers and large corporate firms continue absorbing the vast majority of total profits.

Across the western Kenyan regions of Kericho and Bomet, many local agricultural workers say they cannot cover basic family living expenses, let alone invest in essential protective measures to build future climate resilience on their farms.

These areas are experiencing severe weather volatility this year, including heavy rainfall during usually dry January periods, unseasonal heat in July, intense storm activity and prolonged drought conditions.

open image in gallery Kenyan farmers who grow tea sold in UK supermarkets have warned that climate impacts are hitting yields and their already 'scarce' incomes ( PA )

Nelson Ngeno, manager of Fintea, a union of tea farming cooperatives based in Kericho, said farmers are “really scared” as their livelihoods are “cut short” by the changing conditions.

Production across Fintea’s five cooperatives fell by 30% in May and June this year compared to what their farmers usually harvest during those months, he said.

“Climate is really affecting our farmers,” Mr Ngeno said. “There has been a complete change as far as the weather is concerned.

“It is very serious.”

In January, an unprecendented hail storm damaged thousands of tea plants in the district of Kabartegan, with Fintea estimating losses of 20,000 to 30,000kg daily over four months as the plants recovered.

Lilian Mutai Levin Langot, from the village of Kesebet, was among some 500 tea farmers who lost significant earnings when the storm wiped out her farm.

The 48-year-old smallholder farmer told the Press Association: “It was scary. The hailstones hit everything. On the tea plants, only the stems remained.

“I could not pick anything. It meant there was no income. There was nothing. We just had to survive.”

While she normally earns around 120,000 Kenyan Shillings (Kes) annually (£692), this will likely drop to no more than 90,000 Kes (£520) in 2026.

Ms Langot said she has taken out a loan to get through the year but has still struggled to pay for healthcare fees, school fees for her son and the upkeep of her infant granddaughter.

And having bought a cow and calf to diversify her income, the farmer said she was unable to buy enough feed, so the cow stopped producing milk, and both eventually died.

“It was so hard,” she said, adding that she is “very worried” about such a storm happening again.

“It will be so bad on us,” she said. “When we see the rain, we are just hoping: ‘Don’t let it be the hailstones. Let it just be the rain’.”

Meanwhile, Paul Kipsigei Koech, 50, who lives in nearby Chepchabas, told PA that he is earning so little from his tea farm that he can only provide one meal of mushed-up maize each day for his seven children, wife and elderly father.

Extreme weather events are now happening “once a year”, he said. “You can’t predict like we usually do in the previous (years).”

This, alongside the rising cost of living, is putting further pressure on his ability to make ends meet, with his current income sitting at around 3,000 to 4,000 Kes (£17 to £23) a month, equivalent to less than £1 a day.

“The income is really low to support the entire family,” he said, adding that he is also 80,000 Kes (£462) in debt.

“It is not enough. It is very scarce,” he said. “There is no breakfast. No lunch.”

Asked what he would spend the money on if he received a higher price for his produce, Mr Koech said he would pay the fees so his children – the youngest of which is six – could go to school and eventually help to support the family.

open image in gallery Kenya, which supplies half of all the black tea consumed by Britain, has seen farmers facing unpredictable climate conditions, lower production and quality levels, and rising input costs in recent years ( PA )

“I do not want them to come back to pick tea. I want them to go forward and even get different jobs than what I do,” he said.

Meanwhile, Gladys Maiywa, 50, also from Chepchabas, also earns around 3,000 Kes (£17) a month to support her eight children and sometimes less depending on the weather.

She similarly has sunk 19,000 Kes (£109) in debt to pay for school fees and has an overdraft in the bank of 3,000 Kes.

“It’s very difficult,” she said. “If we get droughts for one, two or three months, we don’t get money. We can’t harvest anything.”

Ms Maiywa said she would spend additional income on her children, their education and build a new home to replace the basic hut they all currently live in.

“I want to see an increase to the rate of pay for our tea,” she added.

And Philip Kitur, a 66-year-old farmer based near Kericho Town, said he has produced 50 per cent less tea than usual for July as climate change and unfair trade practices hit his income.

He said: “A long time ago, the weather was very, very reliable but now the weather patterns have changed.”

His income “just covers the production costs right now”, he said, adding that he has to look for other means of earning money to cover his household’s needs.

“I expect to see less profit this year because of the dry period. We don’t know what’s to come,” he said. “It is very painful.”

open image in gallery These areas are seeing more volatile and extreme weather this year, including wetter conditions in January when it is usually dry, hot temperatures in July when cooler conditions are expected, storms and drought. ( PA )

Their stories come against a wider backdrop of Fintea seeing a drop in the amount of tea it sells on Fairtrade terms from around 5 per cent five years ago to less than 1 per cent today.

This means its farming cooperatives receive less money from “premium payments”, which they can use to invest in climate resilience measures or social impact projects.

Supermarket Lidl last week announced it would be sourcing more tea from Fintea on Fairtrade terms and pay additional money to boost farmers’ incomes, for a new tea called “Way To Go!”, which will hit shelves on Tuesday.

Fintea said the commitment means the percentage of tea it sells on Fairtrade terms may increase to around 2.6 per cent in the coming years.

But Fairtrade is urging more businesses to source tea on Fairtrade terms as the organisation marks the start of its annual “Fairtrade Fortnight” campaign on Monday.

Kerrina Thorogood, partnerships director at the Fairtrade Foundation, said: “Today, just one in five tea farmers in Kenya earns enough income each month to support their families with the essentials.

“As a result, many struggle to invest in their farms, adapt to climate change, and plan for the future.

“Addressing this challenge requires businesses to take responsibility for the prices they pay.”

Hints of an “autumn bounce” were seen in the housing market in September, as the average price tag on a home increased month on month for the first time since May, according to a property website.

The average price of a home coming on the market increased by 0.7% or £2,441 month on month in September, Rightmove said.

Across Britain, the average price tag on a home in September is £367,440, it added.

open image in gallery Rightmove’s map shows average asking price changes across Britain (Rightmove/PA)

This September’s asking price bounce is bigger than the average for the month over the past 10 years, at 0.5%.

September is traditionally a busier period for the housing market as people return from summer holidays, Rightmove said.

It added that heatwaves and the World Cup also created conditions for a particularly quiet summer this year, giving some potential scope for a bigger rebound.

But typical prices remain 0.8% below a year earlier, and 2.3% lower than the start of the summer.

Rightmove also said it is a challenging and crowded market for sellers, with the number of homes available on the market for sale at a 12-year high for the time of year and buyer affordability still stretched.

The Bank of England kept interest rates unchanged at 3.75% last week – but average fixed mortgage rates have still been increasing in recent weeks amid rises in swap rates, which are used to price mortgages.

Finance experts said last week that fixed mortgage rates are influenced by financial markets’ expectations for what will happen, adding that home buyers are expected to be cautious and price-sensitive in the months ahead.

open image in gallery
