Sponsor Message

Yalanda Lattimore, 59, thinks about the career trade-off she has made by volunteering to care for her 1-year-old granddaughter, Mavee. Lattimore provides "granny daycare" one and a half days each week.

She has worked as a blogger and podcaster in Atlanta and now also sells handmade soaps online. But when Mavee came along, Lattimore told her daughter she'd help provide care for the infant — even if it meant she had less time for her soap business and media career.

toggle caption Yalanda Lattimore

"I felt like I could make the sacrifice more than they could, and it truly has been a sacrifice," she said. "You just put things on hold, because your priorities are different."

U.S. workers are staying on the job longer than they used to, with more than 11.7 million Americans age 65 and older in the labor force last month, according to government data.

Lattimore said she hopes to work more but doesn't want to drive for Lyft again, which she did when she was taking care of her ailing mother. She has otherwise struggled to find a job that would let her take off one weekday for childcare and avoid lifting heavy loads.

"Where does flexibility exist at this point?" she said. "Is it anywhere besides the gig economy?"

Harrington Meyer, the Syracuse professor, said she has heard another complaint in her conversations with grandparents: that they are spending too much time with their "parenting" hats on and have fewer opportunities for carefree fun with the kids, a generally agreed-upon right of grandparenthood.

"They would say, 'I would love to take the grandkids to the zoo, but I'm too busy helping them with their calculus or too busy helping them get to flute lessons on time.'" she reported. "They were doing a lot of things that they regarded as parenting and didn't have as much time left over for a trip to the park or something fun and frivolous that they would like to do as grandparents."

Sponsor Message

Making it work

For Mary Jo Galusha, who moved to Delaware to help care for her grandchildren, the lack of pay for being with 23-month-old Robin is possible thanks to her pension from her years as a schoolteacher in Idaho. Her Newark home has a bedroom for her grandchildren, a playroom filled with Legos and even a crafting area for 5-year-old George.

Galusha and her daughter share a Google Calendar where they coordinate care for the kids, and the plan is for Galusha to look after Robin until she starts kindergarten. But Galusha and Bourne, her daughter, review the arrangement every six months or so, and Bourne acknowledges that there is little in the way of a backup plan.

"I'd much prefer to have my mom take care of Robin, but then you always worry, like if in six months she decides that she wants to move and be near another grandbaby, then we'll have to scramble and figure out something else," she said. (Galusha replied from across the table: "No plans for that.")

toggle caption Lianne Milton for NPR

Lattimore, for whom being a grandmother has been an "amazing journey," relishes her days with Mavee. "What you really want is somebody to say you were there, that you were there for them," she said. "Those are the memories that I want."

But Lattimore points out that something has to give in the caretaking formula in general, where parents are often choosing between paying for care or staying home from work. Lattimore remembers trying to "climb the corporate ladder" while she was raising her four and said she wanted to try to spare her daughter the same dilemma.

"When my daughter got ready to start her family, I just didn't want her to go through that," she said. "I wanted her to have the balance. … If work-life balance exists for somebody, I wanted it for my daughter."

World.title: Head of European Investment Bank eyes Canada opportunities as Carney pushes EU ties
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The president of the European Union's investment bank says "the time is ripe" to deepen its co-operation with Canada by exploring how to finance Canadian projects — comments that come as Prime Minister Mark Carney pushes for more EU ties.

"We haven't been very active in Canada until now," said Nadia Calviño, the president of the European Investment Bank (EIB) in an exclusive interview on Rosemary Barton Live that aired Sunday morning.

But Calviño, who is visiting Canada to meet with various federal ministers, said her trip "clearly shows that in Europe, we put our money where our mouth is."

Calviño said the first area where there's a shared interest between the two parties is critical minerals. She also said the EIB is exploring how to get a framework agreement that would enable the bank to invest in critical minerals "and beyond."

"I think the key idea is one that Prime Minister Carney is sharing, which is strategic alliance and strategic co-operation," Calviño told host Rosemary Barton. "We speak the same language, we share the same values."

WATCH | Carney lays out broad strokes of his plan: Carney pledges deeper ties in EU speech but offers few details | Duration closed caption 3:07 A day after the door was opened for Canada to become an 'associate member' of the EU, Prime Minister Mark Carney delivered a speech at the European Parliament pledging deeper ties with Europe, though questions remain on what that includes.

Asked whether the EIB could invest in future oil and liquid natural gas pipelines, Calviño said the bank has "consolidated its role as the climate bank" and is "much more interested in new technologies" and green energy generation.

Calviño's comments come on the heels of Carney's Canada Investment Summit, which the federal government says attracted nearly $500 billion in new investment into Canadian businesses and infrastructure.

Plus, Carney is pushing Canada to deepen its ties to the European Union, though exact details of his vision are unclear.

On Thursday, Carney addressed the European Parliament and outlined a goal to secure "seamless, digital" trade in non-agricultural goods and services, co-operation on computing capacity and AI safety protocols, and exploring an integrated market for financial services.

However, opposition parties have been questioning whether Canada will need to make concessions, particularly after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Canada could become an EU "associate member" — a term that is not a legal designation.

Calviño said she wouldn't waste any time on "the process, the procedures, the names [and] the headlines" and said the EIB is "a very practical organization."

Prime Minister Mark Carney addresses the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, on Thursday. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

"We do investments. We put money. We support projects. We make things happen. And I think that's the approach of Canada, which very much resonates with the way we look at things," Calviño said. "I would say the sky's the limit."

In an interview with CBC's The House this week, Canada's ambassador-designate to the EU, Jonathan Wilkinson, ruled out Canada paying directly into the 27-nation bloc's budget.

"It's a number of specific areas that the prime minister has described as strategic capabilities — those areas where countries really need to have access to certain things that enable them to actually make sovereign decisions," said Wilkinson, who will be sworn in to his new role in the coming weeks.

Latvian MEP weighs in

Rihards Kols, a Latvian member of the European Parliament, told Barton in a separate interview that Carney's EU push is a "geopolitical necessity in these times that we live in."

"Democracies around the world, for the past two decades, are in decline. We're a minority, I would say. We need to stick together," Kols said.

But Kols does have questions about what other Canadian politicians think of the idea, and where they think the Canada-EU relationship is headed.

WATCH | Some urge pumping the brakes on Canada-EU alliance: EU offers Canada 'associate member' status but some urge pumping the brakes | Duration closed caption 3:49 European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen offered Canada a pathway to 'associate membership' status in the 27-member bloc during Prime Minister Mark Carney's alliance-building visit, but Canadian officials say they're not ready to go that far yet.

"We generally understand this is a natural partnership, and we should not delay any of these co-operation elements to bring the EU closer with Canada across the front," Kols said.

Other European politicians who've spoken to CBC News over the past few days have expressed support for Carney's idea, but some worry a formal arrangement will create protracted talks that amount to little progress.

Instead, those European politicians argue the focus should be doing the work of deepening ties — in areas like diplomacy, culture and academic research — rather than debating a formal process.

There's also the question of U.S. President Donald Trump, who has called the Canada-EU idea "laughable." He's also threatened new tariffs if he deems the arrangement to be a "hostile act."

In his speech, Carney said Canada is not "proposing a third bloc in order to become a great power — only with better manners."

WATCH | Trump says closer Canada-EU co-operation is 'laughable': Trump says closer Canada-EU co-operation is 'laughable' | Duration closed caption 0:25 U.S. President Donald Trump threatened the European Union with 'very serious tariffs' or to 'stop trading' if it makes a trade deal with Canada 'with bad intentions.'

"We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so no one, no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law."

Calviño said it's difficult to say whether Canada and the EU would be pushing for closer ties if Trump's trade war had not occurred, but today there's a strong determination from global partners to move forward.

"Everybody's looking at Europe and wants to join forces with Europe because we want to continue to build a world based on mutual respect, on win-win partnerships," Calviño said.

"We are very strong, the European Union is strong, Canada is strong. But we are stronger together."

World.title: Kerry-Lynne Findlay resigns as leader of the B.C. Conservative party
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Kerry-Lynne Findlay has resigned as the leader of B.C.'s Conservative Party effective immediately.

Findlay made the announcement in a social media post Sunday afternoon.

"This was not an easy decision, but I believe it is the right one for our movement and our province," she wrote.

It comes amidst speculation of a snap election and a time of tumult for the Conservative caucus. MLA Linda Hepner left the caucus just hours earlier, joining a growing group of MLAs the party has lost since Findlay was elected leader.

In her statement, Findlay said too much time and attention has been "consumed by internal conflict" and has been "spent fighting amongst ourselves."

But she said the voice of the party’s members — those who elected her leader in May — matters.

"No political party can ask its members for their time, their money, and their trust and then decide their voices only matter when they produce the outcome some people want," it said.

WATCH | B.C. Conservative Party leader resigns: Kerry-Lynne Findlay resigns as leader of the B.C. Conservative Party | Duration closed caption 4:57 Kerry-Lynne Findlay has announced she's stepping down as leader of the B.C. Conservative Party. Her resignation comes less than four months after she took over as leader, and on the same day former Surrey, B.C., mayor Linda Hepner resigned from caucus. The party has lost 14 MLAs since Findlay became leader in May.

She also wrote she has been subject to attacks on her character and threats.

"My children and grandchildren see what is written and said. My family lives with the consequences of decisions I make in public life," she said.

Findlay says she will remain the Conservative candidate in the Abbotsford-Mission byelection set for Sept. 26.

It’s unclear who will lead the party in the interim.



Former party president Aisha Estey says she believes there is a leader who can unite the various factions within the big tent party.

"I think uniting conservatives is inherently very difficult. It needs to be somebody that everybody ultimately respects, and your character and your decision making," she said.



John Rustad, who was also ousted as leader last year after a caucus revolt, says it's a difficult balance.

"It reminds me of the three bears story, you gotta find something that's just right. When I built this party, I made it a very big tent. And obviously that comes [with] challenges when you have a very big tent, because you have people from various perspectives vying for control," he explained.



Claire Rattée, who was among the MLAs who called on Findlay to resign, says her focus now is on the future.



"We're prepared to do the hard work of putting our team back together and ensuring that we're ready to take (the NDP) on in the next election," she said.

There has been widespread speculation that Premier David Eby may call a snap election in the coming days, disrupting municipal elections — set for Oct. 17 — with a provincial vote.



However, it's unclear how Findlay's resignation changes the political calculus.



Hamish Telford, a political scientist at the University of the Fraser Valley, says it would be unusual for a government to call an election when the official opposition has no leader.

"I imagine the NDP war room is in full crisis mode now trying to figure out what to do," he said.

Party turmoil

The resignation comes as Findlay had been facing an internal revolt among her MLAs.

Since she was elected, Findlay has faced criticism from some party members over some of her staff hirings, which several of the departed MLAs said brought the party further to the far-right.

On Friday, three MLAs were ousted, including former party leader John Rustad.

Last month, Reann Gasper also resigned as Abbotsford-Mission MLA to open a path for Findlay to win a seat in the legislature through a byelection.

Ten MLAs have quit the B.C. Conservative caucus since mid-August — the latest being Hepner. Her exit brings the total number of MLAs to leave the B.C. Conservative Party caucus to 14.

Eight of those MLAs on Friday joined CentreBC, which they say will provide a political option to those who felt politically homeless.

At a tense caucus meeting Wednesday night, Rustad and Rattée called on Findlay to resign.

She was defiant Thursday morning, saying in her Union of B.C. Municipalities speech: "I’m not going anywhere."

On Thursday night, Findlay fired three MLAs: Rustad, Rattée and Trevor Halford.

Rustad said he was fired via a late night text message, which Findlay rescinded 15 minutes later. By Friday morning, he was fired again.

Findlay also recently denied having any knowledge about a private investigator allegedly hired by her close political ally, Elaine Allan, who served as party executive director for less than a month in August.

World.title: Long-standing Winnipeg hotel reconnects with 'piece of history' after nearly 120 years
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A long-standing Winnipeg hotel has reconnected with a piece of its history, after an Alberta-based antiques dealer stumbled upon a cash register made for the business more than a century ago.

The register, built by National Cash Register Company in 1907, is engraved with the name of the Northern Hotel and was once a critical part of the Main Street establishment's daily operations.

"It's kind of neat. It's all mechanical — and the fact that it still works, a lot of it is just a testament to the craftsmanship that they did 120 years ago," said hotel owner Keith Horn.

"It's a piece of history."

Horn purchased the register in late July from Franz Giesen, co-owner of Frantic4tiques — an online business based in Mannville, Alta., east of Edmonton.

Giesen said he spotted the cash register for sale on Facebook Marketplace and made the nearly 1,200-kilometre drive from Mannville to Winnipeg to collect it.

"I thought on the way in, I'm like, how cool would it be if I was able to reconnect this cash register with the owner of the Northern Hotel? So then, when I got to the city, I made the phone call," Giesen said.

Franz Giesen, co-owner of Frantic4tiques, found this mechanical cash register that was built in 1907 for the Northern Hotel in Winnipeg. The Alberta-based antiques collector sold it to the hotel's new owner in July. (Tyson Koschik/CBC)

Horn said he was initially skeptical about buying the antique, but came around to the idea after learning more about it.

Giesen used a serial number stamped on the register to determine when it was built. He believes the machine, which is covered in embellishments, was cast in metal.

It weighs more than nine kilograms and still makes a satisfying ring when punching in the numbers, which range in value from five cents to $10.

"Just wondering what, back in 1907, was $10, when rooms back then [only cost] up to $2," Horn said, smiling.

The antique mechanical cash register is engraved with the name of the Northern Hotel. (Tyson Koschik/CBC)

"I guess they were very hopeful."

This particular model included specialty buttons that allowed the hotel to track how many meals or cigars it sold, and was capable of keeping a running total of the day's earnings.

While the exact history of the cash register is murky, but it's nearly as old as the hotel itself, which was built in 1906. Giesen learned the register wound up in the care of a former radio repair shop a short distance from the Northern Hotel sometime in the 1950s.

It was then inherited by the daughter of the radio shop owner, who kept it in her basement until he bought it from her, said Giesen.

"Everything from back then is just out of this world, right? Things were made to last, nothing was made to be tossed away. There is a reason why these things still exist," he said.

Horn said he plans to clean the register, and then put it on display inside the Northern Hotel.

World.title: Patrick Clancy gives first TV interview after Lindsay Clancy mistrial
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This article contains details about violence against children and attempted suicide.

Lindsay Clancy's former husband said he forgave her for killing their three young children in his first televised interview Sunday on CBS News' 60 Minutes since a jury deadlocked in her trial for the children's deaths.

Patrick Clancy talked about his grief, saying he battled suicidal thoughts after the killings and experienced a panic attack while testifying at Lindsay Clancy's trial when attorneys played to jurors his 911 call to report the children's deaths.

At trial, the anguished 911 call included Patrick howling and crying after he discovered the bodies of his children in the family's basement as a confused dispatcher repeatedly asked what happened.

Earlier this month, 11 of 12 jurors were ready to clear Lindsay Clancy of criminal responsibility, with the majority feeling that the Massachusetts mom was in the grip of a rare condition called postpartum psychosis when she strangled her kids in 2023.

But a lone juror sided with prosecutors, who had argued that Clancy knew what she was doing. The deadlock forced a judge to declare a mistrial on Sept. 4.

WATCH | What is postpartum psychosis?: The Lindsay Clancy trial and maternal mental health | Duration 2:13 The trial of Massachusetts mother Lindsay Clancy has put a spotlight on maternal mental health, which some medical experts say may be the only positive outcome in the tragic case. Her legal team argues that she shouldn't be held criminally responsible for the murder of her three children because she was suffering from bipolar disorder and postpartum psychosis.

Clancy says son died in his arms

Patrick Clancy also said his youngest son, Callan, didn't die immediately that fatal day on Jan. 24, 2023, but lived four more days before dying in his arms.

While holding his 8-month-old son, he said he typed with one hand tributes to his other children, Cora, 5, and Dawson, 2, and also forgave his wife.

"I saw headlines that say 'killer mom' and 'baby murderer monster' and none of them were accurate," he said. "I believed that it was her mental illness that caused that."

Calls conspiracy theories a 'distraction'

Clancy said stress from the murders and trial took a toll.

"There was a time I didn't think I would live to see my 35th birthday, and I was completely fine with it," he said.

He also addressed social media conspiracy theories surrounding the case, which have included unfounded claims he was connected to the death of his children.

"It's deeply harmful to the legacy of my children," Patrick Clancy said. "It is a huge distraction from what really matters here, which is perinatal mental health."

His new wife, Dr. Rachel Danis, joined him in the interview, describing Patrick Clancy as the "most selfless and supportive partner."

"I don't understand how the story has been so twisted," she said. "I was just a girl that met a guy running in Central Park on a really cold Saturday. And I don't think there's anything wrong with that."

If you or someone you know is struggling, here's where to look for help:

World.title: Canada's 'Railway City' wants passenger trains back. Like in much of the country, it's not so simple
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Wil Zufelt stands among the remnants of what was once one of Canada's busiest railway hub. He says St. Thomas, Ont., needs to save what's left of its railway history before more of it disappears.

To an outsider, the 3.2-hectare sea of grass surrounding the Elgin County Railway Museum in the heart of St. Thomas, Ont., might look like an urban park. That's not what Wil Zufelt sees.

To him, it's an enormous open wound.

"You say green space," he said. "We're actually sitting in the middle of a brownfield site that was left behind from the railroads."

Built in 1913, the hulking red-brick building was once the Michigan Central Railway Locomotive Shops, where locomotives were maintained and overhauled by a staff of 400 workers. It's one of three survivors of a sprawling railway complex that once had 112 buildings.

The old building is now a museum, but it can't welcome visitors. It's literally crumbling. The city engineer ordered it closed after finding its walls were bowing and its ceiling was unsafe.

'Pay attention to what we're losing'

"People need to wake up," Zufelt said. "Pay attention to what we're losing."

The former Michigan Central Railway Locomotive Shops sit on 3.2 hectares of former railway lands in St. Thomas, Ont. Built in 1913, the building is now home to the Elgin County Railway Museum, but is closed to the public because of structural concerns. (Patrick Morrell/CBC News)

Zufelt heads Railworks, the organization behind three of St. Thomas's surviving railway landmarks. He's launching a campaign to raise $8 million to save and restore the former locomotive shops.

The goal is to turn the old locomotive shops into not just a museum, but an active gathering place at the centre of a redeveloped downtown.

"I want it to be more than alive. I want it to be the centre of St. Thomas," he said. "That's what success is, is putting a heartbeat back in the core and then you have your arteries and everything pumps out from the middle."

By 1914, eight railways converged on St. Thomas, bringing more than 100 trains through the southwestern Ontario city every day. Its location made it a major hub for American rail traffic between Detroit and Buffalo and between New York and Chicago. The cross-border connection was so important, at one point, St. Thomas even had a U.S. consulate.

Today, the community that calls itself the "Railway City" has no rail connection at all.

Tracks that snake everywhere and nowhere

The railways are long gone, but their remains are scattered across the city — empty lots filled with rubble from where railway buildings once stood, abandoned shunting yards, railway spikes that turn up like seashells on a beach and tracks that snake everywhere and nowhere.

The old London to Port Stanley Railway runs past a restored station in St. Thomas before it abruptly ends — disappearing into the grass of a residential neighbourhood.

A section of railway track ends abruptly in St. Thomas, Ont., where a missing connection has been under a federal order to be restored by CN since 1990. Across Canada, communities looking to revive passenger rail are confronting what remains after decades of decline. (Colin Butler/CBC News)

The missing connection was the subject of a 1990 federal transport order requiring CN to replace the missing diamond at its own expense once the line reached CN tracks. But the physical connection was never completed.

Today, part of the former route is blocked by a parking lot enclosed by a fence.

The Canadian Transport Agency told CBC News the order remains in effect and CN's obligation would still apply if the physical connection were made.

CN did not respond to a request for comment by publication time.

What St. Thomas tells us about Canada's railways

St. Thomas is an unusually stark example of what happened in communities across Canada as the railway era receded, according to Thomas Blampied, a historian who studied Canada's railway history at the University of Toronto.

The former Canada Southern Railway Station in St. Thomas, Ont., is one of the surviving landmarks from an era when the city was one of Canada's busiest railway centres. The 1873 building is one of three remaining historic railway buildings in a community that once had 112. (Colin Butler/CBC News)

"Cars started to eat away at passenger revenue from railways and trucks started to take some of the freight traffic," he said.

As passengers moved to cars and freight moved to trucks, railways abandoned increasingly unprofitable routes. They didn't simply stop running trains. Much of the infrastructure was removed with them.

"Do we keep the infrastructure — so the track, all the signals, all the crossing warnings — do we keep it all intact?" Blampied said. "Increasingly, the answer was no."

In some cases, the rails were sold for scrap, in many cases, he said, "it made economic sense to completely withdraw."

But even where the railway lines survived, the network changed.

Canada looks to bring passenger rail back

Anthony Perl, a transportation policy expert at Simon Fraser University, said railways removed passing tracks and other infrastructure once passenger trains disappeared, reshaping the network around the needs of freight.

The Northern Ontario tourism sector are hoping the return of the Northlander passenger train will help bring more people to the region. (Submitted by Ontario Northland)

"We had a great streamlining, or right-sizing, or value engineering, pick your term — of the national rail infrastructure in Canada as passenger trains went away," Perl said. "To optimize it for long, slow freight trains."

He said that matters now because Canada is trying to put passenger trains back on a network that, in many places, was either removed or rebuilt for another purpose.

In Ontario, the province is preparing to restore Northlander passenger service between Toronto and northeastern Ontario, more than a decade after it was cancelled. The federal government meanwhile, is developing Alto, a new high-speed passenger railway between Toronto and Quebec City that would run largely on its own tracks.

Other communities are pushing for passenger rail to return, including on Vancouver Island, in Alberta between Calgary and Banff and in Cape Breton.

The power of owning the tracks

But Canada's railways have something airlines and trucking companies don't: control over the infrastructure they use.

Abandoned freight cars sit on overgrown tracks in a former shunting yard in St. Thomas, Ont., one of the remnants of the city's once sprawling railway network that linked major North American cities. (Colin Butler/CBC News)

"No one is going to build an alternative set of rails across this country under any circumstances," Perl said. "That's why they make the call on whether to put in or take out tracks in particular places."

In St. Thomas, CN has yet to restore the missing connection between London and Port Stanley.

"Even when the Canadian Transportation Agency orders them to do something they don't want to do," he said, "it can take quite a while, if ever, that they will go along with it because they have the ownership of that infrastructure."

Perl argues that kind of power has deep roots in the railway business and points to language the industry has given us.

"To 'railroad someone' is to take advantage and treat someone unfairly or unjustly," he said. "You don't see that with too many other industries."

World.title: ICE agent shot and wounded man in Austin, Texas, officials say
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and wounded a man on Sunday afternoon in the Texas capital of Austin, local officials said, where anti-ICE protesters quickly gathered at the scene.

The man was in serious but stable condition at a hospital after being shot once in the torso on Austin's north side, Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said at a news conference with the city's mayor and other officials present.

The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, didn't immediately respond to requests for details.

Austin police officers were not involved in the operation or the shooting, which occurred after a traffic stop, Davis told reporters.

Austin Mayor Kirk Watson, a Democrat, said he wants the city's police department to be involved in the investigation so it can provide "clear, third-party eyes" in the process. Watson said he does not think it would be appropriate for ICE to conduct the investigation on its own.

People protest where local authorities say a U.S. ICE officer shot and wounded a man Sunday. (Joel Angel Juarez/The Associated Press)

Austin residents have "a right to feel safe in their city," Watson said. A proper investigation will only enhance credibility, he added.

Davis said there were not many facts she could provide so soon after the shooting, but added the police department's special investigation unit was at the scene. She said she did not yet know the nationality of the person who was shot.

A dark blue Toyota Corolla was parked under an overpass with damage to its passenger-side door and what appeared to be bullet holes, local media reported.

A police officer faces demonstrators at the scene. (Nuri Vallbona/Reuters)

A large law enforcement presence was at the scene, along with a crowd of onlookers, along with a crowd of about a hundred protesters. Some demonstrators cursed at police officers holding riot shields, while others yelled out as passing cars honked in support of the protest. One man held a sign saying, "Nobody is safe" and, on the other side, "ICE Nazi."

Asked if Austin authorities knew where the involved federal agent is, given that agents have left states after previous shootings nationwide, the mayor said: "We do not know that. But my hope would be that, an agent that's involved in an officer-involved shooting would not leave the city. Certainly not leave the state."

'This horror has come to our doorstep'

U.S. Rep. Greg Casar, a Democrat representing parts of Austin, called for transparency as the shooting is investigated.

"It is awful that this horror has come to our doorstep," Casar said to reporters. "For Austin to be safe, ICE should end its surge here."

The shooting comes as ICE surges enforcement across the country this summer, producing more than 50,000 arrests a month for the first time in its history in July and August.

In July, an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, of Houston, after federal agents driving unmarked vehicles pursued him while he was taking his construction crew to a job site.

Also in July, 25-year-old Johan Sebastián, a Colombian man, was shot by an ICE officer in Maine. The officer is an Army veteran who has struggled with serious mental health issues since early childhood and never should have been given a badge and gun to patrol American streets, several of his close relatives told The Associated Press.

Bystanders comfort each other while looking over police tape at the scene of the alleged shooting. (Shahrzad Rasekh/Reuters)

The shootings come amid a Trump administration push to carry out mass deportations. While the administration is no longer cracking down on individual cities, arrests are still occurring.

The administration's enforcement efforts were widely condemned last winter after the killings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minnesota.

World.title: 'Agent Layla': Sex assault victim turned secret agent brings her abuser to justice
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This article may affect those who have experienced​ ​​​sexual violence or know someone affected by it.

On a Friday morning in 2021, just a couple of days before Halloween, Vienna Luke zipped up an oversized puffer jacket with a big hood, and put on sunglasses to hide her face.

In a SUV outside her home, plainclothes RCMP officers waited to whisk her away on a secret mission — a face-to-face meeting with the man responsible for the worst night of her life.

Luke, a fitness instructor and mother of two children, was the key undercover agent in an RCMP operation that — if successful — could lead to the rarest of outcomes: a criminal conviction in a sexual assault that had occurred 14 years earlier.

If Luke failed, her case and the truth about what had happened that night would almost surely be lost to time.

The police referred to Luke using a code name: Agent Layla.

'The whole thing really was conditional on me,' said Vienna Luke. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

CBC has obtained the surreptitious recording of that mission. It shows an extremely rare instance of RCMP turning the victim into an agent in her own case.

The RCMP sergeant who led the investigation says it’s an approach that is almost never tried — especially in sexual assault cases.

"For the victim to have the strength, and the investigative team [to have the] determination[...] is almost unheard of," said Sgt. Joëlle LaChance.

Facing the man who assaulted her, her estranged brother-in-law, "Agent Layla" presses him for answers over the course of 70 minutes. Luke ultimately elicits a confession that surpassed even the highest hopes of the RCMP team gathered in a nearby hotel room listening in over a wire. The breakthrough was so moving that it brought tears to a hardened undercover officer accustomed to working with drug dealers and murderers.

"She literally took her life back in her hands," said one of the officers from the undercover unit, working with LaChance.

"There wasn’t a dry eye in that room," said LaChance.

Police hid a microphone in a purse Vienna Luke carried into a meeting with the man who assaulted her. The police set up for the face-to-face meeting in a hotel room above a Vancouver International Airport lounge. (Shawnessy Luke)

That recording — along with interviews from Luke, her middle sister Shawnessy Luke, and the police officers involved in the sting — is part of a new four-part CBC podcast called Personally: Agent Layla.

The podcast details how Luke managed to get the truth, put the man who assaulted her behind bars, and begin to heal from an incident that left her traumatized, detached from her own body, and at odds with members of her family who at times failed to take her side.

(Chloe Cushman)

A night with only one memory

At 20 years old, Luke was living at home with her family in the Vancouver suburbs after attending a Bible school overseas. Her life had been sheltered; she says she had never been kissed, or even held hands with a man.

While she contemplated her future, she decided to move in with her eldest sister, brother-in-law and their sons in the small B.C. town of Fort St. John — a 14-hour drive north from where she was raised.

The welcome to Fort St. John sign at Mile 47 of the Alaska Highway in northeastern B.C. (Matt Preprost/CBC)

Her brother-in-law, Justin Sewell, was a respected veterinarian who was active in a local Christian church. Sewell was 11 years older than her and he had been a trusted member of the family since Luke was a child.

During a week when Luke's sister and nephews were out of town, Sewell proposed a plan. He suggested she get drunk for the first time at home with him, in what he described as a "safe place."

Luke says she had heard of another Christian girl who had done something similar to experiment for the first time with drinking, so she went along with his idea.

WARNING: This story contains graphic details about sexual abuse.

According to testimony presented in court and extensive interviews conducted by the CBC, Luke only sipped the cocktails he made — one of them a Kahlua-based "Brown Cow."

As she and Sewell danced to country music in the living room, Luke remembers her legs buckling. As the world went black, she felt nauseous and thought to herself that drinking alcohol didn’t seem so fun after all.

Aloud, she spoke a phrase that only drives home how naive she was to what was about to happen.

"I just love Jesus," she said. "I just love Jesus. And then I was out."

For Luke, everything about the rest of that night is blank, except for one memory that would both torment her and propel her to seek accountability in the almost two decades to come: a brief moment when she says she awoke mostly naked in her bed.

"I was looking at myself, from above, to my brother-in-law taking off my underwear," she said.

'We gotta tell mom and dad'

In the aftermath of that horrible evening, Luke says she tried to "shelve" what happened. For months, she fought what she described as a war between her body that remembered, and her brain trying to forget.

She moved back home to her parents’ home near Vancouver and didn’t come face-to-face with Sewell again until half-a-year later at Christmas when the entire family went to Florida for a cruise. But when they said their goodbyes at the airport, her middle sister, Shawnessy Luke, noticed something was off.

"I remember it like it was yesterday," Shawnessy Luke said. "The way he hugged her. And I think that’s strange. That’s prolonged. And I knew something was going on."

Shawnessy Luke believed her sister, Vienna, when she began to open up. (Allison Luke)

Shawnessy Luke describes herself as a person with great intuition and "like a dog with a bone." She waited until she and Vienna Luke got back to their parents' home to ask questions. She was doing her laundry in the family’s narrow utility room when she insisted that her sister explain.

"She definitely pulled it out of me," said Vienna Luke. "I did not volunteer."

Vienna Luke told her sister what happened in the days leading up to the drinking game, facts that were accepted in court: How Sewell had held her hand, how he called her up from her basement bedroom to watch a lightning storm and then massaged her back, and how he told her he loved her.

Then she shared how Sewell proposed she get drunk, and how she couldn’t remember much more than that.

"In my moral compass brain, the minute I heard those things, I was like, I don’t need to know anymore, I believe you," said Shawnessy Luke. "We’ve got to tell someone about this because [...] whatever happened to you [...] was wrong."

Shawnessy Luke says she insisted they tell their mom and dad.

Middle sister Shawnessy Luke has stuck by her sister's side through all the steps of the investigation. 'I'm here in support of her going through this process. That's my goal. That's the only reason I'm here.' (Ben Nelms/CBC)

The night in question had happened in June 2007, about 10 years before the #MeToo social movement. As Vienna Luke told her parents about Sewell holding her hand and massaging her back, she stopped short of sharing the most damning memory of all — that she woke up to Sewell removing her underwear. She felt like her parents didn’t know how to handle what she was saying, and didn't have the vocabulary at the time to talk about sexual assault.

"I knew that I couldn’t share more," she said.

Her father called Sewell right away. She didn’t overhear their conversation, but she recalls her father handed her the phone and she found herself suddenly on the line with Sewell.

Vienna Luke pleaded with Sewell to tell his wife what had happened, hoping her oldest sister would take her side. She still doesn’t know if that happened, only that her oldest sister has continued to stand by her husband and is still married to him today.

Her parents declined to be interviewed for this story. In a victim impact statement filed in court, they wrote: "Our effort to uncover the full story was unsuccessful. Lacking information and clarity, we had no path forward. We felt uneasy about what we knew, but did not pursue this matter further."

Years of numbing

In the years that followed, the Luke family struggled with the divide created by that night: Vienna’s oldest sister and Sewell on one side, Shawnessy and Vienna Luke on the other, and their parents trying to walk a line between all three of their daughters.

"It was easier to take Justin for his word," Vienna Luke said. "He was the one that knew what happened. He got to write the story."

Vienna Luke in 2014, seven years after the horrible night. 'I was just a robot,' she said. 'I was going through the motions of what I thought I was supposed to be doing.' (Allison White)

With no clarity about what had actually happened and that one horrific memory of him removing her underwear replaying in her head, Luke says she spent years feeling like a robot trying to numb her pain.

She also moved out of her parents' house and moved to Vancouver, got a job, and met a man who she credits for showing her how to love herself again.

When they started a family, Luke says something inside her started to shift. She knew she’d have to tell her children the truth someday, and something about birth reconnected her to her body.

"My body wasn’t just laboring," she wrote in her journal. "[It was] waking up."

Twelve years after the assault, and weeks after she delivered her second child, Luke called up her sister Shawnessy.

"Hey, I’m ready to deal with this," she said.

So the two sisters made a list.

The sister detectives

Together, they wrote down all the names of people they suspected had soured on Sewell after he had disclosed to his wife and friends two extramarital affairs five years earlier.

Shawnessy Luke's first call was to one of those ex-lovers, a female veterinarian who had worked at Sewell's clinic.

Justin Sewell's veterinarian clinic in Fort St. John, B.C. (Matt Preprost)

In a recording of that phone call shared with CBC and in court testimony, the woman said she and Sewell were discussing previous sexual experiences when he said something shocking.

"So what he told me was that he put ketamine in [Vienna’s] drinks," the ex-lover revealed during a phone call Shawnessy Luke recorded. "But he didn’t know how much was enough to like, make her forget."

The sisters say this new information validated a hunch they had come to believe: that Vienna Luke had been drugged.

It also gave her a little piece of evidence to march into the Vancouver Police Department and report.

'I do my job for the victims'

Vienna Luke's file was transferred up to the small RCMP detachment in Fort St. John. Against all odds, it landed on the desk of Sgt. Joëlle LaChance, a female officer with a special commitment to cases that many officers would simply dismiss as too hard and too old.

"My whole life I have been a champion for the underdog," she said. "Being able to stand up for the victim … it's why I do my job."

'Being able to stand up for the victim — it's why I do my job,' said RCMP Sgt. Joëlle LaChance. (submitted by Joëlle LaChance)

LaChance said she knew Sewell — with his stellar reputation in the community, had a lot to lose. So instead of going directly to the veterinarian to question him, she called on other RCMP units for help, including the undercover unit.

Together, they hatched a plan.

Court records show Sewell had emailed Vienna Luke several times in the years since the night of the drinking game, asking her to accept that he had changed and hoping that the extended family could be together again.

Luke showed the police those emails. Together, they crafted back emails that suggested there could be a possibility for family reconciliation, but first Luke would need the whole truth and they’d have to meet face-to-face.

They pitched Sewell on a plan to fly to Vancouver to meet Luke.

Unbeknownst to Sewell, Luke would be prepared.

Vienna Luke carried this piece of paper with her into the undercover operation at YVR airport. Her notes came from training with the RCMP. (Vienna Luke)

For weeks, she trained, preparing to grill him for the facts. She spent a couple of days in a hotel room, sitting across from an undercover RCMP officer who role played with her. The officer worked to get her comfortable asking tough, direct questions, using words like "vagina" and "ejaculate" — specific terms that would be necessary for charges to be laid.

"This isn’t a trained hitman," the undercover officer said. "She’s very polite, very soft-spoken. And I knew that was exactly the opposite of what we were going to need to do."

Something changed for Vienna Luke when she became a mother. 'My firstborn, [...] my constant reminder that I am lovable,' she wrote in her journal. 'My second child, [...] you showed me a bravery I didn't know I had.' (Ben Nelms/CBC)

On the day of the sting at Vancouver airport, everyone involved held their breath. RCMP had laid the groundwork, but as soon as the tape started recording and Sewell walked in, it would be entirely up to Luke to get the truth.

For the plan to work, Luke would need to be both victim and hero. The RCMP believed it was the best chance at bringing charges. Luke knew it was her only chance to get answers.

"You think I'm exactly the same," Luke remembered thinking. "You think I'm gonna play your same little game, but we've got a new game and I'm writing it."

An extraordinary encounter – and as much truth as she’ll ever get

In the recording, Sewell sits down across from Luke and quickly tries to take control. He claims pornography and a culture that objectifies women is part of why he assaulted her that night.

"Okay, but you’re not actually telling me what happened," Luke replies. "Let’s get back to the night and what actually … happened."

The undercover officer who had spent time coaching Luke for this moment felt proud.

"Take control of that conversation," he said in an interview while listening back to the recording. "Don’t just accept a two-minute fluffy bullshit answer."

An excerpt from the transcript submitted in court of the surreptitious recording between Vienna Luke (VL) and Justin Sewell (JS). (CBC)

Luke persists, peppering Sewell with questions seeking specific details, seemingly undeterred by the fact she’s learning this information about the worst night of her life for the first time.

On tape, Sewell confesses to drugging her, removing her clothing, masturbating and ejaculating twice on her body, and taking 30 photos, including ones where he is spooning her naked body and one where his penis is near her face.

As Luke prepares to wrap up, she lobs an open ended question.

"Is there anything that I’m not asking?" Luke said.

"No reason for me to disclose this. But I took pictures of you at other times," Sewell replied.

His response allowed the RCMP to recommend another charge, this one for voyeurism.

A rare conviction in a historic sexual assault

On the morning of April 26, 2022, Fort St. John RCMP arrested Sewell as he left his home for work.

LaChance said this case was a big deal for the small Fort St. John RCMP detachment. 'People didn't believe we could do it,' she said. 'I believed with Vienna as the agent that we could do it because she was showing the strength and wanting to have justice.' (Tom Summer/CBC)

Sewell pleaded guilty to one count of sexual assault and two counts of voyeurism — one for the photos he took of her the night he assaulted her and one for times he had watched her through her bedroom window. Crown agreed to stay a charge of administering a drug with intent to commit a sexual assault.

In the courtroom, Luke’s mother, father, and Sewell’s supporters listened to the recording from the airport.

A provincial court judge sentenced Sewell to house arrest. Crown appealed and the Court of Appeal judges determined the lower court judge had overstated the mitigating fact of Sewell’s confession.

They issued a sentence of 33 months less a day in prison for his crimes.

Luke asked the court to remove the publication ban on her name — something that is standard in cases of sexual assault to protect the victim’s identity.

As she began to tell friends and acquaintances her whole story, that she was the unnamed victim, she says she realized how important it was to her that she could also say she was the secret agent.

Vienna Luke is telling her story for the first time publicly in a new CBC Podcast called Agent Layla. (Vienna Luke)

"It took this … experiment of the police saying, 'Hey, how about you go undercover as yourself' for me to realize, whoa, look at the advocate I can be for myself," she said.

"I was Agent Layla. That's me."

The CBC podcast Personally: Agent Layla is available wherever you get your podcasts.

World.title: The tangled what-ifs of Alberta separation — from trade and treaties to currency and disaster costs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It’s the big things that might spring to mind first when pondering the consequences of Alberta separation — the potential impacts to the gross domestic product, jobs, wages, debt and such.

This week’s major report by the University of Calgary’s School of Public Policy laid out these figures in sharp relief, with a series of outcomes ranging from modest long-term benefits to massive long-range detriments (and short-term pain in any scenario).

But beyond the headline figures contained in the government-commissioned summary report, we find a series of the U of C academics’ technical papers.

They underpin predictions of an independent Alberta’s debt load and potential job losses by diving into the many complex factors a breakaway republic named Alberta would have to contend with.

When you form a whole new country from the rib of an existing one, there’s a tonne to consider, from tariffs and multilateral agreements to currency, interest rates and treaties — both international and Indigenous.

Or even seemingly smaller (but still billion-dollar) factors, like public-sector pension obligations, and who pays for the aftermath of major floods and wildfires, the kinds of disasters Alberta knows all too well.

So without further ado, here’s a glimpse at the report’s analysis of some of the other challenges of Alberta independence, in the event that the public’s current pro-unity majority shifts dramatically, and opts for independence in two successive referendums, beginning with the one on Oct. 19.

Trade-offs

Owing largely to oil pipelines, Alberta’s trade south of the border is more valuable than its exports to the rest of Canada, the School of Public Policy report notes.

Because of that, the authors suggest it may be most expedient for a new country to strike a direct deal with Washington, rather than try to inject itself into the already rocky talks around the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA).

However, it notes that while the current U.S. administration might offer terms that are beneficial to an oil-producing neighbour, the report adds: “As much as the U.S. depends on Alberta oil and gas exports, Alberta depends on making those exports more, and the U.S. administration knows this.”

Danielle Smith and Donald Trump: future trade dealmakers? (Danielle Smith/X)

Meanwhile, joining CUSMA — does it become CUSAMA? ACUSMA has a certain ring — would provide largely tariff-free access to its big customers, including Mexico. “However, the process could be lengthy,” the report states, a familiar refrain throughout.

Also, ratification to Alberta’s benefit might run into pushback from Democrats in the U.S. Congress, given their historic opposition to the Keystone XL pipeline.

And while Alberta separatists might be wary of global bodies like the World Economic Forum (WEF) and World Health Organization (WHO), they’re more likely to need to get their new country into the World Trade Organization (WTO), World Bank and International Monetary Fund.

“Without membership in these institutions, a separate Alberta would not receive most-favoured-nation tariff rates, making it subject to the same tariff rate as, for example, North Korea,” the report says.

And there’s a wait for that.

The fastest any country has ever gotten into the WTO is three years, and five to seven is more like the “best-case-no-active-opposition” estimate, the report says.

But will there be no opposition? Other countries with their own secessionist movements might be wary of offering a quick embrace of a breakaway ex-Canadian republic.

And domestically, even if there’s a deal reached between Alberta and Canada, the regulatory differences and hiccups of interprovincial trade could get exacerbated when there’s a harder border. There’s a risk “the border ‘thickens’ considerably, in similar fashion to the U.K.’s border with [European Union] countries after Brexit,” the report says.

Money talks

The report notes that the currency question was a major preoccupation during separation debates in Scotland and Quebec.

The dilemma is massive: stick with the loonie, try a Euro-style shared dollar, or strike off with a new Alberta form of money?

While sticking with the Canadian dollar is easiest and quickest, it keeps Ottawa in control.

“A separate Alberta would still be subject to Bank of Canada interest-rate decisions and it would remain reliant on fiscal policy to deal with Alberta-specific shock,” the report states.

A separate Alberta could choose to keep this coin as its legal currency, but it keeps monetary policy control in Ottawa if that's the case. (Paul Chiasson/The Canadian Press)

An Alberta-Canada monetary union, like in Europe, might most resemble the current situation. “It is not obvious, however, that the RoC [rest of Canada] would see great benefit to entering a formal monetary union with a separate Alberta.”

Alberta bucks as legal tender? It’s the most common solution for new nations, the report states.

“The exchange rate for a separate Alberta would likely be quite volatile, as it would largely reflect the price of oil,” it says. “This could cause problems for non-commodity exporters, who would see their export revenues become more volatile in domestic currency terms.”

Of high interest

On top of the big debt Alberta would assume as its share of Canada’s current federal liabilities, the cost of servicing that debt would be greater. Alberta already has to pay higher rates than Canada on interest payments, with a slightly higher credit rating than the country as a whole — a premium currently worth around 0.46 percentage points, the academics’ paper states. The volatility of the fossil fuel economy may make it tough to boost a standalone Alberta’s credit rating, but the study points out that oil-reliant Norway, which has a similarly sized population, has a solid rating — thanks in part to its massive sovereign wealth fund.

However, it adds: “a short-term increase in rates is likely unavoidable” for a new country.

Indigenous treaties

The report actually devotes little specific analysis to the question of First Nations rights, given the lack of international comparators of secession that involves Indigenous land claim matters, and the high degree of uncertainty. (It’s not even certain that courts would allow a secession referendum to go ahead in the first place, given the ruling that blocked a petition for a straight leave-or-stay question.)

Roughly one per cent of Alberta’s land mass is covered by First Nations reserves, over which Ottawa has exclusive legislative authority. But 100 per cent of the province’s territory is covered by Treaties 6, 7 and 8 — agreements to which Alberta is not a signatory. Figuring out longstanding land and rights issues in a separate Alberta would be a “focal point” of separation negotiations, the report says.

Treaty 8 Grand Chief Trevor Mercredi speaks as First Nations chiefs, band councillors and elders gather in March to call on Premier Danielle Smith to end the separation debate. (Jason Franson/The Canadian Press)

“Given the fraught history of Indigenous-settler relations, as well as those with Métis communities, negotiations over treaties, territory, rights and finances will be delicate, complex and protracted. The agreement of all actors cannot be presumed.”

That might be an understatement. Conflict seems highly predictable, given treaty grand chiefs’ vows to strenuously fight separation , and their call for police to investigate Alberta’s premier for treason for planning October’s vote.

In our defence

An independent nation must defend itself, and starting a military would be one of the biggest costs for a separated Alberta. But the $8.3 billion estimate that the School of Public Policy calculates for a transitioning province could be just the start of it.

Would Alberta want to join with Canada, the U.S. and Europe in their continental defence pact, NATO? If so, there are targets Alberta would have to meet — spending two per cent of its total annual economy on defense in the short term, and five per cent by 2035.

Alberta’s GDP is proportionately larger than Canada’s. The school’s report estimates the two per cent target would cost around $10 billion annually, while next decade’s benchmark would run about $25 billion.

That’s a lot of Alberta Air Force jets!

How's the beef?

Alberta’s lucrative agriculture and food trade — hello, cattle country — relies on the Canada Food Inspection Agency’s oversight.

A separate Alberta could hire the province’s former federal inspectors and mimic Canadian policies, but “convincing international buyers these moves are acceptable would be complicated, costly and time-intensive,” the study warns.

Given that overseas product exports would still need to ship from Canada’s coastal ports and piggyback on Canada’s existing supply chains, Alberta officials would have to persuade other countries it was safe to intermingle Alberta-inspected meat or grain with Canadian product in transport.

Would other countries, including Canada, immediately trust Alberta's food-safety inspection system? (Ben Nelms/CBC)

“In the short term, a separate Alberta would likely have to ‘rent’ inspection services from the Canadian government, adding to costs and ceding control of agriculture, processed food and livestock policy to Ottawa,” the report states.

“There are few if any gains imaginable from this scenario, only costs.”

When disaster strikes

The federal government has a long history of playing financial backstop after climate disasters like wildfire and floods. That’s meant a lot of massive cheques cut to Alberta for various non-insurable rebuilding needs.

Ottawa paid around $2.8 billion for damages in the 2013 southern Alberta floods , and ultimately $385 million for the 2016 Fort McMurray wildfire . The wildfire in Jasper National Park — that’s another dicey transfer negotiation in itself — has led to $900 million in federal payments thus far.

Only British Columbia has received more in federal Disaster Financial Assistance Arrangements than Alberta, the report notes.

“A separate Alberta would lose the ability to have such costs borne largely at the national level and would instead need to cover them entirely on its own.”
