World.title: Mexico City’s invisible recyclers fight for rights — and a share of the profits
World.content:
“Living from garbage doesn’t mean we become part of the garbage,” Soledad Mella told a packed auditorium in Iztapalapa, the Mexico City borough most burdened with the megacity’s massive waste stream. “We must dignify and defend our work. But above all, we must organize.”

The energetic grassroots recycler — referred to here in Mexico as a pepenadora — had carried her message all the way from Chile on an international tour through the region. She has carried that message from the streets and landfills of Santiago to international climate conferences and United Nations negotiations.

At Iztapalapa’s Forum on Inclusive Circular Economy, she spoke directly to Mexican pepenadores confronting a pivotal question: Will the country’s new circular economy become a route out of invisibility, or another lucrative industry that leaves them behind?

A push for legal recognition

Mexico is estimated to have some 400,000 pepenadores separating waste in landfills and open-air dumps, according to the forum’s organizers, and more than 2 million people working throughout the informal recycling economy. Many labor in precarious conditions without Social Security, stable wages or legal recognition.

The Sept. 10 forum brought grassroots recyclers together with industry representatives, officials, academics and environmentalists at the Centro Cultural Iztapalapa. The crowd filled the auditorium and spilled into the lobby, where participants exchanged contacts and examined products made from recovered materials.

The event was organized by the alcaldía, or borough, of Iztapalapa and environmental activist Arnold Ricalde, an adviser to Iztapalapa Mayor Aleida Alavez Ruiz. The goal was to shape how Mexico’s new General Circular Economy Law is put into practice — and ensure that grassroots recyclers are not once again left on the margins.

The law, published Jan. 19, seeks to extend the useful life of products, recover and reuse materials and establish “extended producer responsibility,” requiring manufacturers to take greater responsibility for what happens to their products after use.

It also creates a National Circular Economy System charged with developing a national program and coordinating government agencies. Crucially for Soledad’s colleagues, the law formally defines both grassroots recyclers and “inclusive recycling.”

Translating law into action

Much of the practical work remains unresolved, however. The law’s regulations have yet to be published, and questions remain about how recyclers will be registered, gain access to Social Security, form cooperatives and sell materials directly to industry.

René Sánchez Galindo, the Environment Ministry’s director general of legal affairs, said the regulations must balance sharply different interests as rules are developed for each type of product.

“We have to ensure that the measures are viable for everyone: industry, consumers and grassroots recyclers,” he said. “There must be what we call economic viability.”

“We want to help bring these concepts down to earth and bring the spirit of Iztapalapa to the law,” Alavez said. “A law that people don’t know how to use is not operative.”

Iztapalapa as a living laboratory

Iztapalapa has reason to position itself as a laboratory for inclusive recycling. The borough of 1.8 million people is one of the country’s most important centers for the recovery, repair and resale of discarded materials. It also collects roughly 2,200 metric tons of waste every day.

Alfonso González May, the borough’s director general of urban services, said only 2% to 3% of that waste was being separated when the current administration took office. The share has since risen to 8%, with separation taking place along 37 collection routes.

“This 8% has been achieved little by little, through different strategies,” González said. “We don’t want to give the mayor impressive numbers that have nothing to do with reality.”

The borough has expanded a once-weekly collection program for unwanted furniture, appliances and household debris into six weekly “junk days.” The program is intended to prevent residents from hiring informal haulers who may later abandon the items in vacant lots or on street corners.

Local initiatives and youth programs

Another initiative will collect used cooking oil at public markets and government offices. Residents will be encouraged to store the oil in bottles and deliver it separately to municipal collection crews. The oil will then be transferred to a private company for conversion into energy instead of being poured into drains, where it contributes to clogs and flooding.

The borough’s sustainable development office has identified more than 500 local circular-economy enterprises, ranging from cellphone, appliance and shoe repair shops to upholstery businesses and artisans working with discarded cardboard, textiles, wood and plastic.

Its “Soldando Iztapalapa” program trains young people to repair damaged metal furniture. Participants have restored more than 10,000 school desks that otherwise would have entered the waste stream, said Adriana Bustamante Castellanos, Iztapalapa’s director general of sustainable development.

“That means 10,000 objects that are not becoming waste,” she said, “and young people who have acquired knowledge, experience and a sense of service to their community.”

Other initiatives include a public recycling point outside the cultural center, neighborhood composting workshops and an ecocanje program that exchanges recyclable plastics for basic food products and vegetables grown in local greenhouses and community gardens.

National waste challenges

The borough is also developing a composting plant that will use black soldier fly larvae to process organic waste from markets, businesses, child development centers and community facilities.

Those local advances remain small compared with the national scale of the waste problem. Mexico generates more than 139,000 metric tons of urban solid waste daily, according to the federal Environment Ministry’s 2026 national assessment.

Only 5% receives any form of treatment, while 72% undergoes no recovery or valorization process. Of the country’s 2,250 final-disposal sites, just 52 operate as sanitary landfills meeting adequate standards.

Mella came to Mexico with a warning drawn from Chile’s experience. When that country adopted its extended producer responsibility law, she said, grassroots recyclers were initially excluded. They fought their way into the system through political pressure and organization.

Organizing against corporate interests

Mella distilled their demands into three points: formal recognition of recycling as work; dignified conditions supported by equipment, infrastructure and social protections; and payment for the service recyclers provide, rather than compensation based solely on the fluctuating value of the materials they collect.

“The garbage and recycling sector is a business model,” she said. “There are many interests that want to take what belongs to us and remove us from that space.”

Without a just transition that allows grassroots recyclers to compete, she added, “the sharks — the large companies — are going to eat us.”

Abel Balderas, who began working as a pepenador at age 8 and now leads Mexico’s National Recyclers Movement, echoed Mella’s call for organization and recognition.

“We are the experts,” he said. “You are the ones who can teach what can be recycled, what cannot, which material works and which doesn’t.”

Breaking down barriers

Following the presentations, participants divided into five dialogue groups focused on polyethylene terephthalate (PET), other plastics, paper and cardboard, metals and electronics. Each table included recyclers, companies, government officials, academics and civil society organizations.

They were asked to develop recommendations around four central issues: Social Security, tax-system inclusion, training and direct purchases of materials by industry.

At most tables, participants with sharply different interests managed to identify common barriers — particularly the bureaucracy involved in permits and formalization — and develop preliminary proposals.

The metals table proved the most contentious. Facilitator Adelita San Vicente, best known for her decades defending Mexico’s native corn and seeds, struggled as automotive industry representatives, the primary buyer of these materials, raised one objection after another while calling for a zero tax rate.

“Sharks,” she called them afterward, echoing Mella’s warning.

For Mella, legislation alone will not prevent that outcome. Grassroots recyclers must have seats at the tables where regulations and product-specific rules are written.

“If we are not actors and protagonists in this history,” she said, “once again we will be left out of the process.”

Her movement’s slogan reduces that argument to but a few words:

“Recycling without recyclers is garbage.”

Tracy L. Barnett is a Guadalajara-based freelance writer and the founder of The Esperanza Project.

World.title: In photos: The spirit of Mexican independence comes alive in Vienna
World.content:
The little boy, perhaps 3 years old, had everyone’s attention, dancing unrestrained and joyous with his little Mexican flag.

For that moment, he had traded schnitzel for tacos.

Mexico’s Independence Day was celebrated Sept. 12 in Vienna, Austria, for the city’s few but proud Mexican residents in a place appropriately called Mexikoplatz.

The square’s name recognizes a little-known act of courage when, in 1938, Mexico became the only country to lodge an official complaint with the League of Nations against Adolf Hitler’s annexation of Austria.

A Grito de Independencia fit for Vienna

According to Javier Basulto, a minister at the Mexican Embassy in Vienna, there are roughly 2,500 Mexicans living in all of Austria. The embassy, which also represents Mexico in Slovakia and Slovenia, coordinated the celebration alongside the Mexico-Austria Association.

The event showcased traditional dancers, food stands, a cumbia band and even a Grito de Independencia performed by the ambassador himself, José Antonio Zabalgoitia Trejo.

While dancers in Oaxacan dresses warmed up the gathering crowd, it was the Grito de Independencia that officially started the party.

While the ambassador didn’t have a roaring crowd of 300,000 and extravagant fireworks displays, like in Mexico City’s Zócalo, the roughly 500 people in attendance cheered with no less fervor.

Mexico and Austria’s shared history

Despite the jubilant atmosphere, there’s an irony to the whole thing.

In 1864, Habsburg dynasty Emperor Maximilian, younger brother of Austrian Emperor Franz Joseph, was installed as emperor of Mexico, with the backing of Napoleon III of France and Mexico’s conservative faction at the time.

He and his wife, Carlota, transformed Chapultepec Castle, formerly a military college, into a European-style imperial residence that reflected the Habsburg world Maximilian had left behind.

However, it was all for naught. After France withdrew its troops, Benito Juárez’s Republican forces closed in on the crumbling empire. Maximilian was captured at Querétaro in 1867 and executed by firing squad, effectively restoring the Mexican Republic.

But who thinks about executions when a cumbia band is playing, right?

Enter Los Nopaleros, a Vienna-based cumbia and psychedelic Latin-rock band whose members hail from Mexico, Argentina, Colombia and Austria.

The buoyant mood saw kids and the elderly dancing arm-in-arm, as the ambassador was showered with compliments and congratulations.

The wholesome Vienna celebrations were a far cry from the boozy Cinco de Mayo activities that often make headlines in the U.S., and which many mistakenly believe honor Mexican independence

Two distinct cultures, one shared spirit

It’s easy to write events like the one in Austria off as quaint, but they are undoubtedly significant for small communities.

The cultures of Mexico and Austria could hardly be more different. Just compare cumbia to waltzing. The contrasting styles need little explanation.

But small communities all over the world keep themselves alive in much the same way: with food, music, stories and the occasional excuse to crowd together in a public square.

Somewhere in that crowd, the little boy was still dancing, tiny Mexican flag in hand.

For a few hours in Vienna, Mexico was not 6,000 miles away. Its spirit could be felt right there in Mexikoplatz.

Mexico's Independence Day was celebrated Sept. 12 in Vienna's Mexikoplatz for the city’s few bu... 1 of 9

Jimmy Monack is a teacher, photographer and award-winning writer. He profiles interesting people all around the world as well as writing about and photographing rock concerts. He lives in Mexico City. www.jimmymonack.com

World.title: From the archive: How do I know it’s a ‘no’? A comprehensive guide for foreigners
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in November 2024 — is a humorous look at why Mexicans won’t say “no,” and how to know when they’re telling you “no” without actually saying it.

Mexicans are famous for their polite social graces and good humor. Unfortunately, they’re also known for a strong aversion to saying “no” or saying anything negative at all.

But what one sees as polite omission, another might take as flat-out lying. Being polite while also communicating what you mean can be a tricky balancing act; it’s true. And for those of us from more direct cultures, it’s downright opaque. Why would someone just not say what they mean?

Nothing is as simple as it seems, I suppose. Still, there are plenty of recognizable broad strokes we can examine here.

A lesson in keeping the negative to yourself

An impressive example of this tendency came years ago when I lived in Querétaro. I’d been working at a language school then — the kind that says they’ll help with immigration papers but never do. It was someone’s birthday, and teachers and students alike all went out to a bar to celebrate. It was a good time!

The next day, the director of the school told us teachers that one of the students wouldn’t be coming to class that day; there’d been an issue with his car. What was the issue? Someone had broken into it and stolen his car radio and CD player!

And when had this happened? It wasn’t when we were inside the bar, no. It happened at the school before we all left. He’d given some of us a ride, even, and had said nothing about his missing equipment.

It’s been almost 20 years, and I’m still shocked he kept that in.

He didn’t want to say anything about it because he didn’t want to ruin the evening before it had even begun. I myself would have been physically incapable of not saying anything. Just, wow.

Now that I’ve been here a while longer, I’ve seen more examples. People simply seem loath to talk about things that will make people gloomy. What for? We can get sad all on our own, after all.

So the first rule of communication, then, is to not disappoint. That is, of course, if you want the person you’re talking to to feel good. I’d personally rather be momentarily disappointed than later be sitting around like a dummy waiting for someone who’s not going to show, but that’s on me, I guess.

So knowing that “no” is a “no-no word” here, how might you decipher what people mean when they give you an answer?

Words that actually mean ‘no’: a guide for foreigners

Well, that’s just what I’m here to help you with! Below is a list of “actually, that might mean ‘no'” words and phrases.

‘Gracias’

This one is tricky. I sometimes have to stop myself from pedantically saying, “Um, that’s not one of the options for a yes or no question.” I can tell you from experience that challenging someone’s politeness in this way makes you look like an ass.

The way I’ve personally gotten around this is to pause comically and ask, “¿Gracias ‘sí’ o gracias ‘no’?” That will usually get a grin and an actual answer, which, by the way, is almost always “Gracias, no.” Remember that you can use it, too! It’s especially helpful when you’re wandering through a market and merchants are offering their wares. It also usually works if the “market” is coming to you in the form of individual sellers! An emphatic “muchas gracias” will usually transmit the idea that, while you are very grateful for the offer, you will not be purchasing a bottle of perfume on that particular day.

‘A lo mejor sí’

“A lo mejor” is a phrase that means “probably” or “likely.” It’s important to note, then, that all interpretations leave some wiggle room for it maybe not working out. If it doesn’t actually work out, well, they haven’t lied! There was always a chance.

This is, to me, one of the more dismissive ways to say no, a kind of “uh-huh, sure” version. In Mexico, this kind of dismissive “doing what you can to leave the conversation already” is called “dar el avión” (to … give the plane?). And when you “das el avión,” it’s often detectable. There are two likely outcomes of this, then. One is that the other person sighs, gives up and goes on their way. Another is that they get frustrated: “¡No me des el avión!” If that happens, you’d better think of a better, more convincing way to say “no.”

‘Déjame ver/checar’

This one is similar to “a lo mejor sí” in that it’s very likely to be an actual “no.” It means “Let me see” and “Let me check.” Spoiler alert: they will likely conclude, and may or may not tell you, that the result of the seeing/checking was negative.

‘Ahorita’

This is one that my kid uses on me all the time, and it drives me crazy. We speak in English together, so her version is “in a minute.” “Ahorita” could be when someone will definitely do something right then. Or it could mean anywhere from right that moment to when hell freezes over.

In my experience, it’s typically the latter, or after the person’s finally been worn down from enough nagging about it. So beware, people. If you’re hearing “ahorita” from your partner frequently and it’s not turning out to be “right now for real” kind, there will probably be some frustration in your future.

‘Estamos en contacto’

This one is kind of fun because it sounds so official and business-like. “We’ll be in touch.” Oh, will we? Most people don’t intend for this to be a lie; it’s just nicer to say than, “We may never see each other again, I don’t know, but you’re pleasant enough.”

Alas, this is a short list. I’ve got a word limit! But I’d love to hear more examples of “This is what they actually meant” in the comments. Consider this your official call for stories!

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Independence Day fireworks give way to trade deal hopes
World.content:
Listen to this article

Mexico’s Independence Day on Sept. 16 was the focal point this past week, even as less celebratory news circulated. Over the weekend, 21-year-old Spanish exchange student Claudia Tacoronte Aguilera, attending the Autonomous University of Morelos (UAEM) in Cuernavaca, Morelos, was stabbed and killed in Cuautla — the fourth femicide of a UAEM student just this year. On Thursday, Morelos authorities announced the arrest of a suspect, Francisco Javier “N,” but the attack on Tacoronte and the emergency medical response were met with indignation both locally and in Spain.

Also on Sept. 12, Pemex admitted it had contained another oil spill off the coast of Campeche, which the Navy and the state oil company moved quickly to seal and clean up — a contrast to the government’s slower handling of a major spill in February. Meanwhile, the peso spent most of the week trading above 17 to the dollar, weakening toward its worst week since March as markets digested the U.S. Federal Reserve’s decision to raise interest rates for the first time since 2023, narrowing the Mexico-U.S. rate differential.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Industrial activity posts best growth in years

Mexico’s industrial sector delivered its strongest annual performance in nearly three years in July, with industrial activity up 2.4% in seasonally adjusted terms, according to INEGI — triple June’s 0.8% reading and the best showing since November 2023.

Construction led the gains, climbing 6.7% annually, while mining rose 1.6% and manufacturing grew 1.3%. Month-over-month growth was 0.5%, a second straight month of sequential gains. Still, industrial activity is up just 0.4% for the first seven months of 2026, a modest rebound after a 1.3% contraction in 2025, with manufacturing down 0.7% year-to-date. Economists at Grupo Financiero Monex expect only “moderate” growth ahead, citing USMCA-related uncertainty and U.S. tariffs on vehicles, steel and aluminum.

Coahuila is Mexico’s safest state

For the first time, Coahuila topped INEGI’s national safety perception survey, the 2026 ENVIPE, with just 27.8% of residents calling the state unsafe due to crime — a 9.9-point improvement that pushed Baja California Sur out of the top spot.

Coahuila registered only 100 homicides in 2025, a turnaround from more than 1,100 killings in 2012, when cartels such as Los Zetas and the Gulf Cartel dominated large swaths of the state. Analysts credited beefed-up federal forces and prevention programs. Governor Manolo Jiménez Salinas, in office since December 2023, credited “great teamwork.” Nationally, the picture is less rosy: 74% of adults still consider their state unsafe, and México state overtook Morelos this year as Mexico’s least safe state, with 90% of respondents reporting security concerns.

Mexico’s independence is celebrated at home and abroad

On Tuesday night, President Sheinbaum delivered her second Grito de Independencia from the National Palace balcony before a crowd the Mexico City government estimated at more than 300,000 in the Zócalo, marking 216 years since Miguel Hidalgo’s original Cry of Dolores.

Sheinbaum issued 21 arengas honoring independence heroes including Hidalgo, Josefa Ortiz, Leona Vicario and Vicente Guerrero, alongside Mexico’s Indigenous and Afro-Mexican peoples and migrants abroad, several of whom were included in a national Grito for the first time.

Abroad, Iran marked the holiday by lighting Tehran’s Azadi Tower in green, white and red, the first time the landmark has been illuminated in tribute to Mexico — an occasion the Mexican ambassador to Iran called “a great gesture of friendship.” In New York City, Mayor Zohran Mamdani served as grand marshal of Brooklyn’s Mexican Independence Day parade, days after U.S. Vice President JD Vance mocked a Mexican flag-carrying protester at a Dallas rally.

Antitrust regulators probe Liga MX

Mexico’s National Antitrust Commission (CNA) has opened an investigation into whether Liga MX operates as a monopoly, examining whether a small group is unfairly controlling “affiliation, organization and access” to professional soccer competitions in violation of federal competition law. The probe follows Liga MX’s 2020 decision — upheld through the 2026-27 season by the Court of Arbitration for Sport — to scrap promotion and relegation with the second-tier Liga Expansión and end payouts to lower-tier clubs, a move Liga Expansión officials fiercely disputed. No defendants have been named; the probe can run up to 120 business days and be extended. If wrongdoing is found, Liga MX and its clubs could face fines of up to 10% of annual income.

CFE advances Project Oasis in Baja California Sur

The Federal Electricity Commission unveiled Project Oasis BCS, a solar, battery and green hydrogen initiative meant to bring reliable power to the isolated Mulegé region, which has no direct connection to the national grid and has historically relied on fossil fuels.

The project pairs a 72-megawatt photovoltaic plant with a battery system, electrolyzers to produce hydrogen and fuel cells to convert it back into electricity for use when sunlight is scarce. CFE projects the initiative will serve 40,000 households and cut emissions equivalent to taking more than 31,000 vehicles off the road annually. If completed, it would be CFE’s first-ever green hydrogen power generation project.

Democracy index shows modest gains

According to International IDEA’s annual Global State of Democracy report, released on Tuesday, Mexico’s democracy score edged up slightly in 2025 — Sheinbaum’s first full year in office — rising to 1.778 out of 4 from 1.770 the year before. The country improved in rule of law and participation, held steady in rights and declined in representation, its best-ranked category at 83rd out of 173 nations. Mexico ranked in the top 100 in only one of the four measured categories. The report’s authors flagged rising political polarization and “us versus them” identity politics as threats across Latin America, while separately noting democratic backsliding tied to the Trump administration’s consolidation of executive power in the U.S.

Sheinbaum responds to Trump cartel pressure

Responding to a Trump “presidential determination” pressuring Mexico to take “additional action” against cartels and arrest complicit officials, Sheinbaum turned the spotlight on U.S. drug consumption, asking what Washington is doing to curb domestic drug demand, money laundering and the flow of American-made weapons into Mexico.

“We don’t need to be judged from the outside,” Sheinbaum said, insisting “we know what Mexico’s problems are and we act against them every day.” Trump’s determination, submitted to Congress on Tuesday, named Mexico among 23 countries as major drug producers or transit points and singled out Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya — on leave amid U.S. accusations of cartel collusion but still free — as an official Washington wants arrested. The exchange came a week after Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Mexico isn’t doing enough against cartels, even as he acknowledged Mexican efforts had increased.

Record fuel bust in Guanajuato

Authorities announced on Thursday that they had seized 59 million liters of stolen fuel at a property in San José Iturbide, Guanajuato — the largest single-site fuel bust in Mexican history and roughly five times last year’s record seizure in Tamaulipas. The operation traces to a July 3 arrest involving a tanker truck loaded with stolen fuel, which led investigators to the storage facility, capable of holding up to 80 million liters. No arrests had been made as of Friday, and officials say specialized personnel will be needed to safely handle the seized hydrocarbons. Guanajuato’s security minister said the bust would help choke off a funding source for organized crime in a state that has seen four smaller fuel-theft busts this year.

Trade talks hover ahead of US midterms

The fourth round of formal USMCA-related trade talks between Mexico and the United States is tentatively set for next week, with officials on both sides eager to hammer out a deal before U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3, according to sources interviewed by Reuters.

A framework deal would benefit both governments: Trump wants an economic win as he risks losing control of Congress, while Mexico is contending with investor unease and a cooling economy. The push follows the collapse last month of parallel U.S.-Canada trade talks, making the Mexico-U.S. track an effort at an interim bilateral deal.

According to José Medina Mora, president of Mexico’s Business Coordinating Council (CCE), the elimination of Section 232 tariffs, which place duties on aluminum, steel and automobiles, is expected to be a primary focus.

Pups in the news

Rollo, an adopted mixed-breed puppy, is the National Palace’s newest resident, officially tasked with supporting “the emotional well-being of everyone,” per government videos; his brother Theo still awaits adoption, and the palace’s resident cats, including Coco and Zeus, remain in place.

In Morelia, a dog named Maple dressed as a taco stand won the city’s inaugural Patriotic Pup Contest, beating roughly 40 costumed competitors, with runners-up dressed as an elote-and-pork-loin vendor and a pozole bowl nearly twice their size.

Looking ahead

Next week brings a busy convergence of bilateral trade and security missions as well as the potential for currency swings.

The fourth round of USMCA-focused trade talks in Washington, D.C., could yield either a resolution or more setbacks. According to reporting by Politico, a preparatory call between Trump and Sheinbaum on Wednesday may have placed more topics on the discussion table than just Section 232 tariffs. However, Sheinbaum said after the call that “we’re making progress on trade issues.”

Any signs of progress or friction on tariffs are poised to move the peso. Meanwhile, 139 U.S. Army soldiers from the 101st Airborne Division are scheduled to land in Chihuahua on Sept. 20 for 11 days of joint training exercises with Mexican forces at the Centro Nacional de Adiestramiento, the military’s largest training facility.

SEYCHELLES · ECONOMY

Key Facts What happened. Caroline Abel resigned as Governor of the Central Bank of Seychelles on 16 September 2026, after leading the institution since March 2012. Her third term would have run to March 2027.

Caroline Abel resigned as Governor of the Central Bank of Seychelles on 16 September 2026, after leading the institution since March 2012. Her third term would have run to March 2027. How big. Abel steered Seychelles through its 2021 debt restructuring aftermath and an IMF programme totalling about US$105.1 million since May 2023, with roughly US$45 million expected when final reviews win board approval.

Abel steered Seychelles through its 2021 debt restructuring aftermath and an IMF programme totalling about US$105.1 million since May 2023, with roughly US$45 million expected when final reviews win board approval. The catch. The exit comes mid-cycle: the IMF’s final reviews under the Extended Fund Facility and Resilience and Sustainability Facility reached staff-level agreement in March but still await board sign-off.

The exit comes mid-cycle: the IMF’s final reviews under the Extended Fund Facility and Resilience and Sustainability Facility reached staff-level agreement in March but still await board sign-off. Who it hits. The financial sector of a tourism-dependent island economy of about 100,000 people, and every foreign investor holding Seychellois paper who prices central-bank continuity.

The first woman to run the Central Bank of Seychelles steps down with the islands’ IMF programme on track and reserves rebuilt. Her deputy takes over while a successor is chosen.

Caroline Abel, who has led the Central Bank of Seychelles since 2012 and was the first woman to hold the post, resigned on 16 September 2026, fourteen and a half years after taking office. First Deputy Governor Brian Commettant takes over as acting governor while a permanent successor is chosen.

A long tenure ends early

Abel was appointed Governor on 14 March 2012, the first woman to lead the Central Bank of Seychelles, and was reappointed twice. Her resignation, confirmed by the bank and reported by the Seychelles News Agency and Seychelles Nation, takes effect about six months before her third term would have expired in March 2027. No reason for the early departure has been made public. The bank’s statement and government communications have emphasised continuity: Brian Commettant, the First Deputy Governor, assumes the role on an acting basis immediately.

The state she leaves the bank in

By the IMF’s account, the institution Abel leaves is in better shape than the one she inherited. In March 2026 the Fund’s mission reached staff-level agreement on the final reviews of Seychelles’ Extended Fund Facility and Resilience and Sustainability Facility arrangements. Those programmes have anchored policy since May 2023 and are worth about US$105.1 million in total. Roughly US$45 million is tied to the pending reviews. The Fund’s numbers describe a small economy that has stabilised. Growth reached 5.1% in 2025, with inflation just below zero and a primary fiscal surplus of 2.5% of GDP. Public debt stood at 53.6% of GDP, and reserves covered more than four months of imports. The 2026 projection is cooler — 1.5% growth and 2.6% inflation — reflecting a softer tourism cycle.

Why continuity matters here

Seychelles, with about 100,000 people, runs one of Africa’s richest economies per head, built on tourism and fisheries and exposed to both. The central bank’s credibility — rebuilt after the 2021 pandemic shock forced a debt restructuring — is a core national asset. Investors holding Seychellois debt, and donors tracking the climate-linked Resilience and Sustainability Facility, will read the succession as a test of whether policy outlives the governor who personified it.

What this means for expats and investors

For the foreign community in Victoria and the resorts beyond, nothing changes operationally: the rupee regime, the IMF programme and the bank’s senior team remain in place under Commettant. For investors, the near-term marker is the IMF board date for the final reviews; a smooth permanent appointment would close the question Abel’s exit opened.

What Is Not Known

The reason for Abel’s resignation has not been disclosed, and no successor has been named. The timing of the IMF board meeting on the final reviews — and whether the leadership change affects it — is not public. Whether Commettant is a caretaker or a candidate for the permanent post is also unknown.

Key Facts What happened. São Tomé and Príncipe launched a citizenship-by-investment programme in August 2025 under Decree-Law 07/2025: a US$90,000 non-refundable donation to the National Transformation Fund buys eligibility for a passport.

São Tomé and Príncipe launched a citizenship-by-investment programme in August 2025 under Decree-Law 07/2025: a US$90,000 non-refundable donation to the National Transformation Fund buys eligibility for a passport. How big. A family of four pays US$95,000 plus fees of about US$750 per person. In its first five months the programme received 98 applications and approved 27, with processing averaging about two and a half months, according to industry reporting.

What comes next. The government is marketing the programme abroad; BusinessDay this week framed it as part of the islands’ broader terms for foreign capital. São Tomé. The programme sells citizenship for US$90,000, the cheapest on offer anywhere.

The island nation launched a citizenship-by-investment programme in 2025 at half the price of the Caribbean. The first passports are out. The fine print deserves a slow read.

São Tomé and Príncipe, the two-island nation in the Gulf of Guinea, is selling citizenship from US$90,000 — the lowest entry price of any legitimate citizenship-by-investment programme in the world. The scheme opened in August 2025, issued its first passports in January 2026, and is drawing fresh attention as Caribbean programmes hold their prices at US$200,000 or more.

What US$90,000 buys

The structure is simple. A single applicant donates US$90,000 to the National Transformation Fund, a state vehicle intended to finance development projects. A family of four pays US$95,000, with US$5,000 added for each further dependant, plus processing and due-diligence fees of roughly US$750 per head. In return, successful applicants receive full citizenship and a passport, with no residency requirement — there is no obligation to visit, let alone live on the islands. The programme is run by a Citizenship by Investment Unit operated with an international partner under a ten-year mandate, based in Dubai.

The first passports were issued in January 2026, five months after launch. Immigrant Invest, an industry firm, reported 98 applications and 27 approvals in that period. Average processing ran around two and a half months, fast by the standards of an industry where a year is common. Applications from North Korean nationals are excluded; most other nationalities can apply.

Why it is cheap, and what cheap means

The price undercuts every competitor. Dominica and its Caribbean peers start at US$200,000, Vanuatu at US$130,000 and Nauru at US$105,000. São Tomé’s discount reflects what its passport actually delivers. It offers visa-free or visa-on-arrival access to roughly 61 to 90 destinations, depending on the source. That does not include the Schengen area, the United Kingdom or the United States. One genuine advantage is linguistic: as a member of the Community of Portuguese Language Countries, São Toméan citizenship can ease residence routes in Portugal and Brazil.

BusinessDay’s analysis this week put the programme in the context of a fragile archipelago pricing foreign capital carefully: the islands need investment but are wary of the reputational risks that citizenship sales carry. Industry monitors have also begun reporting processing delays stretching beyond eight months as volumes rise — a familiar pattern in young programmes that market speed.

What this means for expats and nomads

For location-independent earners holding weak passports, São Tomé offers the cheapest legal second citizenship on the market — useful as insurance, limited as a travel document. It does not replace a Schengen visa strategy, and anyone buying it for European access is buying the wrong product. For São Toméans, the question is whether the Transformation Fund visibly transforms anything; that answer will take years.

What Is Not Known

The government does not publish application or approval statistics, so industry figures cannot be verified against official data. The exact visa-free destination count varies by source, and no independent audit of the National Transformation Fund’s receipts or spending has appeared. Whether the programme can scale without slowing further, and whether the EU will ever extend visa-free access, are both open questions.

World.title: Central African Republic Signs Mining Deal as CVMR Wins Five Licences
World.content:
CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC · MINING

Key Facts What happened. Montage Afrique, led by CEO Ogochukwu Ezeaku, signed an MoU with the CAR government in Bangui to start mining operations; Mines Minister Rufin Benam Beltoungou represented the state, according to Leadership newspaper.

Montage Afrique, led by CEO Ogochukwu Ezeaku, signed an MoU with the CAR government in Bangui to start mining operations; Mines Minister Rufin Benam Beltoungou represented the state, according to Leadership newspaper. How big. Separately, Canada’s CVMR Corp won five exploration licences covering roughly 2,500 square kilometres, some of it uranium-bearing ground around Bakouma, Africa Intelligence reports.

Separately, Canada’s CVMR Corp won five exploration licences covering roughly 2,500 square kilometres, some of it uranium-bearing ground around Bakouma, Africa Intelligence reports. The catch. An MoU is not a mining permit, and exploration licences are not production. CAR has a long history of announced mining ventures that stalled on security, infrastructure and financing.

An MoU is not a mining permit, and exploration licences are not production. CAR has a long history of announced mining ventures that stalled on security, infrastructure and financing. Who it hits. Mining investors watching Central Africa’s underexplored belt, communities around Bakouma and other licence areas, and a government in Bangui looking for revenue beyond aid and logging.

Mining investors watching Central Africa’s underexplored belt, communities around Bakouma and other licence areas, and a government in Bangui looking for revenue beyond aid and logging. What comes next. Montage Afrique says it is preparing to commence activities. CVMR must now explore and prove resources. Watch for actual ground work, not ceremonies.

Bangui. The government signed a mining accord and granted five uranium licences.

A Nigerian group has signed a mining agreement in Bangui days before reports that a Canadian firm won five exploration licences, including ground with uranium. One of the world’s least-covered mining frontiers is getting attention.

The Central African Republic has signed a memorandum of understanding with Montage Afrique, a Nigerian mining group, to begin mining activities in the country. Mines Minister Rufin Benam Beltoungou attended the signing in Bangui. Days later, Africa Intelligence reported that Canada’s CVMR Corporation has won five exploration licences covering about 2,500 square kilometres, including ground prospective for uranium.

Two doors opening at once

The Montage Afrique agreement was signed in Bangui with the Minister of Mines and Geology, Rufin Benam Beltoungou, in attendance, Leadership reports. The Nigerian group, which presents itself as an African mining investment vehicle, says it is set to commence mining activities in the country. Details of the minerals targeted, the sites and the investment size were not disclosed in the announcement.

The second development is quieter but potentially larger. Africa Intelligence reported on 18 September that CVMR Corporation, a Canadian firm specialising in nickel refining technology, has secured five sought-after exploration licences in CAR covering about 2,500 square kilometres. Part of the licensed ground lies around Bakouma in the east — an area known for uranium, where France’s Orano has retained interests for years without developing them. CVMR’s plans for the licences have not been detailed publicly.

Why CAR, and why now

The Central African Republic sits on significant deposits of gold, diamonds, uranium and iron ore, yet industrial mining has barely begun. Decades of instability, almost no roads or power, and a contested security environment have kept large miners away. The state earns most of its income from aid, forestry and artisanal gold and diamonds. Bangui has been actively courting new investors as it tries to diversify, and Russian-linked operators have shown how quickly licence areas can change hands in this market.

The timing matters. An IMF-backed programme and African Development Bank support have nudged the economy toward modest growth, and the AfDB projects expansion continuing this year. The government is keen to convert geological promise into budget revenue before donor patience thins.

What this means for investors and expats

For mining investors, CAR is the definition of frontier: high geological upside, extreme logistical and political risk, and a licence registry that rewards diligence. The CVMR awards signal that Bangui is willing to allocate serious ground to newcomers. For the small expat community — aid agencies, UN staff, traders — new mining ventures would slowly change the economy outside the capital, but nothing in these announcements moves daily life in Bangui yet.

What Is Not Known

The financial terms of the Montage Afrique MoU, the minerals covered and any timeline to production are undisclosed. For CVMR, the exact licence locations beyond the Bakouma reference, the work commitments attached and the company’s financing are not public. Whether either project survives contact with CAR’s infrastructure and security reality is the standing unknown of every mining announcement in the country.

World.title: Mozambique Gas Revenue Stays Tiny as Debt Nears 96% of GDP
World.content:
Mozambique · ECONOMY

Key Facts — What happened Mozambique’s government projects gas-related state revenue of 5.1 billion meticais (about US$79.8 million) in 2027, equal to 0.27% of gross domestic product.

— How big Total state revenue is projected at 488.3 billion meticais (about US$7.64 billion) in 2027, so gas would contribute roughly 1% of the budget.

— The catch Fitch expects government debt to reach around 96% of GDP over 2026 and 2027, keeping fiscal pressure high.

— Who it hits Budget planners cannot yet rely on liquefied natural gas money to fund schools, health care or debt payments.

— What comes next The only operating project, Coral Sul FLNG, generated about 253 million US dollars in tax revenue between 2022 and 2025.

Mozambique gas revenue will remain a small slice of the state budget in 2027, even as government debt climbs toward 96% of gross domestic product, according to International Monetary Fund and Fitch data.

Mozambique’s liquefied natural gas (LNG) boom is not yet paying the government’s bills. Official projections show gas-related state revenue of just 5.1 billion meticais (about US$79.8 million) in 2027, a fraction of a budget still weighed down by heavy borrowing.

The real Mozambique gas revenue number for 2027

The government’s Medium-Term Fiscal Scenario puts gas-related state revenue at about 5.1 billion meticais (about US$79.8 million) in 2027. That equals 0.27% of gross domestic product (GDP), a strikingly small figure for a country often described as a future gas giant.

Total state revenue is projected at 488.3 billion meticais (about US$7.64 billion) in the same year. Gas money would therefore account for roughly 1% of what the state expects to collect.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) paints a similar picture in its 2026 Article IV review. Total revenue including LNG is projected at 23.9% of GDP in 2027, barely above the 23.7% figure without LNG.

Where the 96% figure actually comes from

The alarming “96%” number circulating in some discussions is not about gas revenue at all. It is a debt projection from Fitch, the credit rating agency.

Fitch says Mozambique’s government debt is expected to reach around 96% of GDP over 2026 and 2027. That is a measure of total public liabilities, not a share of tax income.

Confusing the two would badly misread the country’s fiscal position. Mozambique is not losing 96% of its revenue to gas projects; it is carrying a debt burden close to the size of its entire economy.

Coral Sul FLNG: the only project paying taxes

The only operating LNG project in Mozambique is Coral Sul FLNG, a floating facility in the Rovuma Basin. It generated about 253 million US dollars in tax revenue between 2022 and 2025.

That is real money, but spread over four years it averages roughly 63 million US dollars annually. For a government projecting total revenue of 488.3 billion meticais (about US$7.64 billion) in 2027, it remains a modest contribution.

Other large onshore LNG projects have been delayed or disrupted by instability in Cabo Delgado province. Until they reach production, gas cannot transform the national budget.

The Rovuma Basin and the scramble for gas

The Rovuma Basin in northern Mozambique holds some of the world’s largest untapped gas reserves. Global energy companies and foreign capital are closely tied to expectations of future state revenue from the area.

Mozambique has also passed a sovereign wealth fund law to manage future resource income. The challenge is balancing immediate budget financing against long-term savings for citizens.

This tension sits inside a wider contest for African resources and influence, a dynamic covered in our Africa: The New Scramble pillar. External financing flows through the IMF and LNG-linked investors, giving outsiders a say in Mozambique’s choices.

Security, debt and the wait for bigger gas money

Cabo Delgado’s instability has repeatedly disrupted resource development in the north. Attacks and displacement have slowed projects that were supposed to generate large tax flows by now.

Meanwhile, the government must manage a debt load near 96% of GDP while waiting for gas revenue to grow. That leaves little room for error in public finances.

The IMF’s projections show tax revenue excluding LNG at around 22.6% of GDP in 2027. Adding LNG lifts the total only slightly, confirming that gas is not yet a budget game-changer.

What to watch next

The key date is 2027, when the government expects gas-related revenue of 5.1 billion meticais (about US$79.8 million). Whether that target is met depends on security, project timelines and global gas prices.

Investors and creditors will watch Fitch’s debt ratio closely. If debt stays near 96% of GDP without a revenue surge, Mozambique’s borrowing costs could remain high.

For now, the story is one of patience. Mozambique’s gas wealth is real, but the fiscal payoff is still years away.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much gas revenue will Mozambique collect in 2027? The government projects gas-related state revenue of 5.1 billion meticais (about US$79.8 million) in 2027, equal to 0.27% of GDP. What does the 96% figure refer to in Mozambique? Fitch expects Mozambique’s government debt to reach around 96% of GDP over 2026 and 2027, not 96% of fiscal revenue. Which LNG project is currently paying taxes in Mozambique? Coral Sul FLNG in the Rovuma Basin is the only operating project, generating about 253 million US dollars in tax revenue between 2022 and 2025.

World.title: ECOWAS and France Discuss Terrorism Challenges Across West Africa
World.content:
West Africa · GEOPOLITICS

Key Facts — What happened The Economic Community of West African States and France are coordinating on counterterrorism after West Africa recorded more than 1,800 terrorist attacks in the first half of 2023.

— The numbers Those attacks caused nearly 4,600 deaths, and ECOWAS backed a 2020-2024 action plan with a reported US$2.3 billion budget.

— The catch Niger and Mali accused neighbours in April 2026 of supporting terrorist groups, and Niger’s foreign minister said he meant France.

— Why it matters The Mali-Burkina Faso-Niger bloc has broken with ECOWAS, framing the regional body and France as part of a foreign-interests order.

— What comes next France is moving toward smaller-scale cooperation with coastal states after the end of Operation Barkhane, while ECOWAS keeps seeking regional security funding.

ECOWAS France terrorism talks are intensifying as the Economic Community of West African States keeps a zero-tolerance counterterrorism policy and Paris tries to stay relevant after its military retrenchment from the Sahel.

ECOWAS and France are exchanging views on the challenges related to terrorism in West Africa

The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) and France are exchanging views on the region’s worsening terrorism threat. The dialogue comes as West Africa recorded more than 1,800 terrorist attacks in the first half of 2023, causing nearly 4,600 deaths.

A common counterterrorism position under strain

ECOWAS adopted a common counterterrorism position stating that terrorism is a threat to all member states. The strategy rests on prevention, pursuit and repair as its core pillars.

The bloc also backed a 2020-2024 action plan with a reported US$2.3 billion budget. That plan was designed to fund regional security operations and stabilisation efforts across member countries.

Yet the regional picture has fractured sharply. The Mali-Burkina Faso-Niger bloc has broken with ECOWAS and now frames the regional body and France as part of a foreign-interests order.

France’s shifting military footprint

France’s role has changed after the end of Operation Barkhane, its large-scale military mission in the Sahel. Paris is moving away from big direct deployments and toward smaller-scale cooperation with coastal states and partners.

This retrenchment has left a security vacuum that jihadist groups have exploited. ECOWAS has sought external financing and support from Western and Arab donors for counterterrorism, showing how security, aid and influence are intertwined.

France still wants a seat at the table. The ECOWAS France terrorism dialogue is part of that effort to remain relevant without the heavy footprint of the past.

Accusations fly at the April 2026 forum

In April 2026, Niger and Mali publicly accused neighbours of harbouring, supporting, fuelling, financing and sustaining terrorist groups. Niger’s foreign minister said he meant France.

Reuters reported that the French foreign ministry did not immediately comment on those accusations. The exchange underscored how deeply trust has eroded between Paris and the breakaway Sahel states.

The accusations remain contested. ECOWAS has not endorsed them, and no evidence of state sponsorship was presented at the forum.

How jihadist groups actually fund themselves

Jihadist groups in the Sahel are widely reported to fund themselves through gold, kidnapping, smuggling, livestock theft and local taxation. This is a crucial point in the ECOWAS France terrorism debate.

No proven state sponsorship has been established, despite the accusations from Niger and Mali. The funding model is local and extractive, not dependent on foreign patrons.

That reality complicates the narrative of external backing. It also means military pressure alone cannot choke off the groups’ revenue streams.

The great-power contest behind the security split

The split in West Africa is not only about security doctrine. It is also about who gets to define the region’s political order.

The Mali-Burkina Faso-Niger bloc has turned toward new partners while ECOWAS keeps seeking Western and Arab donor support. This is a classic great-power contest playing out through security alliances.

For investors and professionals watching the region, the ECOWAS France terrorism rift signals deeper instability. It also opens space for other external actors to expand their influence, a pattern covered in Africa: The New Scramble.

What to watch next

ECOWAS will likely push for renewed donor commitments to its counterterrorism agenda. France will try to deepen ties with coastal states that still see Paris as a security partner.

The breakaway Sahel bloc shows no sign of returning to the ECOWAS fold. That means the region’s security architecture will remain divided for the foreseeable future.

The next test will be whether the accusations from Niger and Mali harden into formal diplomatic breaks. If they do, the ECOWAS France terrorism coordination could become even more difficult to sustain.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the ECOWAS France terrorism dialogue about? It is an exchange of views on West Africa’s worsening terrorism threat, with ECOWAS keeping a zero-tolerance counterterrorism policy and France trying to stay relevant after its military retrenchment from the Sahel. How many terrorist attacks did West Africa record in early 2023? ECOWAS leaders said West Africa recorded more than 1,800 terrorist attacks in the first half of 2023, causing nearly 4,600 deaths. Why did Niger and Mali accuse France in April 2026? Niger and Mali publicly accused neighbours of harbouring, supporting, fuelling, financing and sustaining terrorist groups, and Niger’s foreign minister said he meant France.

World.title: Kindiki Coronation in Kiambu Exposes Kenya’s Deeper Power Fight
World.content:
Kenya · POLITICS

Key Facts — What happened Deputy President Kithure Kindiki was crowned by Njuri Ncheke elders in Kirigiti, Kiambu, on August 7, 2026, as spokesman for Mt Kenya East.

— The trigger The ceremony followed Rigathi Gachagua’s impeachment on October 17, 2024, and Kindiki’s swearing-in as deputy president on November 1, 2024.

— The stakes The fight is over control of Mt Kenya’s political machine before the August 2027 election and over who becomes President William Ruto’s heir apparent in 2032.

— The numbers Public Service Cabinet Secretary Geoffrey Ruku claims Mt Kenya East can mobilise more than three million votes for Ruto.

— The accusation Gachagua has accused Kindiki of helping divide the mountain, while Kindiki has urged Mt Kenya to back Ruto’s re-election.

— What comes next Watch whether the East-West split hardens into rival campaign structures as the August 2027 election approaches.

The Kindiki coronation power fight is not about ceremony. It is about who controls Mt Kenya’s votes, state resources and the path to succeed President William Ruto.

Deputy President Kithure Kindiki’s crowning by Njuri Ncheke elders in Kirigiti, Kiambu, on August 7, 2026, has exposed a deeper succession struggle inside President William Ruto’s camp. The ceremony sharpened the East-versus-West split in the vote-rich Mt Kenya bloc.

A coronation that divided the mountain

The Njuri Ncheke elders crowned Kindiki as spokesman for Mt Kenya East, a move framed as cultural recognition. But the timing and location turned it into a political statement.

The episode followed Rigathi Gachagua’s impeachment on October 17, 2024, and Kindiki’s swearing-in as deputy president on November 1, 2024. Gachagua has accused Kindiki of helping divide the mountain.

Kindiki has urged Mt Kenya to back Ruto’s re-election, arguing that keeping Ruto in power best secures the region’s influence and future access to state resources. That argument is the core of the Kindiki coronation power fight.

The real prize is the 2027 machine

The core power fight is over control of Mt Kenya’s political machine ahead of the August 2027 election. It is also about who becomes Ruto’s heir apparent in 2032.

Public Service Cabinet Secretary Geoffrey Ruku has openly pushed a Mt Kenya East political identity. He claims the region can mobilise more than three million votes for Ruto.

That claim matters because Mt Kenya has long been treated as a single voting bloc. Splitting it into East and West would change how campaigns are funded and run.

Money, patronage and the route to State House

Money and patronage remain central to the contest. Analysts cited by the press link the fight to resource-sharing, development promises and access to the executive.

Regional leaders are competing to position themselves as the main conduit to State House. The winner of that contest controls how state resources flow into the region.

This is not only about local symbolism. It is about who commands the route to power, state resources and Kenya’s external economic credibility.

Investor confidence and the wider backdrop

Kenya needs to preserve investor and lender confidence while managing rising domestic tensions. The Ruto administration is still associated with International Monetary Fund-style fiscal tightening and tax pressure after the 2024 unrest.

That makes control of the ruling coalition’s internal base politically and economically critical. A divided Mt Kenya could weaken Ruto’s ability to push through economic policy.

The succession fight therefore reaches beyond campaign politics. It touches the stability that external partners watch when deciding where to place capital in Eastern Africa.

The great-power and regional read-through

Kenya sits at the centre of Eastern Africa’s investment and logistics corridor. Internal coalition stability affects how reliably Nairobi can anchor regional trade and security arrangements.

The wider great-power backdrop is Kenya’s need to manage domestic tensions while keeping lenders and investors engaged. This fits the pattern covered in Africa: The New Scramble, where local power contests shape external economic positioning.

For global readers, the Mt Kenya fight is a signal about Kenya’s political risk premium. A fractured ruling coalition makes policy continuity harder to guarantee.

What to watch next

The immediate question is whether Gachagua builds a rival Mt Kenya West structure. If he does, the August 2027 election could become a contest between two mountain factions.

Watch for whether Ruto publicly backs the East identity or tries to keep the bloc united. His choice will reveal how much leverage Kindiki has gained.

The succession race for 2032 is now effectively open. Every move in Mt Kenya between now and the 2027 vote will be read through that lens.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Rigathi Gachagua accuse Kithure Kindiki? Gachagua has accused Kindiki of helping divide the mountain after Gachagua’s impeachment on October 17, 2024, and Kindiki’s swearing-in as deputy president on November 1, 2024. How many votes does Mt Kenya East claim to control? Public Service Cabinet Secretary Geoffrey Ruku claims Mt Kenya East can mobilise more than three million votes for Ruto.

World.title: Ramaphosa Signs South Africa Public Service Commission Bill Into Law
World.content:
South Africa · POLITICS

Key Facts — What happened President Cyril Ramaphosa signed the Public Service Commission Bill into law on 16 September 2026, repealing the 1997 Act.

— The mandate The new Public Service Commission Act extends oversight to local government, state-owned companies and public entities.

— The structure The Office of the Public Service Commission shifts from a government department into an independent secretariat.

— The timeline A phased 12-month rollout begins for the expanded mandate, with full implementation within three years after that period.

— Why it matters The reform is framed as a step to restore professionalism in the state after years of patronage and weak vetting.

South Africa’s new Public Service Commission Act gives the watchdog independent powers and a wider mandate, including oversight of local government and state-owned companies. The law, signed on 16 September 2026, is the latest move in a broader push to rebuild state capacity.

New law offers public service a shot at redemption: PSC chair Photo By Lance Cheung.

President Cyril Ramaphosa signed South Africa’s Public Service Commission Bill into law on 16 September 2026, repealing the 1997 Act and renaming it the Public Service Commission Act. The reform hands the commission a stronger, more independent role after years of public-service decline.

A watchdog with new teeth

The new Public Service Commission Act creates an independent secretariat, freeing the body from its previous status as a government department. Public Service Commission chair Professor Somadoda Fikeni said the reform allows the institution to “redeem ourselves” after years of decline.

The law also gives the commission power to investigate on its own accord. That marks a shift from a reactive body to one that can initiate probes without waiting for a formal complaint.

Under the Constitution, the Public Service Commission is a Chapter 9-style watchdog that reports to Parliament. Its chair is designated by the President, a structure that has long raised questions about independence.

The money and power stakes

The expanded mandate covers local government, state-owned companies and public entities. That is a significant widening of scope for a body once focused mainly on national and provincial departments.

South Africa’s state-owned companies have been at the centre of governance failures and financial strain for more than a decade. Bringing them under clearer oversight is a direct response to those pressures.

Fikeni framed the reform as part of a broader effort to restore professionalism in the state. The context is a public service weakened by patronage, weak vetting and implementation failures.

A phased path to full implementation

The law introduces a phased 12-month rollout for the expanded mandate. Full implementation is expected within three years after that initial period.

The National Assembly adopted the bill in March 2025, according to the commission’s own 2024/25 annual report. The signing in September 2026 completes a legislative process that stretched across multiple parliamentary sessions.

The phased approach gives the commission time to build capacity for its new responsibilities. It also signals that the government is aware of the operational burden that comes with a wider mandate.

Who gains and who loses

The clearest winners are citizens and investors who want stronger checks on how public money is spent. A more independent commission with investigative powers can act faster on complaints about hiring, procurement and service delivery.

Municipalities and state-owned companies now face a new layer of scrutiny. For managers accustomed to limited oversight, the law raises the cost of poor governance.

Political insiders who benefited from weak vetting may find the new environment less forgiving. The commission’s ability to investigate on its own accord removes a key bottleneck that previously slowed action.

The regional read-through

South Africa’s governance reforms are being watched across Southern Africa. The country remains the region’s largest economy and a benchmark for institutional design.

Weak state capacity is a shared challenge for many governments in the region. South Africa’s attempt to strengthen an independent watchdog could influence similar debates in neighbouring countries.

The reform also fits a wider pattern of institutional repair after periods of political capture. For investors, stronger oversight can reduce risk in public procurement and state-linked contracts.

What to watch next

The first test is the 12-month rollout, which will show whether the commission can staff and fund its new secretariat. Capacity, not legislation, is often the binding constraint in South African governance reform.

Parliament will need to monitor implementation and ensure the commission has the resources to match its expanded mandate. The next annual report will offer the first formal progress check.

For readers tracking the wider contest over African institutions and state capacity, this reform connects to the themes in Africa: The New Scramble. The fight over who controls public institutions is as much about power as it is about policy.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does the new Public Service Commission Act change? It repeals the 1997 Act, creates an independent secretariat, and extends the commission’s oversight to local government, state-owned companies and public entities. When was the Public Service Commission Act signed into law? President Cyril Ramaphosa signed the bill into law on 16 September 2026, after the National Assembly adopted it in March 2025. How long will it take to fully implement the new mandate? The law provides for a phased 12-month rollout, with full implementation expected within three years after that period.

World.title: NamWater to Cut Usakos Water Supply Over Unresolved Debt
World.content:
Namibia · INFRASTRUCTURE

Key Facts — What happened NamWater said it will phase down water supply to Usakos after the town council failed to formally accept conditions in a 25 August letter.

— The deadline Full suspension is threatened for 6–9 October if no deal is reached, with daily interruptions starting Monday.

— The wider debt NamWater was still owed about N$80 million in March 2026, down from N$96 million the previous July.

— Who it hits Usakos residents face overnight cuts and 50 percent weekend reductions, with tanker support for health facilities and schools if needed.

— The balance sheet NamWater’s annual report showed gross trade debtors at N$2.478 billion by 31 March 2025.

NamWater will begin phasing down water supply to Usakos from Monday, with a full suspension threatened for 6–9 October if the town council does not accept conditions set out in a 25 August letter.

NamWater to cut Usakos water over unresolved debt Photo By Lance Cheung.

Namibia’s national water utility, NamWater, said it will cut supply to the central town of Usakos after the local council failed to formally respond to a debt-resolution offer. The move marks one of the sharpest enforcement actions yet in a long-running standoff over unpaid municipal water bills.

What the Usakos water cut means for residents

NamWater said daily interruptions would begin on Monday, alongside overnight cuts and a 50 percent reduction in weekend supply. The utility added that tanker support would be provided for health facilities and schools if the situation worsens.

The town council has not formally accepted the conditions outlined in the 25 August letter, according to NamWater. That failure triggered the phased reduction, which could escalate to a full suspension between 6 and 9 October.

Usakos sits on the main road between Windhoek and Swakopmund, a corridor that carries mining traffic and tourist movement. A prolonged water cut would affect households, small businesses and public institutions in the town.

The money behind the municipal debt crisis

NamWater said it was still owed about N$80 million in March 2026, down from N$96 million the previous July. Several councils, including Usakos, are on repayment plans, but the utility has grown impatient with those that fail to honour commitments.

Earlier reporting put the combined debt of 22 local and regional authorities at N$147 million, with Usakos among the debtors. The gap between what councils owe and what NamWater can recover has become a defining strain on Namibia’s water infrastructure.

NamWater’s annual report showed gross trade debtors at N$2.478 billion by 31 March 2025. That figure captures the broader receivables problem facing the utility, not just municipal arrears.

Why NamWater is taking a harder line now

The utility has shifted from negotiation to enforcement as arrears persist across multiple councils. NamWater said it was reporting progress against what it called a tide of missed fortune, a reference to revenue that remains locked in unpaid bills.

Water utilities across Southern Africa face a similar squeeze: rising operational costs, ageing infrastructure and customers who cannot or will not pay. Namibia’s approach is being watched by neighbouring countries grappling with the same municipal debt problem.

For investors and professionals tracking Namibian infrastructure, the Usakos action signals that NamWater is willing to use supply cuts as a collection tool. That carries political risk, but it also protects the utility’s ability to fund maintenance and new connections.

The regional and resource-politics read-through

Namibia’s water stress sits inside a broader public-finance squeeze and infrastructure crunch. The country is navigating heavy external-interest politics around strategic resources, including China-linked mining investment and a growing Western push around critical minerals and green hydrogen.

Russia’s Africa diplomacy remains a factor in the region’s security and resource calculations, adding another layer to decisions about who finances and controls essential infrastructure. Water supply may seem local, but it underpins mining, energy and industrial expansion.

For readers following the wider contest over African resources, this story connects to the themes tracked in Africa: The New Scramble. Reliable water is a precondition for almost every major project on the continent.

What to watch next in the Usakos standoff

The immediate question is whether the Usakos town council formally accepts NamWater’s conditions before the 6–9 October window. If it does, the phased cuts could be reversed quickly.

If no deal is reached, full suspension would test how the town copes and how the national government responds. NamWater has said tanker support would be available for health facilities and schools, but households and businesses would bear the brunt.

The outcome will also shape how other indebted councils approach their own repayment plans. A hard line in Usakos could push more municipalities to settle, or it could deepen resistance and political fallout.

The longer-term stakes for Namibian water

NamWater’s gross trade debtors of N$2.478 billion by 31 March 2025 show that the utility’s financial health depends heavily on collection. Every unpaid council bill reduces the money available for pipes, pumps and treatment plants.

Namibia is one of the driest countries in sub-Saharan Africa, which makes water infrastructure a strategic asset rather than a routine service. The Usakos dispute is a small but telling test of whether the country can enforce payment discipline without triggering a public backlash.

For global readers, the lesson is familiar: infrastructure only works if someone pays for it. Namibia is now deciding how far it will go to make that principle stick.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is NamWater cutting water to Usakos? NamWater said the Usakos town council failed to formally accept conditions in a 25 August letter about unresolved debt, triggering a phased reduction in supply. When could Usakos face a full water suspension? NamWater threatened a full suspension for 6–9 October if no deal is reached, with daily interruptions starting Monday and overnight cuts already planned. How much does NamWater say it is still owed? NamWater said it was still owed about N$80 million in March 2026, down from N$96 million the previous July, with several councils on repayment plans including Usakos.

World.title: New Costa Rica Law Requires Wildlife Crossings on Public Infrastructure
World.content:
Costa Rica now has a law requiring wildlife crossings on public infrastructure projects, but the regulation that will actually put it into practice could take more than two years to arrive. The rule requires new road, bridge and other infrastructure projects to incorporate mechanisms allowing wild species to move safely across routes that would otherwise fragment their habitat, but before any of that happens the National System of Conservation Areas and the Ministry of Public Works and Transport still have to jointly write the technical regulation defining procedures, responsibilities and criteria for applying it.

Once that regulation takes effect, the conservation agency will then have up to 24 months just to identify the natural corridors wildlife use and the most vulnerable points on existing roads, meaning construction itself is still years away. The law took a long road to get here. It was filed in the legislature back in 2022 by then deputy Ariel Robles Barrantes and spent four years moving slowly enough that it nearly expired under the four year shelf life Costa Rican bills carry before automatic archiving.

Lawmakers voted 53 to 0 in June to extend it just before that deadline, and the bill finally cleared final approval in August with unanimous support. That gap between broad political agreement and years of inaction is a pattern environmentalists and officials both recognize. An environmentalist inside MOPT itself, Andrea Ávila, who runs the ministry’s transportation infrastructure project, has been candid about the reason nothing moved for years before the law passed.

She said every wildlife protection measure taken until now came from individual institutional initiative rather than obligation, and did not rule out a lack of political interest, since no law required new construction projects to include such measures. She specifically pointed to Lanamme, the University of Costa Rica’s highway research institute, saying it makes recommendations nobody follows because they carry no legal weight.

A wildlife biologist from the National University’s conservation institute made a similar point, saying the missing piece was never a shortage of impact studies but a legal framework forcing institutions to act on them. That track record matters because it suggests the coming regulatory delay has less to do with a lack of technical groundwork and more to do with institutional follow through. Much of the mapping work the new law assigns SINAC up to 24 months to complete already exists in some form.

A group tied to Universidad Latina compiled more than 19000 roadkill records dating back to 1996, and one 20-kilometer stretch of route 253 in Guanacaste alone was estimated to see around 7000 roadkill incidents annually as of 2019. Panthera, the University of Costa Rica and the Las Pumas rescue center separately tracked wild cat deaths and found 676 felines, jaguars, pumas, ocelots and margays among them, killed on Costa Rican roads between 2012 and 2025, with more than 4200 animals of all kinds struck between 2013 and the present.

Lanamme has also already developed and field tested a methodology for identifying exactly the kind of crossing points the new regulation calls for. Researchers working along the Barbilla Destierro biological subcorridor as part of the Jaguar Corridor Initiative compared roadkill and wildlife sighting data between a paved and an unpaved section of the same road as far back as 2015, documenting jaguar and margay crossings and raccoons using existing culverts.

A separate scientific guide on wildlife friendly roads, developed jointly by conservation and transportation researchers, has been informing individual projects like the route 32 expansion to Limon since 2014, where aerial rope crossings for monkeys and underground tunnels were installed based on monitoring data from that period. Follow up monitoring across existing structures has recorded 59 wildlife species safely using them, though researchers note some sensitive species such as the margay and spider monkey still show limited evidence the current designs work well for them.

None of that existing work resolves the underlying question of how quickly MOPT and SINAC will move once the regulation is actually written, but it does complicate the idea that a two year timeline for identifying priority corridors reflects how much work remains. Much of the mapping this law calls for has already been done piecemeal by university researchers and conservation groups over more than a decade, without a legal mandate forcing anyone to act on it. Whether the regulation leans on that existing research or starts largely from scratch may end up determining whether the two year estimate holds or stretches further.

World.title: Costa Rica Data Leak Probe Widens as Prodhab Opens Its Own Case
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Agency for the Protection of Inhabitants’ Data (Prodhab) has opened its own investigation into an alleged mass leak of personal data on people in Costa Rica. It is the third public body to formally examine the case, which came to light a week ago. Prodhab opened case file No. 425-09-2026 on its own initiative and formally requested information to clarify what happened. The agency will examine whether there were failures in how personal information was handled.

Its inquiry runs alongside those already under way at the Ministry of Science, Innovation, Technology and Telecommunications (Micitt) and the Public Prosecutor’s Office. The case began on Saturday, Sept. 12, when Micitt’s National Cybersecurity Directorate detected a dark web post from a threat actor claiming to have breached a credit reporting agency. The actor claims to hold more than 400 million lines of data on people in Costa Rica.

According to the actor’s claims, the records include information on the beneficial owners of companies, salaries, home addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, photographs, vehicles, and judicial and marriage records. The actor also claimed to have information on President Laura Fernández.

Micitt has confirmed that a sample of about 10,000 lines released by the actor contains real data. Gezer Molina, the national director of cybersecurity, said the investigation seeks to determine whether a breach actually occurred, when it happened and which system was affected.

Investigators are also trying to establish whether the information comes from a single source or is a compilation of databases obtained earlier. Authorities have not publicly identified the entity the files may have come from. Officials have stressed that the appearance of a database on the dark web does not by itself prove the information is authentic, recent or the product of a single breach.
