However, Butsashvili notes that if the cases were caused exclusively by person-to-person transmission, family members of infected children and other close contacts should already have been infected by this stage.

The specialist says it is essential to quickly establish whether there was a common source of a food product and who was involved in preparing and delivering food to the kindergartens.

She also says employees of companies and institutions supplying food to the kindergartens should be tested. Norovirus can be detected in stool for a certain period after infection, which, according to Butsashvili, can help establish the epidemiological chain.

“It is also necessary to establish whether a product that may have been contaminated is being used elsewhere, how many laboratory samples have been tested, and in how many of them the presence of norovirus was confirmed,” Butsashvili says.

Intensive care physician Ani Kavtaradze also said that the relevant authorities should explain:

How could the virus spread to 22 kindergartens at the same time, and why did more than 100 children in different parts of the capital fall ill at roughly the same time?

Kavtaradze’s main question is that children from different kindergartens clearly had no direct contact with one another. Therefore, she believes it is necessary to determine whether the outbreak could have been caused by a common food product or a problem in the supply chain.

What happened

The Tbilisi Kindergarten Management Agency confirmed on 18 September that dozens of children from public kindergartens in the capital had been taken to clinics with symptoms of intoxication. The children had elevated temperatures, and in some cases nausea and vomiting.

On the recommendation of epidemiologists, seven public kindergartens were temporarily closed.

The Investigation Service of the Ministry of Finance has also launched an investigation into the incident. Officials searched the premises of companies supplying food products to the kindergartens.

The investigation is being conducted under Article 198, Part 2 of the Criminal Code, which concerns the production and sale of products dangerous to human life and health when this poses a threat to life or health.

News in Georgia

World.title: “Whoever stands against the people will not go unpunished” | Video podcast “Protests in Georgia”, day 661
World.content:
For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society.

Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms.

For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti.

In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years.

To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

World.title: South Ossetia election: as expected, former Moscow official Marat Kambolov becomes new president
World.content:
Kambolov becomes South Ossetia president

As expected, Marat Kambolov, the prime minister and acting president of South Ossetia who previously held senior positions in the Kremlin, is winning the snap presidential election held on 18 September.

According to preliminary results, he is securing a convincing victory over his formal rivals – state security officer Murat Valiev, South Ossetian University rector’s state adviser Kazbek Kodoev, and Unity party chairman Zurab Kokoev.

After 40% of the ballots had been counted, CEC head Emilia Gagieva said Kambolov had received 88.4% of the vote. Valiev had 4.3%, Kodoev 1.1%, and Kokoev 1.0%.

Marat Kambolov is a former Moscow official who first appeared in South Ossetia in May 2026 as an adviser to then-President Alan Gagloev. He was quickly granted South Ossetian citizenship and, within a month, rose from minister to prime minister, and then became acting president after Alan Gagloev resigned.

Polling stations were also open in Russia – in North Ossetia and Moscow. According to Emilia Gagieva, turnout was high at all polling stations and no violations were recorded.

According to the CEC, the election was monitored by 66 observers from 15 countries: Russia, Abkhazia, Nicaragua, Belarus, Armenia, Venezuela, Germany, Zimbabwe, Kenya, Mexico, Serbia, Tanzania, Turkey, Uganda and South Africa.

CEC member Dina Ostaeva said that “no complaints or appeals related to violations of electoral legislation or the organisation of voting” had been received during the day.

After polling stations closed at 8pm, a celebratory concert and lottery were held in the city centre, with household appliances, smartphones, TVs, bicycles, vacuum cleaners and the grand prize – a Russian-made Niva Legend car – raffled off.

As soon as the prizes had been handed out, Marat Kambolov took the stage, thanked the people of South Ossetia for taking part in the election and said that, in terms of voter turnout, the election had broken all records.

“Preliminary data show that we have broken all records. Never before have so many people taken part. More voters participated in this election than in any previous one. Only together can we strengthen our Tskhinvali and our Ossetia,” Kambolov said.

One of the voters who cast his ballot for Marat Kambolov believes that the high turnout and the large share of votes he received were not so much the result of political strategists’ work as of people believing in Kambolov and voting “for his authority, for the authority of Russia”.

Blogger Alik Pukhaev expressed hope that the new president would “finally make South Ossetia a state for all Ossetians”.

By this, he means the possibility for all ethnic Ossetians to obtain a South Ossetian passport.

At present, the law provides for citizenship only for people born in South Ossetia and their descendants. Under previous governments, however, there were repeated scandals over the illegal issuance — and even sale — of passports to residents of Chechnya, Ingushetia and Dagestan.

Russian State Duma MP Kazbek Taisaev, who observed the election, said it had been organised “at the highest level – transparently, fairly and openly”.

He also stressed that Russia would continue to provide South Ossetia with comprehensive support.

And that is almost certainly what will happen, given that Marat Kambolov is a Russian official who was clearly sent by the Kremlin with the specific aim of taking the presidency and governing in Russia’s interests rather than those of local politicians pursuing their own agendas.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: EU does not recognise “presidential election” in Georgia’s Russian-occupied Tskhinvali region
World.content:
EU condemns Russia and South Ossetia election

The European Union does not recognise the so-called “presidential election” held on 18 September in Georgia’s Russian-occupied Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia). In a statement, the EU Delegation said the results of the election have no legal effect.

Georgia’s Foreign Ministry also condemned the so-called “presidential election”, calling it a violation of Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

The EU statement says it does not recognise the constitutional and legal framework, including recent amendments, under which the election was held in the Russian-occupied region, which unilaterally declared its secession from Georgia.

“The EU strongly condemns Moscow’s actions aimed at installing a Russian official as the de facto president of South Ossetia, Georgia’s occupied breakaway region,” the statement said.

The EU also expressed concern over the signing of the so-called “Treaty on Deepening Allied Cooperation” on 9 May 2026 and criticised Russia’s attempts to strengthen its control over South Ossetia in the political, military, economic and judicial spheres.

The EU considers these steps contrary to a peaceful resolution of the conflict and paving the way for the future illegal annexation of the Russian-occupied region.

“Such actions systematically deepen divisions, threaten regional security and stability, and constitute a flagrant violation of international law,” the EU statement said.

The bloc reaffirmed its commitment to a peaceful resolution of the conflict in Georgia, including through its co-chairmanship of the Geneva International Discussions and the activities of the European Union Monitoring Mission in Georgia.

The EU called on Russia to respect Georgia’s sovereignty and cease all actions undermining its territorial integrity.

“The European Union reaffirms its unwavering support for Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders,” the statement said.

On 18 September, snap “presidential elections” were held in Russian-occupied “South Ossetia”. Four candidates took part.

However, calling it an “election race” would only be accurate in a very loose sense, as it was clear from the outset that the overwhelming favourite was so-called “acting president” and “prime minister” Marat Kambolov, who arrived in the region from Russia in May 2026.

Unlike Kambolov, the other three candidates were residents of South Ossetia. But that was where their advantage ended. Most experts described them as “technical candidates” — people who were not seriously trying to compete for the presidency:

Zurab Kokoev, leader of the Unity party;

Kazbek Kodoev, an independent candidate and adviser to the rector of South Ossetia University;

Murat Valiev, a candidate nominated by the Patriots of Alania party and an employee of the state security service.

None of them campaigned among the population. They presented their views on the development of so-called South Ossetia only during live televised debates.

World.title: Pashinyan’s salary to nearly double as Armenian civil servants set for pay rises from 2027
World.content:
Salary increases for public officials in Armenia

From 1 January 2027, senior Armenian officials will receive higher salaries. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, for example, will earn 2,662,000 drams ($7,353), up from the current 1.5 million ($4,143). Deputy prime ministers’ salaries will rise to 2,163,000 drams ($5,975), from 1,289,000 ($3,560).

The increases will apply not only to the executive branch, but also to the legislative and judicial branches. The state budget will allocate 25 billion drams ($69 million) for this purpose. The government has already approved the draft. Parliament must now approve it.

“How does this public official live? How does he buy a suit and a watch? We never assess the negative impact [of this factor] on the development of our state. But the effect is highly negative. If we do not solve this problem, it will lead to disasters,” Nikol Pashinyan said during a discussion of the draft.

The ruling party views the decision as a reform. The prime minister said he was confident that failing to implement the project would mean “keeping Armenia stuck in place and continuing to subordinate the logic of the state to the logic of corruption”.

However, the opposition warns that such decisions will further deepen the sense of social injustice.

“Citizens often become disillusioned and leave the country not only because of economic difficulties, but also because of a sense of injustice,” former MP Garnik Danielyan said.

Salary increases in figures

Under the proposed amendments to the law “On remuneration for persons holding public office”:

the president of Armenia will earn 2,662,000 drams ($7,353), up from the current 1,664,000 drams ($4,596);

the speaker of the National Assembly will earn 2,496,000 drams ($6,895), up from 1,497,600 drams ($4,137);

MPs will earn up to 1,497,600 drams ($4,137), up from 832,000 drams ($2,311);

the president of the Constitutional Court will earn 2,412,800 drams ($6,665), up from 1,664,000 drams ($4,596);

the prosecutor general will earn 1,830,400 drams ($5,056), up from 1,248,000 drams ($3,447);

the ombudsman will earn 1,830,400 drams ($5,056), up from 998,400 drams ($2,758).

Governors, deputy ministers and deputy speakers of parliament will also receive higher salaries.

The stated amounts include taxes and other mandatory payments.

Ruling party representative’s assessment and opposition response

Eduard Aghajanyan, an MP from the ruling party, told journalists:

“The public administration system has consistently faced difficulties attracting highly qualified specialists. The issue became particularly acute after the 2018 revolution, when the logic of working within the system changed radically. Systemic corruption was eradicated, and the motivation mechanisms were completely restructured.

At the same time, pay levels made the public administration system unattractive to highly qualified professionals.

We have been at the helm of government for eight years now. I believe that the decision to address this issue is somewhat overdue.

I welcome the government’s decision. I am confident that it will produce the desired results in attracting highly qualified professionals.”

Former MP from the opposition Armenia bloc Garnik Danielyan wrote on his Facebook page:

“According to official data for 2024, Armenia’s poverty rate stands at 21.7%. One in four children lives in poverty, while thousands of families continue to face severe social hardship. People struggle to meet their basic needs. Moreover, in the 21st century, Armenia has recorded cases of people dying from hunger.

In your 2021 election programme, you [addressing the authorities] promised to halve the poverty rate by 2026. Poverty has not declined. But you yourselves are now living better. You no longer buy vacuum cleaners or televisions on instalment plans. Instead, you are accumulating assets.

Of course, no one objects to high salaries for public officials. But given this level of poverty, should the priorities not be addressing social problems, creating new jobs and ensuring decent living conditions for people?

And this is happening while Armenia’s public debt has already exceeded $14 billion. Housing and employment remain critical issues for thousands of Karabakh Armenians. Hundreds of people still live in temporary shelters, and many are forced to buy groceries on credit.

Clearly, political calculations also lie behind this decision — namely, preserving loyalty within the state system.”

Comments from Armenian residents on social media

The decision to raise the salaries of senior public officials has sparked heated discussions on social media. Most users criticised the authorities. Here are some of their comments:

“Of course, raising the salaries of civil servants and public officials is important. But we must not forget a phenomenon that is shameful for Armenia. Librarians receive the lowest salaries [75,000 drams — $208]. Raise them!”

“After spending days and nights thinking about the people, the ‘democratic’ government decided to raise its own salaries by 60–80%. Meanwhile, citizens earning 80,000–150,000 drams ($220–414) can continue entering shops full of goods. As prices rise rapidly, they must painfully choose whether to buy food for their child or shoes for themselves.”

“They are setting their salaries higher than those of members of the British royal family. And they are paying for all this with our taxes. They will bleed us dry. This is only the beginning.”

“The [prime minister] claims that raising his salary and those of other officials is necessary to prevent a catastrophe. According to this passionate speaker, a ‘catastrophe’ is when someone asks where an official got his suit or watch. I wonder who will ask him what he plans to spend those 2,662,000 drams — around $7,400 — a month on, considering how expensive he is for the state. For nine years now, you have paid neither rent nor utility bills, car expenses, petrol or maintenance costs.”

Salary increases for public officials in Armenia

World.title: Tbilisi condemns “presidential election” in Georgia’s Russian-occupied Tskhinvali region
World.content:
Georgia condemns Russia over South Ossetia election

Georgia’s Foreign Ministry condemned the so-called “presidential election” held on 18 September in the Russian-occupied Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia), calling it a violation of Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

According to the ministry’s statement, “the opening of polling stations by Russia in the occupied territory without the consent of the Georgian government is a gross violation of Georgia’s sovereignty and another manifestation of Russia’s policy aimed at the de facto annexation of Georgia’s regions.”

Georgia’s Foreign Ministry said that holding the so-called election violates fundamental norms and principles of international law and cannot legitimise the occupation regime in Tskhinvali or change the region’s status under international law as part of Georgia.

“Holding any so-called elections in Georgia’s occupied territories, which are under military occupation and the effective control of the Russian Federation, while internally displaced persons and refugees are not given the opportunity to return to their homes safely and with dignity, is illegal and cannot have any international legal consequences,” the ministry said.

Tbilisi also condemned Russia’s decision to open polling stations for the Russian State Duma election in occupied Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region from 18 to 20 September.

The Foreign Ministry called on the international community to properly assess and condemn Russia’s actions and ensure an appropriate international legal and political response.

“Georgia continues to call on the international community to firmly protect Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders and support a peaceful resolution of the conflict,” the statement said.

World.title: Armenia’s anti-corruption campaign: law on confiscating illicit assets takes effect
World.content:
Armenia’s law on confiscating illicit property

A large-scale anti-corruption campaign is unfolding in Armenia . As part of the campaign, the state is confiscating assets belonging to members of the country’s former financial and political elite.

The authorities say they are moving from high-profile political accusations to a systematic effort to recover illegally acquired property. The list of people accused of corruption whose numerous properties and business assets have been frozen includes former Armenian president Robert Kocharyan , Prosperous Armenia party leader Gagik Tsarukyan, and former finance minister and ex-head of the State Revenue Committee Gagik Khachatryan. Prosecutors accuse those involved in these high-profile cases of money laundering, bribery and abuse of office.

At the same time, the debate in Armenia goes beyond how they managed to amass such wealth. It also concerns whether the process complies with the law, whether the authorities apply the law equally to everyone, and whether the confiscated property is genuinely being returned to the people.

About the law

Armenia’s Law on Confiscation of Property of Illicit Origin has been in force since 2020. The authorities adopted it “to strengthen the fight against corruption and restore social justice”. The law applies to assets worth more than 50 million drams ($132,120). It allows the state to confiscate property if its owner cannot prove that the income used to acquire it came from legal sources.

According to the Prosecutor General’s Office, between 2018 and the first half of 2026, the state and local communities recovered assets worth approximately 304 billion drams (around $840 million). More than two-thirds of that amount — about $562 million — was recovered over the past three and a half years.

Comment from lawyer Aram Orbelyan

“The Law on Confiscation of Property of Illicit Origin contains fundamental contradictions. In international practice, confiscation models are clearly separated. One involves checking declarations: if a person cannot explain their income, the state confiscates the property. The other involves confiscation following proof of a crime. Our lawmakers, however, have mixed everything together into complete confusion.

The grounds for an investigation are chaotic. Half of the provisions are linked to criminal cases, including cases that authorities have suspended or closed on non-exonerating grounds. The other half allows officials to launch confiscation proceedings based simply on ‘operational information’. As soon as any intelligence report appears, law-enforcement agencies immediately begin examining a person’s property, going back as far as 1991.”

The factual vacuum of the 1990s

“What political statements describe as ‘plunder’ is often impossible to prove in court because the circumstances of that era were different. In the 1990s, non-monetary transactions, including agricultural exchanges, were widespread. There was no clear system of tax and customs control. Vehicle databases only appeared in the early 2000s, while electronic tax records emerged in 2013.

Moreover, the law at the time did not require businesses to keep documents for more than five years. This has naturally created an information vacuum today. Young prosecutors fail to take this historical context into account, leading to dead ends in court.”

Intrusion into private life and the political context

“The extent of the intrusion into private life raises serious questions. The law allows investigators to examine years of bank statements belonging to any relatives of a person under investigation. As a result, investigators and prosecutors gain access to strictly personal spending unrelated to corruption: where people went on holiday, what they ordered in cafés and what illnesses they received treatment for.

Society sees this mechanism exclusively as a ‘law to recover what former [authorities] stole’. Legally, however, the law should target corruption as such, rather than individuals. To ensure that anti-corruption tools do not appear politically selective, they must operate universally. They should apply to all elites, regardless of their current political status or affiliation with the ruling camp.

Authorities must examine both the past and the present transparently, without politically motivated cases, while taking limitation periods and the economic realities of earlier years into account. The process should objectively target illicit property, rather than serve as a selectively applied repressive tool.”

Comment from Varuzhan Hoktanian, an expert at Transparency International’s Anti-Corruption Centre

“The law sparked legal disputes from the outset, which led to a review of its constitutionality by the Constitutional Court. The court, in turn, sought an expert opinion from the Venice Commission. International experts offered two key recommendations. First, the confiscation of property for the benefit of the state should take place through separate civil proceedings, rather than criminal prosecution resulting in imprisonment. Second, some responsibility for proving the lawful origin of assets should fall on the owner.

It is often extremely difficult to prove that property has a corrupt origin. For example, Kocharyan’s case involves the signing of government decisions. For the charges to stand, the prosecution must prove that he deliberately approved specific decisions in the expectation that the assets would eventually pass to his family. This is extremely difficult to establish, so the evidence often appears unconvincing. The situation is compounded by the absence of a mandatory declaration system in the 1990s. As a result, it is now virtually impossible to confirm that property was acquired legally.”

Discrimination or fight against corruption?

“Applying legal mechanisms exclusively to one group of people discredits the anti-corruption institution itself, turning the law into a tool of political pressure. Attempts to deprive opponents of financial resources by seizing their property create a risk of completely clearing the political field. If this is combined with double standards during elections — harsh punishment, including arrests, for vote-buying while ignoring the abuse of administrative resources — the system of checks and balances itself collapses. Ignoring any of these abuses leads to dictatorship.”

What happens to confiscated property?

“The legal question is only one side of the problem. The question of what happens to confiscated property after the state receives it is no less important.

I recall a similar confiscation from Soviet history — the dekulakisation campaign of the late 1920s and early 1930s. We later learned about the grave consequences it caused, including the Holodomor. As it turned out, the party nomenklatura ultimately received everything that the authorities had seized. Today, these assets could likewise pass to new wealthy individuals or another nomenklatura. Once again, ordinary people would receive nothing.

When people talk about confiscating property, they mean both financial assets and movable and immovable property. For example, someone may have built a luxurious house and live in it. If we return to the Soviet example, after the October Revolution, the authorities seized property from wealthy people and turned luxury homes into communal apartments. That will not happen in our case. No one plans to move an ordinary citizen into someone else’s mansion. This raises the question: who received the mansion belonging to formerprimeministerformer prime minister Hovik Abrahamyan, or the Golden Palace hotel in Tsaghkadzor?

The situation is also problematic here. Even if a new wealthy owner buys these properties, a change of government could lead to their seizure again, with the authorities claiming that the original confiscation was unlawful.

Moreover, the phrase ‘returning property to the people’ sounds somewhat abstract to me. The trend shows that confiscated real estate goes not to the people, but to another wealthy person close to the authorities. And the public will ask: ‘What do we get out of it?’

Let me give you an example. There used to be a kindergarten in our courtyard. A newly wealthy owner acquired it through an illegal transfer. If the state takes the building back today and restores its former status as a kindergarten, then yes, that would mean ‘returning it to the people’.

In other cases, this could become a vicious circle in which each successive government dispossesses the previous one. This is quite dangerous, especially in the context of investment. Investors should not have to fear that the authorities might dispossess them tomorrow.”

How can confiscated funds be used?

“As for monetary confiscations, the seized funds go into the budget, into what is known as a ‘common pot’. It is unclear how the authorities then spend this money. These are not earmarked revenues, so the authorities decide how to use them.

It would be better to classify these revenues as earmarked funds and regulate them by law, directing the money towards social programmes designed to improve citizens’ welfare.”

Armenia’s law on confiscating illicit property

World.title: Poll: Do Abkhazia residents consider voting in Russia’s State Duma elections important? Video
World.content:
Russia’s State Duma elections will take place on 20 September. As most residents of Abkhazia hold dual Abkhaz-Russian citizenship, they can also take part in the vote. In the republic, which has a population of 250,000, as many as 35 polling stations have opened, and campaigning is in full swing.

Ahead of the election, we asked residents of Sukhum whether they planned to vote and whether they believed doing so would make a real difference.

The poll produced highly contradictory responses. Some people do not want to spend their day off voting in another country. Others consider it very important because, “if things go badly in Russia, things will get very hot here in Abkhazia too”.

Rustam: “For some reason, Russia is placing great importance on Abkhazia at the moment, and they really want all residents to take part in these elections. Perhaps it does not even matter how people vote, because there is no alternative. What matters is showing the turnout — that people are actively and collectively going to the polls, thereby acknowledging the assistance Russia provides to Abkhazia.

Personally, I will not vote because I see no point in it. If the [Yabloko party] had not been barred from the election, I would definitely have voted. Or I would have supported the Communists. As things stand, I do not want to spend my day off that way.”

Eliso: “I will definitely go to the polls and vote.

I will not say whom I will vote for. But as a Russian passport holder, I have the right to influence the composition of the State Duma, because the decisions made there directly affect us.

As a woman and a future mother, I want Abkhazia residents with Russian citizenship to be able to receive child benefits. I believe this bill should be among the first issues considered by the new parliamentary term.”

Timur: “I always vote in every election, both ours and Russia’s. My choice may almost never win, but I want to feel involved and have at least some opportunity to influence events. Russia directly affects us, and by voting I make my small contribution to what is happening in Abkhazia today.”

Almaskhan: “I will not vote. I never take part in elections and I am not interested in politics. I do not even know which parties are currently running or what they decide. Everything is done without us anyway. We live in a reality that we simply have to adapt to. It is impossible to change anything with a ‘tick’ on a ballot — everything has already been decided.”

Liana: “I will see how things go on Sunday, but I am not particularly keen. I do not even know whom to choose. The only party I hear about is United Russia, because its s are everywhere. Everyone says it is the strongest party. And Kiriyenko (the Kremlin’s overseer of Abkhazia — JAMnews) is a member, so apparently everything here is done through them. If I go, I will probably vote for them.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Will Abkhaz vote in Russia’s State Duma elections?

World.title: Uzbekistan’s mortgage lending reaches $1.5B in 8M2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 21. Commercial banks in Uzbekistan extended 18.3 trillion soums (about $1.5 billion) in mortgage loans to 59,200 individuals from January through August 2026, up 4.9 trillion soums (around $414.4 million) from the same period last year.

This was reflected in the statement by the Central Bank of Uzbekistan.

According to the bank, the average interest rates on mortgage loans issued during this period ranged from 16.9% to 21.6%, depending on the source of funding.

The primary housing market accounted for the majority of mortgage lending, with 74% of total loans directed toward newly built housing. The remaining 26% went to purchases in the secondary housing market.

According to Trend’s calculations, primary-market mortgage lending amounted to approximately 13.54 trillion soums (around $1.1 billion), while secondary-market lending totaled about 4.76 trillion soums (around $402.3 million). The difference between the two segments was therefore roughly 8.78 trillion soums (approx. $742 million), with lending to new housing nearly 2.85 times higher than lending to the secondary market.

The data also show that younger and middle-aged borrowers accounted for most mortgage recipients. Borrowers aged 31-50 represented 64% of the total, while those aged 18-30 accounted for 26%.

Borrowers aged 18-30 represented approximately 15,400 people, while the 31-50 age group accounted for about 37,900 borrowers. Together, the two groups represented 90%, or roughly 53,300 individuals, of all mortgage borrowers during the eight-month period.

The average mortgage size can also be estimated from the total lending volume and number of borrowers. Calculations show that 18.3 trillion soums (around $1.5 billion) distributed among 59,200 borrowers corresponds to an average mortgage of approximately 309 million soums (approx. $26.113) per borrower. This is an aggregate average and does not indicate the typical loan size for an individual borrower.

The increase in total mortgage lending of 4.9 trillion soums (about $414 million) indicates continued expansion in housing finance compared with the same period of 2025. At the same time, the dominant share of lending to the primary market points to sustained financing demand for newly constructed housing.

Uzbekistan’s mortgage market in January-August 2026 was characterized by both higher lending volumes and strong concentration in the primary housing segment. Interest rates remained relatively high, while the distribution of borrowers indicates that people aged 18-50 accounted for the overwhelming majority of mortgage demand.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s manufacturing grows up to 38.9% in January-August 2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 21. Kazakhstan's manufacturing sector demonstrated substantial growth across multiple high-value segments in January-August 2026, according to data from the Bureau of National Statistics of Kazakhstan.

Leading the expansion, the production of basic pharmaceutical products and pharmaceutical preparations surged by 38.9%, while the manufacturing of finished metal products, except machinery and equipment, increased by 33.3%. Significant gains were also observed in the chemical industry, which grew by 27.3%, and mechanical engineering, which expanded by 21.2%. Food production and the manufacturing of rubber and plastic products rose by 12.9% and 18.5%, respectively.

According to Trend calculations, the average growth rate across these five leading segments reached 26.7%, more than three times the manufacturing sector's overall growth rate of 8.4%, reflecting a structural shift toward higher value-added goods. Meanwhile, the overall index of physical volume for the manufacturing sector reached 108.4% compared to the corresponding period of 2025.

In contrast, the mining and quarrying sector recorded an industrial production index of 95.7%, weighed down by declines in the extraction of crude oil to 91.6% and natural gas to 94.6%. According to Trend calculations, the gap between manufacturing and mining performance reached 12.7 percentage points in January-August 2026, up from 13.4 percentage points a month earlier, as the divergence between accelerating manufacturing output and decelerating resource extraction highlights Kazakhstan's ongoing industrial diversification efforts.

The currency conversions are based on the official exchange rate of 1 USD = 444.88 tenge as of September 17, 2026.

World.title: Tajikistan's chemical output jumps 1.6 times in 7M2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 21. Chemical production in Tajikistan amounted to 483.1 million somoni ($52.4 million) in the period from January through July 2026, increasing 1.6 times compared with the same period in 2025.

The information was announced by the Agency on Statistics under the President of the Republic of Tajikistan.

According to the Statistics Agency, in July 2026, chemical production amounted to 115.4 million somoni ($12.5 million), increasing 1.7 times compared with July 2025. For comparison, chemical production increased by 20.6% in July 2025 compared with July 2024, while January-July 2025 output increased by 7.4% year-on-year.

"Overall manufacturing production in Tajikistan amounted to 20.32 billion somoni ($2.2 billion) in January-July 2026, increasing by 24.7% compared with January-July 2025. In July 2026, manufacturing output reached 2.78 billion somoni ($301.9 million), up 18% year-on-year. For comparison, manufacturing production increased by 9.6% in July 2025 compared with July 2024, while January-July 2025 manufacturing output increased by 6% compared with the same period of 2024, the Agency on Statistics noted.

Total industrial production in Tajikistan amounted to 39.46 billion somoni ($4.28 billion) in January-July 2026, increasing by 13.1% compared with January-July 2025. In July 2026, industrial production reached 5.74 billion somoni ($621.8 million), up 9.4% compared with July 2025.

Furthermore, in July 2025, total industrial production increased by 23.6% compared with July 2024, while January-July 2025 industrial output increased by 24.5% year-on-year.

Trend’s analysis indicates that continued expansion in chemical production could increase the contribution of the chemical industry to Tajikistan’s manufacturing sector and support greater domestic production of industrial inputs and processed goods. If the average monthly chemical production recorded during January-July 2026 is maintained through the end of the year, annual output could reach approximately 828.2 million somoni ($89.8 million), based on a simple Trend calculation.

If chemical production maintains a more moderate annual growth rate of 20-30 percent in 2027, output could potentially reach around 994 million to 1.08 billion somoni ($107.8-117.1 million). Further expansion could support the development of domestic manufacturing and reduce reliance on some imported chemical products, although the actual results would depend on investment, production capacity, access to raw materials, and market demand. These forward-looking figures are Trend calculations based on January-July 2026 data and hypothetical growth scenarios, not official forecasts.

World.title: DPP drops murder charge against final suspect in Omega Ruston shooting
World.content:
Murder charges over the fatal shooting of Gold Coast man Omega Ruston have been dropped against alleged longtime person of interest Paul Younan.

Mr Younan, a former Nomads Outlaw Motorcycle Club member, had his murder charge discontinued in the Brisbane Magistrates Court on Monday.

The prosecutor told the court the "the crown offers no evidence in respect to that charge of murder".

It had been alleged Mr Ruston was standing next to his car on the side of the Gold Coast Highway at Burleigh Heads when a passenger in another car shot him twice.

Police had previously said they believed the two cars were part of a road rage incident just minutes before the 32-year-old was shot.

A crime scene was declared at Burleigh Heads following the death of Omega Ruston. (ABC News)

Cold case

A full review into the unsolved homicide was launched in 2020 by the Homicide Cold Case Investigation Team and Gold Coast Criminal Investigation Branch.

Authorities launched a fresh appeal a year later, saying there had been a forensic breakthrough in DNA, fingerprint and ballistics evidence, and announcing a $250,000 reward for information leading to a conviction in the case.

In 2022, detectives charged four men in relation to the death, including Mr Younan, who was arrested by highway patrol officers and New South Wales' bikie-busting Raptor Squad while travelling on the M4 at Huntingwood in NSW.

When Mr Younan was granted bail in August 2022, concerns were raised about whether an eyewitness to the shooting would give evidence.

Supreme Court Justice Melanie Hindman in granting bail noted the crown had been asked to produce a statement from an eyewitness who had been given the code name A.

She said the crown had failed to produce the statement.

Police have spent 17 years attempting to gather evidence. (ABC TV News)

Justice Hindman said the statement was supposed to have identified the applicant as the shooter in the killing.

But she stated, there was doubt that the statement "in fact existed in written form".

She said: "[This] casts serious doubt on whether witness A is a cooperative witness and is likely to give evidence in accordance with what police have said that witness A can give.

"Counsel for the crown properly and candidly conceded to the court that without the evidence of witness A, the crown case against the applicant on the murder charge is unlikely to be able to proceed."

Justice Hindman also said the crown had been invited to produce the witness statement on a confidential basis without the applicant or his legal representatives being able to view the same, and without waiving public interest immunity in the document.

But she said the crown did not produce the statement.

Bail was granted, with Mr Younan's wife involved in providing a surety of $5.5 million, according to the Justice Hindman's judgment.

Mr Younan has 27 remaining charges of perjury in relation to the case, which are set to heard in the Brisbane Magistrate Court on October 12.

Omega Ruston is survived by his two children. (Supplied: Ruston family)

Family say they are disappointed by the outcome

Mr Ruston's brothers, Nicholas and Chris Ruston, told ABC News they were floored at the Director of Public Prosecutions' (DPP) decision to discontinue the charges.

"The DPP has decided that the accused has no charges to stand for … we're deeply saddened," Nicholas Ruston said.

Omega Ruston was 32 years of age when he died. (Supplied: Ruston family)

"We're at a complete loss with the criminal justice system … for a state that's promoting being tough on crime and illegal firearm use, it's a real slap in the face for us."

Mr Ruston said the family had hoped the charges would progress to trial.

Nicholas (left) and Chris Ruston say their family is deeply disappointed and angered by the decision to drop charges against Mr Younan. (ABC News)

The family had previously been told that Mr Younan was the prime suspect in the police investigation.

Murder charges against previously co-accused Toni Elbayeh and Hysam Hamdan were dropped last October, while an accessory-after-the-fact charge against Brent Simpson was also discontinued.

'We've lost faith'

Although the family spoke highly of the work cross-border investigation between Queensland and New South Wales Police in the past 17 years, Chris Ruston said he had lost hope they would ever see justice.

"We've never had a chance to grieve properly. Two young children have had to grow up without a father," he said.

The Ruston family fears it will never get justice for their son, brother and father. (Supplied: Ruston family)

"We just hope and pray that someone who does know [what happened], who was there, eventually comes forward."

Nicholas Ruston said there was not a day that goes by where the family were not thinking of Mr Ruston and hoping to get closure.

"The DPP seems to have closed the courtroom doors on this matter and are handballing it on. [The case] could go to the coroner's court," he said.

"We're not feeling as if we're ever going to get closure or a sense of justice. We've lost faith."

World.title: Breaking: H5 bird flu found in four sea lions, including a pup, on SA islands
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

South Australia’s sea lion population is increasingly being impacted by the H5 bird flu, with four of the mammals – including one pup – testing positive for the virus.

The sea lions were among several found dead on the North Page and South Page islands, a key breeding location for the animals between the South Australian mainland and Kangaroo Island.

There has also been a mass mortality event involving crested terns on the Pages, with about 900 of the birds found dead.

SA Environment Minister Emily Bourke said out of 10 deceased sea lions available for testing, three adults and one pup returned positive results.

The results bring the total number of South Australian sea lions with bird flu up to five, following a positive case at Kangaroo Island's Seal Bay last week.

There have been significant fears from environmentalists that the virus could devastate the sea lion population, which is recorded as endangered on international threatened species lists.

Ms Bourke said discussions are underway with the federal government to gain approval for a vaccine trial targeting mammals.

She said a separate trial aimed specifically at birds has been underway at Cleland Wildlife Park, with more than 150 vaccines administered since last month.

"We are pulling every lever possible to show we are willing, able and capable of participating in a national vaccine program," she said.

Separately, magpies have also tested positive at Hindmarsh Island, which Ms Bourke said was indication the virus would eventually travel further inland.

"We've seen it in Monarto, we've seen it in metropolitan areas, within inland areas in South Australia," she said.

"This isn't a coastal issue ... it is a national issue, and it is being addressed that way."

The government said two dead sea lions on Liguanea Island, off the southern point of Eyre Peninsula, were also tested but returned negative results for bird flu.

World.title: 'Not enough' mental health beds in Tasmania after arson attack, union warns
World.content:
The loss of the only dedicated public mental health facility in Tasmania's north-west will place a "huge" strain on a health system already at crisis point, the health union says.

The Spencer Clinic, which operates out of Burnie's North West Regional Hospital, suffered extensive damage following an allegedly deliberately lit fire on Saturday night.

Police have charged a 28-year-old woman with one count of arson.

The fire damaged one part of the clinic but the smoke reached most areas. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Robbie Moore, from the Health and Community Services Union (HACSU), told ABC Northern Tasmania the clinic's 19 beds were full at the time of the incident.

He said the facility had been operating over capacity for most of the past 12 months.

An interim arrangement has led to Spencer Clinic patients being transferred to North West Private Hospital and Launceston General Hospital, with some to be moved to Royal Hobart Hospital later today.

"Both of those other two [public] hospitals are at capacity as well so there's not really enough beds to cover this," Mr Moore said.

"Anybody needing services into the future is going to continue to have major issues moving forward."

Firefighters were called to the scene on Saturday night. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Mr Moore is travelling to Burnie today to meet with frontline workers. He says he is concerned for the staff.

"They've been through a very traumatic event on Saturday night," he said.

"They're obviously very concerned about how they support the people that would be in the Spencer Clinic at the moment and making sure that everyone is getting all the support and debriefing and things like that need to occur."

The ward was full when it was evacuated. (Tasmanian government)

Mr Moore said there would be scope for more hospital-in-the-home care — a virtual way to look after patients — to help with the lack of beds.

"It's obviously very early days, but they [the department] are looking at all the options for being able to support people in all the different ways," he said.

" But it also does demonstrate that there was no ability to deal with a situation like this within the mental health area. "

Mr Moore and the health department both reiterated that anyone in the region suffering a mental health crisis should still present to the North West Regional Hospital emergency department or call Triple Zero in an emergency.

The loss of the ward will have flow-on effects to other hospitals. (Tasmanian government)

Department will try to fast-track new clinic

It is expected the Spencer Clinic will be unable to treat patients for an extended period.

Tasmanian health secretary Dale Webster told 936 ABC Hobart it was too early to tell if the current clinic would ever reopen.

"The fire service still hadn't handed it back to us late yesterday," he said.

The North West Regional Hospital mental health patients were moved to other hospitals. (ABC News)

"So the first opportunity for building surveyors and insurance assessors to get into the unit is likely to be today or tomorrow and that means that we'll need to wait on that advice before we can actually make decisions about which way forward."

He said he was glad no-one was injured.

"The staff did a fantastic job and emergency services were on site very, very quickly so more damage was prevented," he said.

A woman has been charged with arson over the fire. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

He said the health department was working on longer-term solutions to keep patients near home.

The state government had already announced plans to replace the Spencer Clinic with a $40 million mental health precinct.

The new precinct is set to provide places for 22 patients by mid-2028.

"I've talked to our infrastructure team yesterday and I'm meeting with them today," Mr Webster said.

"We will do everything we can to get that unit online before the mid-2028 current deadline."

World.title: NRL set to act over 'embarrassing' referee abuse
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The NRL has threatened to ban spectators who threw projectiles at referee Ashley Klein, with the league's integrity unit investigating the aftermath of Sunday's semifinal in Auckland.

Footage from after full-time in Newcastle's 12-10 win over the Warriors at Eden Park showed a raft of bottles, cups and rubbish being thrown at Klein as he walked from the field.

Projectiles thrown at ref as Knights win Projectiles have been thrown at the NRL refereeing crew following Newcastle's upset semifinal win over the New Zealand Warriors.

Klein had to be protected by security as fans abused the veteran referee and threw projectiles.

The NRL immediately launched an investigation into potential breaches of its spectators' code of conduct.

An integrity unit investigator had been at the ground.

"If found guilty, they [the fans] will be banned for a period of time from attending NRL games," ARL Commission chair Peter V'landys said.

Auckland police have since confirmed no arrests were made.

They said there were "no issues to note", other than two pitch invaders.

The Warriors exited the finals following the loss to the Knights. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

Sunday's crowd of 48,511 marked the largest ever for a rugby league match in New Zealand, after the NRL made the call to move the match from Mount Smart Stadium.

The spectator abuse came after two contentious calls went against the Warriors late in the match, including a decision not to penalise Tyson Frizell for an escort in the dying minutes.

Warriors great Shaun Johnson hit out at the response of spectators after the match, labelling it "embarrassing".

"It leaves a bit of a sour taste in your mouth [after] what has been an unbelievable night with the colours, the energy, the happiness and celebration," Johnson said on Sky NZ's coverage.

"But there is just no need for it. It's just embarrassing.

"Ashley Klein has probably refereed the best game of rugby league I have seen in a long time tonight.

Hawks fans facing bans Hawthorn supporters who threw bottles at umpires after a controversial finals exit face lengthy bans if identified by the AFL and Victoria Police.

"He didn't take any gamesmanship in terms of people laying down. He didn't let people approach him whingeing.

"He didn't make the game about him. He let the players come and play and they dictated the outcome."

Warriors coach Andrew Webster vented his frustration in the post-match media conference, highlighting a bunker strip call on Te Maire Martin and the decision not to penalise Frizell for a possible escort on Leka Halasima.

"The last one, [when] two points would have drawn the game, he [Frizell] is going across Leka, pretending to try and catch the ball, which they've told us you can't do," Webster said.

The incident came after AFL umpires also had bottles and cans thrown at them while leaving the MCG following Hawthorn's nine-point loss to the Brisbane Lions in Saturday night's preliminary final.

The AFL has condemned the behaviour and warned of minimum five-year bans for any fans found responsible.

AAP

World.title: Everything you need to know about the 2026 Brownlow Medal count
World.content:
The AFL's grand final week is here, and will begin as usual with the awarding of the Brownlow Medal tonight.

The best-and-fairest player of the 2026 season will be presented with the AFL's highest award at the end of the evening, with a first-time winner widely expected to be crowned.

The fashion on display beforehand on the red carpet will also be a big focus of attention.

Here is what you need to know about the AFL's night of nights.

What time is the 2026 Brownlow Medal?

The Brownlow Medal count will be held tonight, Monday, September 21, with the broadcast coverage starting at 7:30pm (AEST) and the count getting underway from 8pm.

Red carpet guests arrive from 5:15pm. The mark of the year winner will be announced at 8:35pm, and the goal of the year at 9pm.

How can I watch and follow the Brownlow Medal?

ABC Sport will be live blogging all the action with every vote from every round at abc.net.au.

The broadcast of the event from Melbourne's Crown Palladium will be on Channel 7 and 7Plus.

Who is the favourite to win the 2026 Brownlow?

Collingwood's Nick Daicos is the unbackable favourite.

As a demonstration of his favouritism, most bookmakers have listed him at $1.01 to win.

However, Daicos was also the strong favourite to win last season before coming second to the Gold Coast's Matt Rowell by seven votes.

Other players in the discussion are Geelong's Bailey Smith, Bulldogs captain Marcus Bontempelli, and Carlton star Patrick Cripps.

Can umpires access stats when they give their votes?

Traditionally umpires haven't had access to game stats when they cast their votes directly after a match.

That has changed this year, after St Kilda's Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera was controversially deemed as not being the best player on the field in a game against Melbourne last season, despite being the clear star on the day.

This season umpires were given access to stats, including: kicks, handballs, disposals, marks, contested marks, tackles, goals, behinds, goal assists, score involvements, clearances, contested possessions, hitouts, kick-ins, intercept marks, intercept possessions and spoils.

Can the banned Sydney Swans players receive votes in the Brownlow?

Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon were all banned from playing finals after breaching club standards.

The players were also deemed ineligible of making the All Australian team, with Heeney and Warner both likely to have been named if not for the ban.

However, all players will be able to receive votes in the Brownlow, and all votes will count.

Heeney is considered a top 10 prospect in the award.

How does the Brownlow work?

Unlike other awards, the Brownlow Medal is decided by the votes of the umpires.

For every game of the home-and-away season (not counting finals), umpires award votes to the three best players on the field.

The best player is given three votes, the second-best two votes, and the third-best one vote.

The votes are kept secret and are revealed round-by-round at the ceremony.

The player who ends with the most votes at the end of the season is crowned the Brownlow Medal winner.

The award is for the fairest and best players, so those who have been suspended for a week or more during the season are ineligible. Corey McKernan (1996) and Chris Grant (1997) are the most recent examples of ineligible players notching the most votes, while Jobe Watson won the medal in 2012 before having it rescinded in the wake of Essendon's supplements scandal.

In the event of a tie, the Brownlow can be shared, as was the case in 2003 when Adelaide's Mark Ricciuto, Collingwood's Nathan Buckley and Sydney's Adam Goodes shared the medal.

World.title: Coldplay singer reveals how Shane Warne introduced him to John Farnham
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Coldplay has sold out stadiums around the world, but the band's lead singer has declared that he can't compete with Australian music legend John Farnham's voice.

International and Australian performers came together to celebrate Farnham's music career at a charity concert in Melbourne last night, raising money for head and neck cancer.

Coldplay frontman Chris Martin recorded a special song to be played at the concert called A Better Singer Than Me.

"I'm really sorry I can't be with you," he told a sold-out crowd at the Rod Laver Arena show.

"John, I send you all my love.

"Shane Warne is the person that told me about how great you are.

"And this is a song about that and about you."

Loading...

Farnham's son, James Farnham, said in a social media post that the original song was a "wild" surprise.

"I knew Chris Martin was doing the show, but I had no idea what he was actually doing," he said.

"This video is me out in the crowd, watching it for the first time.

"I still can’t believe he wrote a song for my dad."

The song explained how Martin was introduced to Farnham's music during a trip to check in on bushfire-impacted communities in Victoria after the devastation of Black Saturday in 2009.

"My friend Shane said to me, 'There's been a bloody big bushfire. It's something you should see. I'm going in up to Kinglake to check on how they are and I made us a mix tape, we can listen in the car,'" Martin sang.

" 'And I really do love Coldplay. I love Coldplay, it's true. But my favourite is John Farnham, he's a better singer than you.' "

Farnham performed You're the Voice, backed by Coldplay, at the Sound Relief concert at the SCG in 2009 to raise money for communities affected by the Black Saturday bushfires.

Martin also referred to this in his song, with tongue-in-cheek lyrics saying singer-songwriter Natalie Imbruglia suggested that Farnham would be the better choice to lead a relief show.

"She said, 'Here's what you can do. You can call John Farnham, he's a better singer than you,'" Martin sang.

John Farnham and Chris Martin performed together at the Sound Relief concert in 2009. ( AAP: Joe Castro)

Farnham was unable to attend the Melbourne concert due to deteriorating health, with his family releasing a statement on the weekend.

His star power was still felt during the show, as other entertainers took to the stage to perform beloved songs from the 77-year-old's catalogue.

Jessica Mauboy, John Stevens, Jack Jones, Mahalia Barnes and Human Nature opened the show with a medley of Farnham songs.

Hugh Jackman and Celine Dion were also beamed into the arena from abroad, both performing Farnham songs that had inspired them.

Martin sang that Farnham's songs would keep living even once "we've all gone".

World.title: Investor saves Brisbane bowling club in $6m deal
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Coorparoo Bowls Club will no longer be demolished to make way for high-rise apartments, after the club was snapped up by a local investor for $6 million.

It comes after a multi-year-long campaign by the club's committee, which were due to be evicted in May this year.

Instead, the site was bought by Coorparoo local Will Griffin from Griffin Hospitality Group in a deal inked with Bowls Queensland.

As part of the deal, Griffith Hospitality will keep both of the bowling greens, one of which will be used for competitions and the other for casual players.

Coorparoo Bowls Club has been operating for 97 years. (612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

Bowls Queensland chief executive Fletcher Dyson told 612 ABC Brisbane the organisation turned down much higher offers to ensure the bowling greens would remain.

"We turned a million dollars down to get this result," he said.

"It wasn't about money. It was all about keeping bowls on the site and embracing Coorparoo Bowls Club as a community hub."

Mr Griffin said he planned to renovate the clubhouse, bar and kitchen, while keeping the feel and character of Coorparoo Bowls Club intact.

Both of the bowl greens will be maintained under the deal. (612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

"We see an enormous opportunity to give Coorparoo Bowls Club a bright new future while respecting everything that has made this venue so special for almost 100 years," Mr Griffin said.

"Our ambition is for people to be able to come to Coorparoo Bowls Club to play bowls, enjoy a meal, catch up with friends, bring the family, or simply be part of the community."

The existing Coorparoo Bowls Club committee, which campaigned to save the club, will continue to run it with a five-year lease.

Committee chairman Mark Delbridge said the deal was a triumph for the club members who fought to save the club.

"This is a really exciting new chapter for Coorparoo Bowls Club," he said.

"Our members are incredibly proud of the club's history, and the opportunity to see the venue renewed while keeping bowls at the heart of the site is a fantastic outcome."

World.title: Trump’s war is strangling the world
World.content:
BusinessMarketsInterest rates Opinion Trump’s war is strangling the world Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist September 21, 2026 — 12:00pm

September 21, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Kevin Warsh explained why the US Federal Reserve Board had lifted its policy rate for the first time in three years last week, he studiously avoided any direct references to the war in the Middle East. Three things had changed, he said, since the Fed’s July meeting, when the Fed left the federal funds rate (the equivalent of the Reserve Bank’s cash rate) unchanged: the US economy had strengthened, inflation hadn’t slowed and the “geopolitical landscape” was one of “shocks and uncertainty”. Donald Trump’s administration has dug itself quite a hole in the Middle East. AP With the US 10-year bond yield, the world’s risk-free benchmark for assets, trading around 5 per cent, Warsh said economic strength, a surge in artificial intelligence-related expenditures and “hotspots” around the world – particularly the differences between the spot prices of energy and the “so-called crack spreads” – were driving long-term yields. While Warsh might add growth and AI investment to the influences on US inflation, that begs the question of why other developed economies with less growth and lower AI investment – from Australia and Japan to the European Union – are also wrestling with persistently high inflation and their central banks are also raising their policy rates.



The answer lies within the Middle East. The war in the Middle East has driven up oil prices from around $US70 a barrel to over $US100 a barrel (it traded at almost $US110 a barrel on Friday) and, more particularly, has had a more dramatic impact on gasoline and diesel prices. Related Article Opinion

Interest rates Why higher interest rates are the new normal Clancy Yeates Deputy business editor In the US, the average price of gasoline ahead of the attacks on Iran by the US and Israel in February was $US3.18 a gallon, with the average price of diesel $US3.70 a gallon. Today, the average gasoline price is $US4.47 a gallon and that of diesel $US6.50 a gallon – a record. The same holds true around the world, with the price of diesel at record levels in Europe and Asia and likely to surge further during the northern hemisphere winter. Crude oil supply out of the Middle East is still well below pre-war levels despite some oil now being shipped out of the Strait of Hormuz, a big lift in production outside the region, and the world’s strategic oil reserves still being deployed.



The picture for refined products like petrol and diesel is worse. Not only have crude supplies been diminished, but the refining infrastructure in the Middle East has been targeted and significantly damaged by Iran. Ukraine’s campaign of drone attacks on Russia’s refineries, which have turned the world’s third-largest exporter of diesel into an importer, has compounded the damage. Fed chair Kevin Warsh carefully avoided mentioning the war in the Middle East last week. Bloomberg While Donald Trump has blamed Ukraine for the soaring prices of gasoline and diesel (and told Ukraine to stop targeting Russia’s refineries), Russia produces less than half the volumes of diesel of the Middle Eastern exporters. The world is producing about 4.2 million barrels of diesel a day less than it did a year ago, with the refineries in the Middle East operating at about a quarter of their pre-war levels and Russia’s production cut by about a third, according to the International Energy Agency.



Related Article Opinion

Oil As Trump’s Iran war drags on, we’re facing the next oil crunch Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist With the war on Iran now into its seventh month, with no end in sight and Iran and the Houthis now increasingly targeting strategic oil infrastructure in the region – including the Saudi Arabian refineries and its pipeline to the Red Sea that had allowed up to 5 million barrels a day to bypass the Strait of Hormuz – there’s little likelihood of the prices of either crude oil or, more critically, the prices of the refined products that businesses and households actually consume, subsiding. In fact, with the largest-ever release of the 400 million barrels of oil from strategic reserves now slowing – the IEA says 320 million barrels have been released – a new and even more threatening phase for oil and refined product prices might be ahead, given that the Trump administration appears clueless when it comes to devising a way to extricate itself from its stalemated adventurism in the Middle East. That implies more rate rises in the US and elsewhere. With 24 hours of the Fed’s 25 basis point rate rise, the Bank of Japan followed up with a 25 basis point hike of its own. The European Central Bank raised its policy rate by the same amount earlier this month and Bank of England has foreshadowed rate increases if energy prices remain elevated.



Both inflation rates and interest rates have been significantly higher in the past than they are today, but their threat today relates to the record levels of global debt, particularly government debt. Global public debt is just under 100 per cent of global GDP, with the largest economies – notably the US and China – driving most of the growth. In the US, there’s a 50 per cent chance of another rate rise next month and a 90 per cent chance of it occurring by the end of the year, with at least two more pencilled in by the markets for 2027. It is the interaction between that debt and interest costs that are surging in response to the inflationary impacts of the war in the Middle East, as well as the extraordinary call on capital markets for the financing of artificial intelligence and the physical infrastructure that supports that sector, which is a threat to stability. The International Monetary Fund’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, said at the weekend that governments must do more to reduce their budget deficits and rein in global debt, which she said was projected to reach 100 per cent of global GDP by 2029, or two years earlier than the fund had previously expected. “We have been advocating with the US to pay attention to the fiscal position,” she said.



“Out of our conversations with [Treasury] Secretary [Scott] Bessent, there is an understanding that this is not sustainable, that the US has to gradually bring deficit and debt down.” To date, while presiding over deficits that have grown to 2 per cent of US GDP and a $US4 trillion increase in government debt since January last year – before Trump even reaches the halfway mark of his second term as president – Bessent’s only strategy for dealing with the exploding debt and deficits has been, unsuccessfully, to try to manipulate the bond market with his bond buybacks. He – and other officials in similar positions – has also been replacing maturing longer-term bonds with those of much shorter duration, which carry significantly lower yields, to reduce their interest costs. International Monetary Fund managing director Kristalina Georgieva. AP Refinancing debt that costs 5 per cent with bills or notes that have yields that might be 25 to 100 basis points less might lower a government’s interest costs, but increase its vulnerability to external shocks.



If Warsh and his peers continue to do the heavy lifting of using the only tool at their disposal – higher interest rates – to lower inflation, of course, whatever savings that might be available from exploiting the shape of yield curves would be overwhelmed by the overall rise in interest rates. Related Article Opinion

Global economy The four horsemen of the apocalypse are coming for the global economy In the US, there’s a 50 per cent chance of another rate rise next month and a 90 per cent chance of it occurring by the end of the year, with at least two more pencilled in by the markets for 2027. If diesel and other refined products continue to climb and continue to feed into transport costs and end-prices for businesses and consumers, most of the developed world will be challenged by increased inflation and rising interest costs that eat away at their capacity to fund measures that are more productive and popular than servicing their debts. World.title: Neighbour pays $1.68m for unit with garage, beating five first home buyers
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Neighbour pays $1.68m for unit with garage, beating five first home buyers Carmen Forward September 21, 2026 — 11:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A three-bedroom art deco apartment in Waverley was snapped up by an upstairs neighbour for $1.68 million at auction on Saturday, giving them ownership of half of the building and garage access. As a ground floor unit, the property at 2/4 Kent Street came with one of only two lock-up garages in a boutique block of four. The eastern suburbs property was one of 796 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney last week. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 48 per cent from 481 reported results throughout the week, while 177 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. Although the early result is a fall of five percentage points from last week’s preliminary reading, it remains just above the low of 47 per cent it reached in June as buyers stepped back following the May budget’s changes to the tax treatment of investment properties.



Related Article Auctions ‘We got a house’: Inner west semi sells for $311,000 above reserve Six parties registered for the Waverley unit, five were first home buyers, and all except one participated. Bidding opened at $1.4 million, below its $1,585,000 guide and rose in $25,000, $5000 and $1000 increments. When nobody budged despite further attempts to secure more bids, it sold under the hammer for $80,000 above its $1.6 million reserve for $1.68 million. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. McGrath’s Charles Stevens said that, other than the upstairs neighbour, the auction didn’t draw any investors.



“The two downstairs apartments, both have garages, and then the two upstairs don’t have a garage,” Stevens said. “The majority of people coming through were in the first home buyer category … we had 12 people who came back for more than one inspection.” “You can see the ocean from the sunroom,” he added. The vendors are an investor sibling pair. The flat last traded for $520,000, since 2002, records show. In Drummoyne, a waterfront apartment with Sydney Harbour views at 12/74 Wrights Road sold for $2,161,000.



Ten people registered for the three-bedroom apartment which had no guide. Buyers were mostly downsizers, and two were builders seeking to renovate and flip. Five were active in the ring. Bidding opened at $1.8 million and a $100,000 offer instantly took the price above its $1.85 million reserve, so it was announced as on the market. There were a flurry of bids in large and small increments until it sold for $311,000 above reserve for $2,161,000. Ray White’s Mario Carbone said it was a no guide campaign under instructions from the solicitors, “because it had to be sold, it was a deceased estate”. He said that buyer feedback was between $1.5 million and $1.7 million. Carbone said the waterfront home drew the interest of downsizers due to its lift access.



Related Article Auctions Enmore vendors cut price hopes as Sydney’s clearance rate drops “We’re having good numbers through our open homes, but buyers are still proceeding with an element of caution because of everything that’s happening in the economy,” he said. “When buyers see value, they will come, they will compete and they will purchase.” The buyer is a local downsizer. Nearby, a well maintained Stanmore terrace at 82 Northumberland Avenue drew three registrations. Two competed for the Federation style inner west two bedder.



Initially, the property was guided at $1.65 million, but then lifted to $1.7 million midway through its campaign. Bidding opened at $1.69 million with $10,000 bids dished out quickly for most of the rapid auction before it sold above its reserve for $1,872,000 to a buyer from Canberra. The underbidder is looking to upsize from an apartment. Ray White’s Matt Carvalho said it “was quite a strong auction in terms of bidding. It was really just two people that just fought it out. “A lot of other auctions are … holding back, whereas this was actually a competitive fast auction, which was nice to see,” he said.



Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Moguls behind Kylie Jenner-endorsed sunglasses brand list Byron Shire mansion The investment property was held for 20 years. It last traded for $585,000 in 2006, records show. LJ Hooker’s head of research Mathew Tiller said Domain’s clearance rate of 48 per cent for Sydney was “not a good start” to the spring selling season. “We’re not seeing as much listing activity at the start of spring as we would normally see at this time of year.” He said properties were sitting on the market for a little bit longer now. “Those who aren’t under pressure to list have begun to hold off a little bit to see how the market pans out,” he said. “We probably just have to get through the RBA decision the week after next. If that’s a hold, then it will probably be OK for spring. If it is an increase, then it will obviously dent buyer confidence again.”

World.title: Warriors want answers from NRL over ‘escort’ play at end of Knights match
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Warriors want answers from NRL over ‘escort’ play at end of Knights match Christian Nicolussi September 21, 2026 — 11:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Warriors have contacted the NRL over a number of contentious calls in Sunday’s semi-final loss to Newcastle, including the late-game decision not to penalise Tyson Frizell for an escort play that could have sent the match into extra time. The non-call on the Frizell play came after the NRL last week sent out a reminder to clubs still in the finals race that referees would clamp down on escorts after the Dolphins accused the Warriors of getting away with the same tactic in week one of the finals. Loading “We’ve already asked the NRL for a couple of explanations, so we’ll wait to hear back,” Warriors CEO Cameron George said. “It was disappointing because a warning was sent out to the clubs about [escorts] this week; it was extremely obvious that’s what occurred with [Frizell].



“Then to have no review or anything done by the referee, it was disappointing. We have to move on.” The Warriors had already used their captain’s challenge, which meant they could not ask for the Frizell play to be reviewed by the bunker. Loading The bunker had minutes earlier ruled that centre Ali Leiataua had got a thumb to an intercept attempt, and Te Maire Martin was controversially ruled to have stripped the ball from Greg Marzhew in a tackle with more than one defender involved. As coach Andrew Webster said after the heartbreaking 12-10 loss to the spirited Knights: “I thought they were trying to find ways to take it off us.”



Fan frustration spilled over after the game with a handful of spectators throwing bottles onto the field in the direction of referee Ashley Klein. NRL investigators have already started analysing TV footage to identify the culprits. View post on X “We had close to 49,000 fans, which meant we broke a record, and while I know we can all get frustrated, that behaviour is unacceptable and poor,” George said. “I know the stadium and the NRL are looking at it. Whatever action they take, we will support.”



ARL Commission chairman Peter V’landys added: “We began an investigation immediately on breaches of the NRL spectators’ code of conduct. Related Article Opinion
