World.title: In Washington, temples to Trump’s ego lie ruined. And another is on the way
World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaTrump's America In Washington, temples to Trump’s ego lie ruined. And another is on the way Michael Koziol September 21, 2026 — 11:49am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It was deathly quiet outside the John F. Kennedy Memorial Centre for the Performing Arts on Friday afternoon. Ordinarily, the storied cultural institution would have been preparing for an evening of performances: an opera, perhaps, or musical theatre. Instead, the building was closed, its white Italian marble exterior surrounded by scaffolding, temporary chain-link fences and security guards patrolling the perimeter. Scaffolding covers the signage where a court ordered the Trump administration to remove Donald Trump’s name. AP The Kennedy Centre – so named for the assassinated Democratic president – was abruptly shuttered last week following a vote by its board. The board is chaired by President Donald Trump, who gutted the previous board and installed loyalists with the explicit intent of making him chair. The centre’s closure did not change much, in practical terms. The only programming on Friday night was a free, unticketed show by “master illusionist” Michael Grandinetti, which proceeded at an expansion site outside the main Kennedy Centre building.



That is because artists and arts lovers have largely given the Kennedy Centre a wide berth since Trump began taking over the venue last year and had his name inscribed on the side of the building. Performers cancelled shows, donors withdrew and ticket sales nosedived. Last October, The Washington Post calculated 43 per cent of tickets remained unsold for the typical autumn production. Things have only worsened since. Staff and programs have been slashed, and the budget is in disarray. Protesters on Friday night linked hands to form a human chain around the Kennedy Centre. AP This giant of American cultural life – and a living memorial to one of the country’s slain presidents – now lies empty and sad. It is a cautionary tale; a temple to the tragedy of ego. The stalemate may continue. Trump secured the money, $US257 million, from Congress for a major two-year renovation, which he and his board argue is sorely needed. But he is refusing to begin the work unless he can put his name back on the building.



It’s not just his name; court documents show Trump is insisting on three things. One is changing the plaque on the front of the building to read: “The John F. Kennedy Memorial Centre for the Performing Arts, renovated and restored by President Donald J. Trump.” Second, when his Trump Kennedy Centre Fund reaches an endowment of $US100 million, he proposes to add: “Endowed by the Trump Kennedy Centre Fund” to the plaque. Finally, he wants to name the surrounding area “President Donald J. Trump Plaza”. The board approved these proposals last month. The Reflecting Pool outside the Lincoln Memorial remains drained and fenced off to visitors. AP Last week, a federal judge appointed by Barack Obama, Christopher Cooper, put a stop to this. He is the same judge who last year ordered Trump’s name be taken off the building, as Congress had named it in honour of President Kennedy alone. Now, Cooper said, the administration “plays word games” to try to skirt the ruling. “Alone means alone,” Cooper ruled. “The board cannot honour both President Kennedy and President Trump without running afoul of the terms of the injunction and the board’s own governing statute.”



Trump has defended this narcissism by arguing he is saving the Kennedy Centre from certain ruin. He says he raised the $US257 million from Congress himself (“they gave it to me because it’s me”) and would have to keep raising funds after he leaves office because the centre has always lost money. “That place is a dump. It’s been a dump for years. I’m ready to fix it,” he said. “I think the Trump administration should be recognised as having saved the Kennedy Centre because nobody else can do it.” US President Donald Trump spoke about the Kennedy Centre last week, with John F. Kennedy’s nephew, Robert F. Kennedy Jr, behind him. AP One may well scoff at the idea of Trump, who somehow paid no income tax for many years, fundraising for the arts after he departs the White House. And if the centre was such a dangerous “dump”, why was it chosen to host the FIFA World Cup draw late last year, a major event attended by Trump, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and FIFA president Gianni Infantino?



The building may be deserving of a renovation – and nobody is opposing that – but there’s no doubt Trump and his acolytes have milked that for all it’s worth. When a five-foot piece of ceiling plaster collapsed during a storm this month, the debris wasn’t cleaned up: as The New York Times reported on Sunday, staff “left the mess on the carpet for nearly two weeks”, documenting it as part of a brief on the building’s decay. One need not venture far to see another victim of Trump’s egomania. Down at the National Mall, the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool is still blocked off by fencing – more than two months after it was drained again to repair a botched job by the contractor. Trump says the “Triumphal Arch” he intends to build across the river near Arlington Cemetery will have snipers and be stocked with ammunition. Bloomberg No work was being done on Saturday morning when this masthead visited, although bobcats and trailers sat strewn around the pool’s barren surface and on the nearby grass. What was once a rush job to be finished for Independence Day is now languishing in the incomplete basket. And across the river, Trump has just announced that his planned Triumphal Arch will be stuffed with drones, snipers and ammunition, turning it into a “military complex”. This was apparently at the military’s request, despite the Pentagon being a stone’s throw away.



Related Article Donald Trump Trump’s ‘triumphal arch’ is bigger than ever, and even the expert who proposed it is worried There is an obvious reason for this change – Trump has learnt from the White House ballroom that declaring something a security necessity can generate a lot of leverage. The courts allowed him to continue work on the underground military parts of the ballroom while pausing work on the above-ground sections. Washington is a grand city of monuments to American endeavour and excellence. This president wishes to turn them into monuments to his own ego, or, as things stand, leave them to rot when he cannot get his way. World.title: Fresh hope in investigation into death of pregnant nurse suspected of being Ivan Milat’s first victim
World.content:
NationalNSWCrime Fresh hope in investigation into death of pregnant nurse suspected of being Ivan Milat’s first victim Anne Worthington Dimity Clancey and September 21, 2026 — 11:48am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The family of Keren Rowland, who suspect she was Ivan Milat’s first victim when she was brutally murdered more than five decades ago, hopes a $500,000 reward will bring new leads on one of Australia’s most baffling unsolved homicide cases. The ACT government on Monday announced the substantial reward for information that leads to an arrest, 55 years after the 20-year-old pregnant woman’s body was found in a pine plantation on the outskirts of Canberra. Keren Rowland was five months pregnant when her body was found dumped in a shallow grave in Fairbairn Forest near Canberra airport. 60 Minutes “Keren and her unborn baby deserve the truth to come out. That child would be 55 this year,” Keren’s brother Steve Rowland said. Keren’s loved ones have long suspected the dental nurse was serial killer Milat’s first victim, 18 years before he killed and dumped the bodies of seven young backpackers in the Belangalo State Forest.



In June, at a NSW Parliamentary Inquiry into unsolved murders and missing people, NSW Police confirmed a taskforce set up in the early ’90s to investigate the backpacker murders had concluded they too believed Milat was “highly likely” to have killed Keren. That information was passed to ACT police, but Steve Rowland says they’ve struggled to get answers about what police did to further their own investigations into Keren’s death. Ivan Milat in jail in 1997. “I haven’t been trying to catch the police out. I haven’t been trying to see if they’ve done right, or they’ve done wrong. I’ve just been trying to find out what happened to my sister, but they made every turn very tight, and it was really difficult to find out anything.” ACT Police Minister Dr Marisa Paterson said the reward would be “a strong incentive for someone to tell police what they know.”



ACT Chief Police Officer Scott Lee acknowledged “that significant time has passed” but “that doesn’t mean there isn’t someone out there that knows what happened.” Related Article Exclusive

Crime Milat linked to cold cases in Tasmania, South Australia, police list reveals The reward was one of five announced, with Lee saying these matters were the “ones most likely to have witnesses or information that can assist police.” For Steve Rowland, who was only 16 when his sister vanished, the long-awaited cash reward brings a bittersweet mix of raw emotion and profound frustration. “We’ve been fighting for eight years for this reward, someone must know something whether it’s related to Milat or not, someone knows something. That figure could draw something from even the Milat family.”



Steve admitted he isn’t entirely hopeful the reward will instantly bring justice after years of police dead ends and lost evidence, but he hopes the money will help bring closure to decades of grief. Anyone with information should contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Drill blitz serves up 10.72g/t WA gold for Great Southern
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Drill blitz serves up 10.72g/t WA gold for Great Southern Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Penny Taylor September 21, 2026 — 11:47am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Great Southern Mining has punched into high-grade gold within fresh rock at Golden Boulder, part of its 100 per cent-owned Duketon gold project near Laverton in Western Australia, extending mineralisation up to 45m down-dip as a major drilling campaign probes the scale beneath its shallow footprint. First assays cover 2436m from 19 holes of a planned 14,000m reverse circulation (RC) program, with the drilling concentrated on the northern 450-metre section of Golden Boulder’s 3.5km Main Line trend, one of three parallel mineralised corridors alongside its Eastern Line and Ogilvies prospects. Another 48 holes, representing 5428m of completed drilling from Main Line and Eastern Line, await assays. Great Southern Mining reverse circulation drilling at the Golden Boulder gold discovery within its Duketon Gold Project near Laverton, Western Australia. The standout 10-metre hit ran 2.62 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 20m, including 2m at 10.72g/t and 1m at 2.20g/t. Another hole returned 8m at 2.24g/t from 102m, including 2m at 7.20g/t, while 7m at 2.45g/t from 41m contained 1m at 6.91g/t. Deeper intervals included 3m at 3.07g/t from 105m, 3m at 3.32g/t from 121m and 4m at 1.85g/t from 145m, including 1m at 6.62g/t. All except one of the 19 holes returned mineralised intercepts above 0.7g/t, with high grades occurring in both the weathered oxide zone near surface and the underlying fresh rock. Reported lengths are downhole, with true widths yet to be confirmed.



‘There is potential for a much larger gold system that could support multiple open-pit operations, all within 20km of operational gold processing facilities.’ Great Southern Mining managing director Matthew Keane Golden Boulder carries a rich goldfield pedigree. More than 50 historical workings pepper the area across a 3.7km strike, with records showing 1915 tonnes of ore were mined at 28.6g/t for 1761 gold ounces between 1900 and 1955. More recently, 2025 drilling struck 5m at 14.6g/t gold from 41m, including 1m at 70.9g/t, adding modern high-grade smoke to the old workings. The latest results appear to provide a glimpse beneath those shallower historical and modern results, extending mineralisation up to 45m down-dip. However, few holes have reached beyond 150m below surface, leaving much of Golden Boulder’s depth potential still untested. Drilling has now moved to the southern reaches of Main Line, where drill lines from the 2025 campaign were widely spaced up to 400m apart. Great Southern Mining managing director Matthew Keane said: “These results support our view that Golden Boulder and the wider Duketon Gold Project have potential for significant scale. The latest results highlight the propensity for high-grades both in the shallow oxide zone and continuing at depth into fresh rock.”



Modelling and interpretation at Golden Boulder are underway to assess continuity between multiple stacked quartz-vein lodes carrying pyrite and arsenopyrite within basalt and minor dolerite. Great Southern will assess the growing RC dataset before planning follow-up drilling, with a resource estimate also possible subject to interpretation of the results. In parallel with the action at Golden Boulder, another batch of assays is waiting in the wings from Amy Clarke, Great Southern’s emerging gold discovery just 3km to the northeast. Results from its first RC program of 18 holes totalling 2248m are expected in coming weeks, with mineralisation already defined across a 4.7km strike. Adding further intrigue is Golden Boulder’s prime geological address. It sits on the same interpreted structure as Regis Resources’ greater-than-2-million-ounce Rosemont deposit 26km away, where mineralisation extends beyond 700m below surface. Great Southern’s wider Laverton ground also sits between Regis’ 12-million-ounce-plus Duketon camp and Genesis Minerals’ 6-million-ounce Laverton tenure, while Keane says operational gold processing facilities lie within 20km. Further afield, diamond drilling has wrapped up at Mt Dillon’s massive gold-copper target within Great Southern’s Edinburgh Park project in northern Queensland. Core logging and processing are now underway. The company has a deal with mining giant Gold Fields, which can earn up to 75 per cent by sole-funding $15M of exploration. The arrangement allows Great Southern to retain exposure to the Queensland project while focusing its own resources on its WA gold portfolio. With drilling ongoing at Golden Boulder and a torrent of assays in the lab from two separate large-scale systems, Great Southern now has plenty of shots on goal as it looks to prove whether Duketon has the makings of an emerging gold camp in one of WA’s most prolific gold districts. World.title: Newcastle’s rise from spoon to prelim is remarkable. But the Panthers are the big winners
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Opinion Newcastle’s rise from spoon to prelim is remarkable. But the Panthers are the big winners Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist September 21, 2026 — 11:45am

September 21, 2026 — 11:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The winners of the Sunday smash-up in Auckland were undoubtedly Penrith, kicking back and watching next week’s opponents belt each other senseless. Even though the Warriors were their own worst enemy in the 12-10 loss to the Knights, succumbing to the pressure of the Eden Park occasion and panicking their way to defeat, Newcastle’s rise from wooden spoon to preliminary final is fabulous. Loading Nobody gets juiced on underdoggery like the Knights. They are the envy of the Tigers, Dragons, Titans and Eels, who remain stuck in the cellar and who, if they’re smart, will study closely everything the Knights have done this year. It’s difficult to manufacture team spirit, happiness and harmony without winning first, but under Justin Holbrook the Knights have produced the egg without needing the chicken.



Newcastle will be rank outsiders on Sunday – but they were rank outsiders in New Zealand, too. Ref justice for Wahs Make it make sense! Not that it was the reason the Warriors lost, but the non-penalty call on Newcastle’s Tyson Frizell in the final minute, when he clearly blocked Warriors kick chasers, shows what a rabbit hole the video officiating system has descended into. Throughout the match, every bunker call turned into a philosophical discussion of how many angels can dance on the head of a pin.



To their credit, the bunker officials avoided making absolute howlers. The absolute howler came when referee Ashley Klein missed Frizell’s infringement, which should have given the Warriors a shot at a penalty goal from right in front and a chance at extra time (in which, the way they were playing, they would surely have lost). Loading The Warriors had lost their challenge on a fingertip call a few minutes earlier. So, do we want to eliminate technology and go back to crucial on-field refereeing mistakes like this? Clearly not. But the tech-assisted challenge system hasn’t stopped it happening either. And nobody understands why the bunker can intrude on the game unprompted and correct many referee rulings or take a player out due to a head knock, but not correct a glaring error like this.



My brain hurts even thinking about it. Rugby league is a simple game played by simple people, refereed by an overcomplicated Rube Goldberg machine. Tyson Frizell and the Knights celebrate a stunning win in Auckland. But it came amid plenty of controversy. Getty Images When NRL supremo Peter V’landys sits down with his rules officials in the summer, item one has to be unpicking this tangle of wires and knobs. The end result is what matters, and the end result on Sunday was a shower of bottles and other projectiles raining from the stands onto the referee – just like before we had video technology.



Even in victory, Robbo’s still not happy On Saturday, the Roosters’ win over Cronulla echoed their win in the corresponding match two years ago over Manly. Nicho Hynes after the head knock that forced him out of Saturday night’s heavy loss to the Roosters. NRL Photos Then, Jake Trbojevic and Tolu Koula were knocked out in the opening minutes, and it was game over. This time, it was an early exit for Cronulla’s Nicho Hynes, whose concussion at least absolves him from the usual blame for another Sharks finals loss.



Two years ago, the Roosters followed their thumping semi-final win with a heavy loss in Melbourne. The Dolphins in Brisbane may not have the same aura as the Storm of 2024, and the Roosters have a fighting chance this Friday. But an NRL week wouldn’t be complete without the squeaky wheel of Trent Robinson needing some oil. Daly Cherry-Evans will get one last visit to Suncorp Stadium before moving to the Super League. Getty Images A handsome 46-10 win didn’t quite fill the hole. This week’s complaint-but-not-a-complaint was about the six-day turnaround before the preliminary final. “It’s a little bit surprising that this has happened. I wouldn’t say it’s happened too often,” Robinson said of his team having two six-day turnarounds during the finals.





The position, selected from members of V’landys’ own board, is meant to be an independent “guardrail” on his authority. In case you’re wondering why they would bother, remember that autarchs never win 100 per cent of the vote. It’s always 98 per cent or 99 per cent, just so you know it’s not some kind of fait accompli handed down from above.

World.title: Diana’s brother is right to be furious with Charles over Harry and William
World.content:
WorldEuropeRoyal family Opinion Diana’s brother is right to be furious with Charles over Harry and William Eleanor Mills Journalist September 21, 2026 — 11:45am

September 21, 2026 — 11:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Next year will mark the 30th anniversary of the death of Princess Diana but still it makes headlines. The latest furore is about her brother Charles Spencer – he of the Westminster Abbey eulogy – who has written a new book called Swan Song: Diana, My Sister. The big reveal is a heated conversation (actually it sounds more like a full-blown row) between Spencer and the then-Prince Charles over whether or not the young princes, William and Harry, should walk behind their mother’s funeral cortege. “What empathy-free monsters ever thought it was appropriate for children of 15 and 12 to have to walk so far, in the glare of the entire global media, when their beloved mother had just died? Reuters The book says that, during the row, Spencer said the idea was “barbaric” while the King said he had walked behind the gun carriage at Lord Mountbatten’s funeral and that it was tradition. Spencer apparently riposted that Charles had been 30 when Mountbatten died (in 1979) and it wasn’t the same. And the King “went nuts”. Touché. I have to say I agree with Spencer. Whatever you think of Princess Diana’s brother (and he’s certainly a colourful piece of work with many alleging he has written this book to raise cash for his latest divorce) he was right about the boys. What empathy-free monsters ever thought it was appropriate for children of 15 and 12 to have to walk so publicly, so far, in the glare of the entire global media, when their beloved mother had just died unexpectedly in a car accident? The death of a parent in early adolescence is traumatic enough anyway, without that deep personal grief having to be performed (and contained) in front of hundreds of millions of people. Prince Harry says in his memoir Spare how traumatic it was. He told Newsweek in 2017: “I don’t think any child should be asked to do that, under any circumstances. I don’t think that would happen today”.



Prince William is much more stiff upper lip, but he has said that he felt completely numb and disorientated and described Diana’s death as “an earthquake which split my mind and life”. Of the walk behind the coffin specifically, he said: “It wasn’t an easy decision” – an oblique reference to the rows that surrounded it, perhaps – “and it was sort of a collective family decision to do that. It was one of the hardest things I have ever done, but there was this element of duty and responsibility that you have to do things you don’t want to do”. Princes William and Harry with their father during Diana’s funeral. AP Ouch. Both boys have also talked of the overwhelming pressure they felt not to cry in public. Spencer was right to call it “barbaric”. We shouldn’t be surprised that those tumultuous events continue to reverberate down the decades; I expect that they will echo down the centuries. The tragedy of Diana’s hounding by the paparazzi, our collective insatiable curiosity about her life and the tawdriness of her death at 36 in a Mercedes driven by a drunk chauffeur in the employ of an alleged sex-criminal (Mohamed Fayed), is a saga for the ages. But even if it hadn’t been so public, losing a parent so young is the kind of blow that defines your life, whether you are prince or pauper. William has spoken about the pain of not having his mother around to see his own children grow up. (How he must have felt when his wife, Catherine, had cancer and his children faced losing their own mother at a young age doesn’t bear thinking about... Poor William.) And it is clear to all of us that Prince Harry is still acting out the trauma of losing his mum so young. It is there in his terror of something awful happening to his own wife or children, expressed in his ongoing rows with the authorities over security and press coverage.



Of course, funerals and the arrangements around them are a notorious flashpoint. Decisions have to be made while emotions are running high. Grief makes people irrational – their normal boundaries have been breached; we are oversensitive and not as tolerant of the foibles or perspectives of others as we might usually be. It is incredibly easy, in such a situation, to say something we later regret. And all families have their undercurrents and unspoken tensions, particularly between siblings and in-laws. Funerals bring out the best, but also the worst in us. I don’t know a single family who hasn’t experienced some kind of row or tension around a funeral – whether it’s over who should speak, how it should go, who should do what, who pays, and whether it’s what the departed would have wanted (too many of us haven’t had that conversation while we could…) Cruse, a bereavement support service, says such rifts and troubles around a death are all too common. Sometimes how we feel about the deceased is uncomplicated: we totally loved them, we totally didn’t. But often we are ambivalent (like Prince Charles, who, according to Spencer, was furious that Diana had eclipsed him). In death, ambivalence hits you in the face like stepping on a rake – wham! When someone dies there is no longer any time to work out your difficulties; those tricky emotions have nowhere to go. We’re sad, we’re angry about things that have happened and we have nowhere to put those feelings. So they get projected on to other family members. This is particularly true in our Western, uptight culture where we don’t have a tradition of howling our collective grief together, or banging our chests in outlandish communal displays of emotion. The funeral arrangements, or arguments over money, become the outlet instead. Given the immensity of what happened with Princess Diana it is not surprising emotions still run hot. My heart goes out to all of them. So much grief, such a huge tragedy, reverberating down the years, down the centuries. They may be royal, but in grief we are all too human.



Eleanor Mills is a former editorial director of The Sunday Times and editor of its magazine. She is now a columist for the UK Telegraph. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Trump’s war is strangling the world
World.content:
BusinessMarketsInterest rates Opinion Trump’s war is strangling the world Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist September 21, 2026 — 12:00pm

September 21, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Kevin Warsh explained why the US Federal Reserve Board had lifted its policy rate for the first time in three years last week, he studiously avoided any direct references to the war in the Middle East. Three things had changed, he said, since the Fed’s July meeting, when the Fed left the federal funds rate (the equivalent of the Reserve Bank’s cash rate) unchanged: the US economy had strengthened, inflation hadn’t slowed and the “geopolitical landscape” was one of “shocks and uncertainty”. Donald Trump’s administration has dug itself quite a hole in the Middle East. AP With the US 10-year bond yield, the world’s risk-free benchmark for assets, trading around 5 per cent, Warsh said economic strength, a surge in artificial intelligence-related expenditures and “hotspots” around the world – particularly the differences between the spot prices of energy and the “so-called crack spreads” – were driving long-term yields. While Warsh might add growth and AI investment to the influences on US inflation, that begs the question of why other developed economies with less growth and lower AI investment – from Australia and Japan to the European Union – are also wrestling with persistently high inflation and their central banks are also raising their policy rates.



The answer lies within the Middle East. The war in the Middle East has driven up oil prices from around $US70 a barrel to over $US100 a barrel (it traded at almost $US110 a barrel on Friday) and, more particularly, has had a more dramatic impact on gasoline and diesel prices. Related Article Opinion

Interest rates Why higher interest rates are the new normal Clancy Yeates Deputy business editor In the US, the average price of gasoline ahead of the attacks on Iran by the US and Israel in February was $US3.18 a gallon, with the average price of diesel $US3.70 a gallon. Today, the average gasoline price is $US4.47 a gallon and that of diesel $US6.50 a gallon – a record. The same holds true around the world, with the price of diesel at record levels in Europe and Asia and likely to surge further during the northern hemisphere winter. Crude oil supply out of the Middle East is still well below pre-war levels despite some oil now being shipped out of the Strait of Hormuz, a big lift in production outside the region, and the world’s strategic oil reserves still being deployed.



The picture for refined products like petrol and diesel is worse. Not only have crude supplies been diminished, but the refining infrastructure in the Middle East has been targeted and significantly damaged by Iran. Ukraine’s campaign of drone attacks on Russia’s refineries, which have turned the world’s third-largest exporter of diesel into an importer, has compounded the damage. Fed chair Kevin Warsh carefully avoided mentioning the war in the Middle East last week. Bloomberg While Donald Trump has blamed Ukraine for the soaring prices of gasoline and diesel (and told Ukraine to stop targeting Russia’s refineries), Russia produces less than half the volumes of diesel of the Middle Eastern exporters. The world is producing about 4.2 million barrels of diesel a day less than it did a year ago, with the refineries in the Middle East operating at about a quarter of their pre-war levels and Russia’s production cut by about a third, according to the International Energy Agency.



Related Article Opinion

Oil As Trump’s Iran war drags on, we’re facing the next oil crunch Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist With the war on Iran now into its seventh month, with no end in sight and Iran and the Houthis now increasingly targeting strategic oil infrastructure in the region – including the Saudi Arabian refineries and its pipeline to the Red Sea that had allowed up to 5 million barrels a day to bypass the Strait of Hormuz – there’s little likelihood of the prices of either crude oil or, more critically, the prices of the refined products that businesses and households actually consume, subsiding. In fact, with the largest-ever release of the 400 million barrels of oil from strategic reserves now slowing – the IEA says 320 million barrels have been released – a new and even more threatening phase for oil and refined product prices might be ahead, given that the Trump administration appears clueless when it comes to devising a way to extricate itself from its stalemated adventurism in the Middle East. That implies more rate rises in the US and elsewhere. With 24 hours of the Fed’s 25 basis point rate rise, the Bank of Japan followed up with a 25 basis point hike of its own. The European Central Bank raised its policy rate by the same amount earlier this month and Bank of England has foreshadowed rate increases if energy prices remain elevated.



Both inflation rates and interest rates have been significantly higher in the past than they are today, but their threat today relates to the record levels of global debt, particularly government debt. Global public debt is just under 100 per cent of global GDP, with the largest economies – notably the US and China – driving most of the growth. In the US, there’s a 50 per cent chance of another rate rise next month and a 90 per cent chance of it occurring by the end of the year, with at least two more pencilled in by the markets for 2027. It is the interaction between that debt and interest costs that are surging in response to the inflationary impacts of the war in the Middle East, as well as the extraordinary call on capital markets for the financing of artificial intelligence and the physical infrastructure that supports that sector, which is a threat to stability. The International Monetary Fund’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, said at the weekend that governments must do more to reduce their budget deficits and rein in global debt, which she said was projected to reach 100 per cent of global GDP by 2029, or two years earlier than the fund had previously expected. “We have been advocating with the US to pay attention to the fiscal position,” she said.



“Out of our conversations with (Treasury) secretary (Scott) Bessent, there is an understanding that this is not sustainable, that the US has to gradually bring deficit and debt down,” she said. To date, while presiding over deficits that have grown to 2 per cent of US GDP and a $US4 trillion increase in government debt since January last year – before Trump even reaches the halfway mark of his second term as president – Bessent’s only strategy for dealing with the exploding debt and deficits has been, unsuccessfully, to try to manipulate the bond market with his bond buybacks. He – and other officials in similar positions – has also been replacing maturing longer-term bonds with those of much shorter duration, which carry significantly lower yields, in order to reduce their interest costs. The International Monetary Fund’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, said at the weekend that governments must do more to reduce their budget deficits and rein in global debt. AP Refinancing debt that costs 5 per cent with bills or notes that have yields that might be 25 to 100 basis points less might lower a government’s interest costs, but increase its vulnerability to external shocks.



If Warsh and his peers continue to do the heavy lifting of using the only tool at their disposal – higher interest rates – to lower inflation, of course, whatever savings that might be available from exploiting the shape of yield curves would be overwhelmed by the overall rise in interest rates. In the US, there’s a 50 per cent chance of another rate rise next month and a 90 per cent chance of it occurring by the end of the year, with at least two more pencilled in by the markets for 2027. World.title: Neighbour pays $1.68m for unit with garage, beating five first home buyers
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Neighbour pays $1.68m for unit with garage, beating five first home buyers Carmen Forward September 21, 2026 — 11:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A three-bedroom art deco apartment in Waverley was snapped up by an upstairs neighbour for $1.68 million at auction on Saturday, giving them ownership of half of the building and garage access. As a ground floor unit, the property at 2/4 Kent Street came with one of only two lock-up garages in a boutique block of four. The eastern suburbs property was one of 796 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney last week. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 48 per cent from 481 reported results throughout the week, while 177 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. Although the early result is a fall of five percentage points from last week’s preliminary reading, it remains just above the low of 47 per cent it reached in June as buyers stepped back following the May budget’s changes to the tax treatment of investment properties.



Related Article Auctions ‘We got a house’: Inner west semi sells for $311,000 above reserve Six parties registered for the Waverley unit, five were first home buyers, and all except one participated. Bidding opened at $1.4 million, below its $1,585,000 guide and rose in $25,000, $5000 and $1000 increments. When nobody budged despite further attempts to secure more bids, it sold under the hammer for $80,000 above its $1.6 million reserve for $1.68 million. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. McGrath’s Charles Stevens said that, other than the upstairs neighbour, the auction didn’t draw any investors.



“The two downstairs apartments, both have garages, and then the two upstairs don’t have a garage,” Stevens said. “The majority of people coming through were in the first home buyer category … we had 12 people who came back for more than one inspection.” “You can see the ocean from the sunroom,” he added. The vendors are an investor sibling pair. The flat last traded for $520,000, since 2002, records show. In Drummoyne, a waterfront apartment with Sydney Harbour views at 12/74 Wrights Road sold for $2,161,000.



Ten people registered for the three-bedroom apartment which had no guide. Buyers were mostly downsizers, and two were builders seeking to renovate and flip. Five were active in the ring. Bidding opened at $1.8 million and a $100,000 offer instantly took the price above its $1.85 million reserve, so it was announced as on the market. There were a flurry of bids in large and small increments until it sold for $311,000 above reserve for $2,161,000. Ray White’s Mario Carbone said it was a no guide campaign under instructions from the solicitors, “because it had to be sold, it was a deceased estate”. He said that buyer feedback was between $1.5 million and $1.7 million. Carbone said the waterfront home drew the interest of downsizers due to its lift access.



Related Article Auctions Enmore vendors cut price hopes as Sydney’s clearance rate drops “We’re having good numbers through our open homes, but buyers are still proceeding with an element of caution because of everything that’s happening in the economy,” he said. “When buyers see value, they will come, they will compete and they will purchase.” The buyer is a local downsizer. Nearby, a well maintained Stanmore terrace at 82 Northumberland Avenue drew three registrations. Two competed for the Federation style inner west two bedder.



Initially, the property was guided at $1.65 million, but then lifted to $1.7 million midway through its campaign. Bidding opened at $1.69 million with $10,000 bids dished out quickly for most of the rapid auction before it sold above its reserve for $1,872,000 to a buyer from Canberra. The underbidder is looking to upsize from an apartment. Ray White’s Matt Carvalho said it “was quite a strong auction in terms of bidding. It was really just two people that just fought it out. “A lot of other auctions are … holding back, whereas this was actually a competitive fast auction, which was nice to see,” he said.



Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Moguls behind Kylie Jenner-endorsed sunglasses brand list Byron Shire mansion The investment property was held for 20 years. It last traded for $585,000 in 2006, records show. LJ Hooker’s head of research Mathew Tiller said Domain’s clearance rate of 48 per cent for Sydney was “not a good start” to the spring selling season. “We’re not seeing as much listing activity at the start of spring as we would normally see at this time of year.” He said properties were sitting on the market for a little bit longer now. “Those who aren’t under pressure to list have begun to hold off a little bit to see how the market pans out,” he said. “We probably just have to get through the RBA decision the week after next. If that’s a hold, then it will probably be OK for spring. If it is an increase, then it will obviously dent buyer confidence again.”

World.title: In Washington, temples to Trump’s ego lie ruined. And another is on the way
World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaTrump's America In Washington, temples to Trump’s ego lie ruined. And another is on the way Michael Koziol September 21, 2026 — 11:49am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It was deathly quiet outside the John F. Kennedy Memorial Centre for the Performing Arts on Friday afternoon. Ordinarily, the storied cultural institution would have been preparing for an evening of performances: an opera, perhaps, or musical theatre. Instead, the building was closed, its white Italian marble exterior surrounded by scaffolding, temporary chain-link fences and security guards patrolling the perimeter. Scaffolding covers the signage where a court ordered the Trump administration to remove Donald Trump’s name. AP The Kennedy Centre – so named for the assassinated Democratic president – was abruptly shuttered last week following a vote by its board. The board is chaired by President Donald Trump, who gutted the previous board and installed loyalists with the explicit intent of making him chair. The centre’s closure did not change much, in practical terms. The only programming on Friday night was a free, unticketed show by “master illusionist” Michael Grandinetti, which proceeded at an expansion site outside the main Kennedy Centre building.



That is because artists and arts lovers have largely given the Kennedy Centre a wide berth since Trump began taking over the venue last year and had his name inscribed on the side of the building. Performers cancelled shows, donors withdrew and ticket sales nosedived. Last October, The Washington Post calculated 43 per cent of tickets remained unsold for the typical autumn production. Things have only worsened since. Staff and programs have been slashed, and the budget is in disarray. Protesters on Friday night linked hands to form a human chain around the Kennedy Centre. AP This giant of American cultural life – and a living memorial to one of the country’s slain presidents – now lies empty and sad. It is a cautionary tale; a temple to the tragedy of ego. The stalemate may continue. Trump secured the money, $US257 million, from Congress for a major two-year renovation, which he and his board argue is sorely needed. But he is refusing to begin the work unless he can put his name back on the building.



It’s not just his name; court documents show Trump is insisting on three things. One is changing the plaque on the front of the building to read: “The John F. Kennedy Memorial Centre for the Performing Arts, renovated and restored by President Donald J. Trump.” Second, when his Trump Kennedy Centre Fund reaches an endowment of $US100 million, he proposes to add: “Endowed by the Trump Kennedy Centre Fund” to the plaque. Finally, he wants to name the surrounding area “President Donald J. Trump Plaza”. The board approved these proposals last month. The Reflecting Pool outside the Lincoln Memorial remains drained and fenced off to visitors. AP Last week, a federal judge appointed by Barack Obama, Christopher Cooper, put a stop to this. He is the same judge who last year ordered Trump’s name be taken off the building, as Congress had named it in honour of President Kennedy alone. Now, Cooper said, the administration “plays word games” to try to skirt the ruling. “Alone means alone,” Cooper ruled. “The board cannot honour both President Kennedy and President Trump without running afoul of the terms of the injunction and the board’s own governing statute.”



Trump has defended this narcissism by arguing he is saving the Kennedy Centre from certain ruin. He says he raised the $US257 million from Congress himself (“they gave it to me because it’s me”) and would have to keep raising funds after he leaves office because the centre has always lost money. “That place is a dump. It’s been a dump for years. I’m ready to fix it,” he said. “I think the Trump administration should be recognised as having saved the Kennedy Centre because nobody else can do it.” US President Donald Trump spoke about the Kennedy Centre last week, with John F. Kennedy’s nephew, Robert F. Kennedy Jr, behind him. AP One may well scoff at the idea of Trump, who somehow paid no income tax for many years, fundraising for the arts after he departs the White House. And if the centre was such a dangerous “dump”, why was it chosen to host the FIFA World Cup draw late last year, a major event attended by Trump, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and FIFA president Gianni Infantino?



The building may be deserving of a renovation – and nobody is opposing that – but there’s no doubt Trump and his acolytes have milked that for all it’s worth. When a five-foot piece of ceiling plaster collapsed during a storm this month, the debris wasn’t cleaned up: as The New York Times reported on Sunday, staff “left the mess on the carpet for nearly two weeks”, documenting it as part of a brief on the building’s decay. One need not venture far to see another victim of Trump’s egomania. Down at the National Mall, the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool is still blocked off by fencing – more than two months after it was drained again to repair a botched job by the contractor. Trump says the “Triumphal Arch” he intends to build across the river near Arlington Cemetery will have snipers and be stocked with ammunition. Bloomberg No work was being done on Saturday morning when this masthead visited, although bobcats and trailers sat strewn around the pool’s barren surface and on the nearby grass. What was once a rush job to be finished for Independence Day is now languishing in the incomplete basket. And across the river, Trump has just announced that his planned Triumphal Arch will be stuffed with drones, snipers and ammunition, turning it into a “military complex”. This was apparently at the military’s request, despite the Pentagon being a stone’s throw away.



Related Article Donald Trump Trump’s ‘triumphal arch’ is bigger than ever, and even the expert who proposed it is worried There is an obvious reason for this change – Trump has learnt from the White House ballroom that declaring something a security necessity can generate a lot of leverage. The courts allowed him to continue work on the underground military parts of the ballroom while pausing work on the above-ground sections. Washington is a grand city of monuments to American endeavour and excellence. This president wishes to turn them into monuments to his own ego, or, as things stand, leave them to rot when he cannot get his way. World.title: Fresh hope in investigation into death of pregnant nurse suspected of being Ivan Milat’s first victim
World.content:
NationalNSWCrime Fresh hope in investigation into death of pregnant nurse suspected of being Ivan Milat’s first victim Anne Worthington Dimity Clancey and September 21, 2026 — 11:48am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The family of Keren Rowland, who suspect she was Ivan Milat’s first victim when she was brutally murdered more than five decades ago, hopes a $500,000 reward will bring new leads on one of Australia’s most baffling unsolved homicide cases. The ACT government on Monday announced the substantial reward for information that leads to an arrest, 55 years after the 20-year-old pregnant woman’s body was found in a pine plantation on the outskirts of Canberra. Keren Rowland was five months pregnant when her body was found dumped in a shallow grave in Fairbairn Forest near Canberra airport. 60 Minutes “Keren and her unborn baby deserve the truth to come out. That child would be 55 this year,” Keren’s brother Steve Rowland said. Keren’s loved ones have long suspected the dental nurse was serial killer Milat’s first victim, 18 years before he killed and dumped the bodies of seven young backpackers in the Belangalo State Forest.



In June, at a NSW Parliamentary Inquiry into unsolved murders and missing people, NSW Police confirmed a taskforce set up in the early ’90s to investigate the backpacker murders had concluded they too believed Milat was “highly likely” to have killed Keren. That information was passed to ACT police, but Steve Rowland says they’ve struggled to get answers about what police did to further their own investigations into Keren’s death. Ivan Milat in jail in 1997. “I haven’t been trying to catch the police out. I haven’t been trying to see if they’ve done right, or they’ve done wrong. I’ve just been trying to find out what happened to my sister, but they made every turn very tight, and it was really difficult to find out anything.” ACT Police Minister Dr Marisa Paterson said the reward would be “a strong incentive for someone to tell police what they know.”



ACT Chief Police Officer Scott Lee acknowledged “that significant time has passed” but “that doesn’t mean there isn’t someone out there that knows what happened.” Related Article Exclusive

Crime Milat linked to cold cases in Tasmania, South Australia, police list reveals The reward was one of five announced, with Lee saying these matters were the “ones most likely to have witnesses or information that can assist police.” For Steve Rowland, who was only 16 when his sister vanished, the long-awaited cash reward brings a bittersweet mix of raw emotion and profound frustration. “We’ve been fighting for eight years for this reward, someone must know something whether it’s related to Milat or not, someone knows something. That figure could draw something from even the Milat family.”



Steve admitted he isn’t entirely hopeful the reward will instantly bring justice after years of police dead ends and lost evidence, but he hopes the money will help bring closure to decades of grief. World.title: Drill blitz serves up 10.72g/t WA gold for Great Southern
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Drill blitz serves up 10.72g/t WA gold for Great Southern Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Penny Taylor September 21, 2026 — 11:47am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Great Southern Mining has punched into high-grade gold within fresh rock at Golden Boulder, part of its 100 per cent-owned Duketon gold project near Laverton in Western Australia, extending mineralisation up to 45m down-dip as a major drilling campaign probes the scale beneath its shallow footprint. First assays cover 2436m from 19 holes of a planned 14,000m reverse circulation (RC) program, with the drilling concentrated on the northern 450-metre section of Golden Boulder’s 3.5km Main Line trend, one of three parallel mineralised corridors alongside its Eastern Line and Ogilvies prospects. Another 48 holes, representing 5428m of completed drilling from Main Line and Eastern Line, await assays. Great Southern Mining reverse circulation drilling at the Golden Boulder gold discovery within its Duketon Gold Project near Laverton, Western Australia. The standout 10-metre hit ran 2.62 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 20m, including 2m at 10.72g/t and 1m at 2.20g/t. Another hole returned 8m at 2.24g/t from 102m, including 2m at 7.20g/t, while 7m at 2.45g/t from 41m contained 1m at 6.91g/t. Deeper intervals included 3m at 3.07g/t from 105m, 3m at 3.32g/t from 121m and 4m at 1.85g/t from 145m, including 1m at 6.62g/t. All except one of the 19 holes returned mineralised intercepts above 0.7g/t, with high grades occurring in both the weathered oxide zone near surface and the underlying fresh rock. Reported lengths are downhole, with true widths yet to be confirmed.



‘There is potential for a much larger gold system that could support multiple open-pit operations, all within 20km of operational gold processing facilities.’ Great Southern Mining managing director Matthew Keane Golden Boulder carries a rich goldfield pedigree. More than 50 historical workings pepper the area across a 3.7km strike, with records showing 1915 tonnes of ore were mined at 28.6g/t for 1761 gold ounces between 1900 and 1955. More recently, 2025 drilling struck 5m at 14.6g/t gold from 41m, including 1m at 70.9g/t, adding modern high-grade smoke to the old workings. The latest results appear to provide a glimpse beneath those shallower historical and modern results, extending mineralisation up to 45m down-dip. However, few holes have reached beyond 150m below surface, leaving much of Golden Boulder’s depth potential still untested. Drilling has now moved to the southern reaches of Main Line, where drill lines from the 2025 campaign were widely spaced up to 400m apart. Great Southern Mining managing director Matthew Keane said: “These results support our view that Golden Boulder and the wider Duketon Gold Project have potential for significant scale. The latest results highlight the propensity for high-grades both in the shallow oxide zone and continuing at depth into fresh rock.”



Modelling and interpretation at Golden Boulder are underway to assess continuity between multiple stacked quartz-vein lodes carrying pyrite and arsenopyrite within basalt and minor dolerite. Great Southern will assess the growing RC dataset before planning follow-up drilling, with a resource estimate also possible subject to interpretation of the results. In parallel with the action at Golden Boulder, another batch of assays is waiting in the wings from Amy Clarke, Great Southern’s emerging gold discovery just 3km to the northeast. Results from its first RC program of 18 holes totalling 2248m are expected in coming weeks, with mineralisation already defined across a 4.7km strike. Adding further intrigue is Golden Boulder’s prime geological address. It sits on the same interpreted structure as Regis Resources’ greater-than-2-million-ounce Rosemont deposit 26km away, where mineralisation extends beyond 700m below surface. Great Southern’s wider Laverton ground also sits between Regis’ 12-million-ounce-plus Duketon camp and Genesis Minerals’ 6-million-ounce Laverton tenure, while Keane says operational gold processing facilities lie within 20km. Further afield, diamond drilling has wrapped up at Mt Dillon’s massive gold-copper target within Great Southern’s Edinburgh Park project in northern Queensland. Core logging and processing are now underway. The company has a deal with mining giant Gold Fields, which can earn up to 75 per cent by sole-funding $15M of exploration. The arrangement allows Great Southern to retain exposure to the Queensland project while focusing its own resources on its WA gold portfolio. With drilling ongoing at Golden Boulder and a torrent of assays in the lab from two separate large-scale systems, Great Southern now has plenty of shots on goal as it looks to prove whether Duketon has the makings of an emerging gold camp in one of WA’s most prolific gold districts. World.title: Newcastle’s rise from spoon to prelim is remarkable. But the Panthers are the big winners
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Opinion Newcastle’s rise from spoon to prelim is remarkable. But the Panthers are the big winners Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist September 21, 2026 — 11:45am

September 21, 2026 — 11:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The winners of the Sunday smash-up in Auckland were undoubtedly Penrith, kicking back and watching next week’s opponents belt each other senseless. Even though the Warriors were their own worst enemy in the 12-10 loss to the Knights, succumbing to the pressure of the Eden Park occasion and panicking their way to defeat, Newcastle’s rise from wooden spoon to preliminary final is fabulous. Loading Nobody gets juiced on underdoggery like the Knights. They are the envy of the Tigers, Dragons, Titans and Eels, who remain stuck in the cellar and who, if they’re smart, will study closely everything the Knights have done this year. It’s difficult to manufacture team spirit, happiness and harmony without winning first, but under Justin Holbrook the Knights have produced the egg without needing the chicken.



Newcastle will be rank outsiders on Sunday – but they were rank outsiders in New Zealand, too. Ref justice for Wahs Make it make sense! Not that it was the reason the Warriors lost, but the non-penalty call on Newcastle’s Tyson Frizell in the final minute, when he clearly blocked Warriors kick chasers, shows what a rabbit hole the video officiating system has descended into. Throughout the match, every bunker call turned into a philosophical discussion of how many angels can dance on the head of a pin.



To their credit, the bunker officials avoided making absolute howlers. The absolute howler came when referee Ashley Klein missed Frizell’s infringement, which should have given the Warriors a shot at a penalty goal from right in front and a chance at extra time (in which, the way they were playing, they would surely have lost). Loading The Warriors had lost their challenge on a fingertip call a few minutes earlier. So, do we want to eliminate technology and go back to crucial on-field refereeing mistakes like this? Clearly not. But the tech-assisted challenge system hasn’t stopped it happening either. And nobody understands why the bunker can intrude on the game unprompted and correct many referee rulings or take a player out due to a head knock, but not correct a glaring error like this.



My brain hurts even thinking about it. Rugby league is a simple game played by simple people, refereed by an overcomplicated Rube Goldberg machine. Tyson Frizell and the Knights celebrate a stunning win in Auckland. But it came amid plenty of controversy. Getty Images When NRL supremo Peter V’landys sits down with his rules officials in the summer, item one has to be unpicking this tangle of wires and knobs. The end result is what matters, and the end result on Sunday was a shower of bottles and other projectiles raining from the stands onto the referee – just like before we had video technology.



Even in victory, Robbo’s still not happy On Saturday, the Roosters’ win over Cronulla echoed their win in the corresponding match two years ago over Manly. Nicho Hynes after the head knock that forced him out of Saturday night’s heavy loss to the Roosters. NRL Photos Then, Jake Trbojevic and Tolu Koula were knocked out in the opening minutes, and it was game over. This time, it was an early exit for Cronulla’s Nicho Hynes, whose concussion at least absolves him from the usual blame for another Sharks finals loss.



Two years ago, the Roosters followed their thumping semi-final win with a heavy loss in Melbourne. The Dolphins in Brisbane may not have the same aura as the Storm of 2024, and the Roosters have a fighting chance this Friday. But an NRL week wouldn’t be complete without the squeaky wheel of Trent Robinson needing some oil. Daly Cherry-Evans will get one last visit to Suncorp Stadium before moving to the Super League. Getty Images A handsome 46-10 win didn’t quite fill the hole. This week’s complaint-but-not-a-complaint was about the six-day turnaround before the preliminary final. “It’s a little bit surprising that this has happened. I wouldn’t say it’s happened too often,” Robinson said of his team having two six-day turnarounds during the finals.





The position, selected from members of V’landys’ own board, is meant to be an independent “guardrail” on his authority. In case you’re wondering why they would bother, remember that autarchs never win 100 per cent of the vote. It’s always 98 per cent or 99 per cent, just so you know it’s not some kind of fait accompli handed down from above.

World.title: Diana’s brother is right to be furious with Charles over Harry and William
World.content:
WorldEuropeRoyal family Opinion Diana’s brother is right to be furious with Charles over Harry and William Eleanor Mills Journalist September 21, 2026 — 11:45am

September 21, 2026 — 11:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Next year will mark the 30th anniversary of the death of Princess Diana but still it makes headlines. The latest furore is about her brother Charles Spencer – he of the Westminster Abbey eulogy – who has written a new book called Swan Song: Diana, My Sister. The big reveal is a heated conversation (actually it sounds more like a full-blown row) between Spencer and the then-Prince Charles over whether or not the young princes, William and Harry, should walk behind their mother’s funeral cortege. “What empathy-free monsters ever thought it was appropriate for children of 15 and 12 to have to walk so far, in the glare of the entire global media, when their beloved mother had just died? Reuters The book says that, during the row, Spencer said the idea was “barbaric” while the King said he had walked behind the gun carriage at Lord Mountbatten’s funeral and that it was tradition. Spencer apparently riposted that Charles had been 30 when Mountbatten died (in 1979) and it wasn’t the same. And the King “went nuts”. Touché. I have to say I agree with Spencer. Whatever you think of Princess Diana’s brother (and he’s certainly a colourful piece of work with many alleging he has written this book to raise cash for his latest divorce) he was right about the boys. What empathy-free monsters ever thought it was appropriate for children of 15 and 12 to have to walk so publicly, so far, in the glare of the entire global media, when their beloved mother had just died unexpectedly in a car accident? The death of a parent in early adolescence is traumatic enough anyway, without that deep personal grief having to be performed (and contained) in front of hundreds of millions of people. Prince Harry says in his memoir Spare how traumatic it was. He told Newsweek in 2017: “I don’t think any child should be asked to do that, under any circumstances. I don’t think that would happen today”.



Prince William is much more stiff upper lip, but he has said that he felt completely numb and disorientated and described Diana’s death as “an earthquake which split my mind and life”. Of the walk behind the coffin specifically, he said: “It wasn’t an easy decision” – an oblique reference to the rows that surrounded it, perhaps – “and it was sort of a collective family decision to do that. It was one of the hardest things I have ever done, but there was this element of duty and responsibility that you have to do things you don’t want to do”. Princes William and Harry with their father during Diana’s funeral. AP Ouch. Both boys have also talked of the overwhelming pressure they felt not to cry in public. Spencer was right to call it “barbaric”. We shouldn’t be surprised that those tumultuous events continue to reverberate down the decades; I expect that they will echo down the centuries. The tragedy of Diana’s hounding by the paparazzi, our collective insatiable curiosity about her life and the tawdriness of her death at 36 in a Mercedes driven by a drunk chauffeur in the employ of an alleged sex-criminal (Mohamed Fayed), is a saga for the ages. But even if it hadn’t been so public, losing a parent so young is the kind of blow that defines your life, whether you are prince or pauper. William has spoken about the pain of not having his mother around to see his own children grow up. (How he must have felt when his wife, Catherine, had cancer and his children faced losing their own mother at a young age doesn’t bear thinking about... Poor William.) And it is clear to all of us that Prince Harry is still acting out the trauma of losing his mum so young. It is there in his terror of something awful happening to his own wife or children, expressed in his ongoing rows with the authorities over security and press coverage.



Of course, funerals and the arrangements around them are a notorious flashpoint. Decisions have to be made while emotions are running high. Grief makes people irrational – their normal boundaries have been breached; we are oversensitive and not as tolerant of the foibles or perspectives of others as we might usually be. It is incredibly easy, in such a situation, to say something we later regret. And all families have their undercurrents and unspoken tensions, particularly between siblings and in-laws. Funerals bring out the best, but also the worst in us. I don’t know a single family who hasn’t experienced some kind of row or tension around a funeral – whether it’s over who should speak, how it should go, who should do what, who pays, and whether it’s what the departed would have wanted (too many of us haven’t had that conversation while we could…) Cruse, a bereavement support service, says such rifts and troubles around a death are all too common. Sometimes how we feel about the deceased is uncomplicated: we totally loved them, we totally didn’t. But often we are ambivalent (like Prince Charles, who, according to Spencer, was furious that Diana had eclipsed him). In death, ambivalence hits you in the face like stepping on a rake – wham! When someone dies there is no longer any time to work out your difficulties; those tricky emotions have nowhere to go. We’re sad, we’re angry about things that have happened and we have nowhere to put those feelings. So they get projected on to other family members. This is particularly true in our Western, uptight culture where we don’t have a tradition of howling our collective grief together, or banging our chests in outlandish communal displays of emotion. The funeral arrangements, or arguments over money, become the outlet instead. Given the immensity of what happened with Princess Diana it is not surprising emotions still run hot. My heart goes out to all of them. So much grief, such a huge tragedy, reverberating down the years, down the centuries. They may be royal, but in grief we are all too human.



Eleanor Mills is a former editorial director of The Sunday Times and editor of its magazine. She is now a columist for the UK Telegraph. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: NRL: Eden Park boss urges tougher action on unruly sports fans after Warriors' loss
World.content:
The boss of the country's biggest stadium wants the government to crack down on unruly sports fans and follow Australia's lead when it comes to handing out punishments.

On Sunday night, Eden Park hosted the NRL semifinal between the Warriors and the Newcastle Knights in front of a record home crowd of 48,511.

The Warriors lost 12-10, and referee Ashley Klein and his officials were booed off the park after two contentious late decisions went against the home side.

Bottles, cans and rubbish were thrown from the crowd towards the officials as they left the field after the final whistle.

Eden Park chief executive Nick Sautner said this was an "isolated incident at the end of the game".

He said the stadium was working with the NRL and the Warriors "to ensure that if able to identify those individuals, we'll work with them to see what the appropriate penalty would be to put in place".

Sautner pointed to a similar incident in Australia over the weekend at an AFL preliminary final in Melbourne, and suggested New Zealand should take note of how that was dealt with.

"Just looking across the ditch, the AFL had a similar incident with over 40,000 projectiles thrown onto the MCG, and they do have strict penalties in Australia with up to $5000 fines and five-year bans," Sautner said.

"We have raised the issue with the previous government around pitch invasions and the issue of projectiles, and we'll be doing the same with the current government to see what mitigations are being put in place to ensure that if people do partake in this sort of activity, the appropriate penalties will be implemented."

Sunday's game was the first NRL match the Warriors had hosted at Eden Park since 2014, and Sautner said no incidents were reported to the stadium via the safety reporting number.

An NRL spokesman said in a statement: "All supporters who attend NRL games are subject to the NRL Spectator Code of Conduct.

"The safety of match officials, along with players, officials and fans is paramount. Anyone found breaching the required standards can expect to be subject to significant sanctions, including being banned from venues."

Sautner said the safety of their staff, the players, fans, and also the referees was of "critical importance to us".

"I just want to reiterate, and I think everyone who attended the fixture would say the atmosphere was electric, the on-field performance wasn't what we'd all hoped for, but we don't want that isolated incident to overshadow such a memorable moment at our national stadium."

He could understand some Warriors fans being upset by the actions of others.

"I think emotion plays a huge part in sport, and unfortunately those emotions have probably got the better of some of those fans that attended.

World.title: Incident involving two Air New Zealand pilots reported to Civil Aviation Authority
World.content:
An incident involving two Air New Zealand pilots in the United States has been reported to the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA).

The CAA would not comment further, saying the airline was responsible for employment matters relating to its staff, ''and CAA cannot comment on those matters".

The aviation watchdog says it considers all information brought to its attention, "and determine whether any regulatory action is required".

The statement by CAA stems from a public post in which allegations are made about an altercation between two pilots earlier this month.

Air New Zealand chief safety and Risk Officer McGraw said in a statement "we are aware of a matter between two crew members off duty in the United States which is currently being investigated. There was no incident onboard the aircraft".

Passengers reported flight disruptions as a result, with flight departures from San Francisco to Auckland on September 6 and 7 cancelled.

According to the online post - which was put to Air New Zealand - passengers were told that the pilot scheduled to operate their flight was no longer able to operate the service.

"To get you on your way, we have arranged a replacement pilot, who is on their way to operate your flight to Auckland. Before they can do so, they are required to complete their mandatory minimum rest period.''

World.title: Pacific news in brief for 21 September
World.content:
Pacific

Most Pacific countries were among 34 nations which did not vote on a decision to admit Palestine to the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA).

Leaders from across the region are making their way to New York for assembly week.

The UN said the vote became necessary in the wake of a US decision to deny visas to, and revoke visas from, representatives of Palestine.

Vanuatu voted in support of Palestine's participation in the 81st UNGA, as did 151 other member states, while three were opposed and four abstained.

Vanuatu

Vanuatu is considering linking marine weather warnings to permissions for allowing varioius categories of vessels.

The Vanuatu Daily Post reported that the proposal could see regulations potentially determining which boats can operate under particular weather and sea conditions.

Minister for Climate Change and Meteorological Services Ralph Regenvanu proposed the idea after last week's MV Matui disaster in which dozens of passengers are feared to have died.

Regenvanu said the disaster reinforces the need to turn weather warnings into clearer guidance for sea travel.

He said vessel operators need clearer guidance on whether their vessels can safely operate under particular conditions.

The proposed approach would reduce the need for vessel captains to interpret general weather warnings themselves.

Fiji

A Fjian farmer has given up her cattle as water supply dwindles.

Sunita Devi said sometimes there is no water for the animals, and when they are thirsty, they cry and she also cries because she could not do much to provide water.

The Fiji Sun reports the family relies on a shared water tank, and Devi said she could not prioritise her animals and garden when neighbouring families also needed water.

She said the growth of the animals and the garden will be affected with El Niño and climate change.

Devi said the only solution they found was to quit the gardening and sell and give away the animals.

Federated State of Micronesia

The US deputy secretary of state Christopher Landau says the US intends to give disaster relief to the Federated States of Micronesia (FSM).

On a visit after the Pacific Islands Forum, Landau looked at the recovery efforts following Typhoon Sinlaku's damage in Chuuk State.

He announced the US intends to provide over US$100 million to support disaster relief and reconstruction in FSM, delivering on commitments under the Compact of Free Association.

Landau also visited Solomon Islands and Kiribati, after earlier attending the Pacific Forum leaders summit.

Tonga

Deputy Prime Minister Dr Viliami Latu says no village should be considered too small to get weather warnings.

Islands Business reported Dr Latu spoke at the opening of the Pacific Meteorological Council.

He said the value of weather and climate services should not be measured by how sophisticated the technology is; but whether people receive information they can understand and act upon.

He said no community should be considered too remote to receive an effective warning.

Tonga

A Tongan man has been sentenced to life imprisonment on methamphetamine-related charges.

Teau 'i Mo'unga Faletau was convicted of arranging the transportation of more than five kilograms of meth to New Zealand in 2024.

Matangi Tonga reported that a co-defendant, Mafi Fatongiatau Lutui, was acquitted of a similar count in this case, which involved police informants.

Because the quantity exceeded five kilograms, life imprisonment was the only sentence legally available.

Tonga Police generic Facebook / Tonga Police

Meanwhile, Tongan police arrested three individuals on suspicion of importing drugs on Monday.

The arrests were made after police seized approximately 200 grams of methamphetamine during a raid.

In a statement, police said they have charged a 36 year old female from Halaleva and two males, aged 68 and 45, both from Vaini.

Fiji

Fiji says it has three key priorities for the COP31 climate talks, to be held in Turkey in November.

Permanent Secretary for Environment and Climate Change, Sivendra Michael, said Fiji will host the Pacific pre-COP negotiators' meeting in Nadi on 1 and 2 October.

The Fiji Sun reported the government's priorities are fairer access to climate finance; putting the ocean on the negotiating table; and keeping the 1.5-degrees Celsius warming limit goal within reach.

Michael, who co-chairs the Ocean and Climate Dialogue under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, said the Pacific is pushing to formally place oceans on the COP agenda for the first time.

Australia

Australia's right-wing One Nation Party says it would preserve the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme (PALM) while slashing in-bound temporary migration across the board.

One Nation has been the second-highest polling party in Australia since February.

The party said it wants to reduce the number of temporary visa holders, as well as those in the country unlawfully, by 750,000 over three years.

It would combine this with an annual cap of 130,000 in the country at a time.

Leader Pauline Hanson said both the Labor and Liberal parties have sacrificed Australian living standards to serve vested interests demanding continued mass migration.

However, working visas tied to employer demand, such as the PALM scheme, will be maintained.

World.title: 'A full-body experience': Life amongst plants at Allan Herbarium
World.content:
"People say, what's that? Are you working with dead plants in a plant morgue? And I say, 'Wow, it's a full-body experience working in here.'"

Germany-born Dr Ines Schönberger, the collections manager at the Allan Herbarium in Lincoln, Christchurch, showed Kadambari Raghukumar - host of RNZ's Here Now podcast - around the labyrinth of botanical archives: more than 800,000 plant specimens, with about 3000 to 5000 being added every year.

"A full body experience" - life amongst plants at the Allan Herbarium Here Now Download MP3 19m

A herbarium - if you're anything like Ines - can be a sensory treasure trove, and she says that almost every single specimen tells a story. Some of those stories date way back, with cabinets that store specimens collected by Joseph Banks and Daniel Solander during Captain James Cook's first voyage to New Zealand, circa 1770.

Ines was born in South Germany and dropped roots in the South Island a few decades ago. She met her husband in Germany while working in a collection in a very small herbarium of a botanical society in Regensburg.

"We worked together and we hung out. After three months he had to go back to New Zealand and so he said, 'Oh, you have to come with me.' We were very lucky to arrange a scholarship from the German exchange service for me to come to New Zealand."

The Allan Herbarium was founded in 1928 with HH Allan as the botanist in Palmerston North. It later moved to Lincoln sometime in the late 1950s, and Ines has managed the herbarium since 2007. But it didn't all begin with plants for her.

"I wasn't a plant taxonomist, really, by training. I didn't do a degree in biology for plants. I wanted to become a vet because I loved animals so much.

"But when you study zoology you have to dissect animals, and I didn't like this. Then I had to put my sausage dog down, and I didn't like this either. So I said, 'That's me done for zoology. I will turn to plants.'"

Kadambari Raghukumar/RNZ

It's a relatively quiet afternoon in the herbarium, but Ines said there's normally a big group of volunteers helping with pressing specimens. Part of her role is to work with community volunteers who help organise and preserve specimens that the centre receives from all across the country.

They're currently pressing some specimens of the invasive Madagascar Ragwort

A large number of specimens stored in the herbarium have historically been treated with mercuric chloride to control insect pests.

"We alert everyone coming in here that there might be still traces of mercury on some of the sheets," Ines said. "We are very cautious about it. Every sheet which [has] ever been in contact with mercuric chloride has to be stamped."

Kadambari Raghukumar

Ines pulls out a very large, fluffy, dry, yellowish ball that resembles a spongy brain. This one here is known as a species of vegetable sheep.

"This is a New Zealand native shrubby daisy," she explains.

It's accompanied by a glass plate negative of two men carrying something that looks like a sheep made of vegetables lying on a stretcher.

"So you can just imagine this plant, a big cushion growing in the scree fields up in the southern mountains. This picture was taken in 1906 to be exhibited in the World Exhibition in Christchurch."

Kadambari Raghukumar/RNZ

Climate change elevates the importance of this collection.

"As you see some plants, New Zealand native plants, suddenly found in places where they weren't before. So a collection like this, with these immense samples from throughout the decades, can answer so many questions. Never know what we can do in a collection like this regarding the distribution, climate change, global warming."

Kadambari Raghukumar/RNZ

Germany is known for major historical contributions to biological taxonomy and classification methods that are even in use today, thanks to people like Adolf Engler and Alexander von Humboldt.
